questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Hypokalemia is shown by all. Except?
questions.explanation: Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) is a group of disorders characterized by metabolic acidosis due to renal impairment. RTA Type 4 (Hyperkalemic RTA) is unique because it is characteristically associated with hyperkalemia (high potassium) rather than hypokalemia. This is usually caused by hypoaldosteronism or resistance to aldosterone. RTA Type 1 (distal, Option A) and RTA Type 2 (proximal, Option B) both typically lead to hypokalemia due to increased distal delivery of sodium or defective bicarbonate reabsorption, respectively. Ureterosigmoidostomy (Option D), a surgical procedure where ureters are diverted to the sigmoid colon, also causes a classic hypokalemic hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis because the intestinal mucosa absorbs chloride and secretes potassium and bicarbonate. Clinically, identifying the potassium level is the most useful first step in narrowing the differential diagnosis for a patient with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Management of RTA4 focuses on dietary potassium restriction and potentially fludrocortisone or diuretics to lower serum potassium levels
questions.learning: Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) is a group of disorders characterized by metabolic acidosis due to renal impairment. RTA Type 4 (Hyperkalemic RTA) is unique because it is characteristically associated with hyperkalemia (high potassium) rather than hypokalemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient is diagnosed with recurrent genital infections. In which of the conditions does her male partner need to be treated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichomoniasis

The male partner should be treated with a single dose of oral metronidazole in cases of recurrent Trichomonas infection.

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. It can cause symptoms such as vaginal discharge, itching, and irritation in females, and urethritis or prostatitis in males.

Since trichomoniasis is transmitted through sexual contact, both partners should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection.

The treatment options in case of Trochomoniasis include:

* An oral dose of metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days or single oral dose of metronidazole 2 g

* Vinegar douche to lower the vaginal PH

* Trichofuran suppositories

* Betadine gel

Other Options:

* Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of bacteria in the vagina and is not typically considered a sexually transmitted infection. Treatment of male partners is not routinely recommended.

* Candida albicans is the fungus responsible for most cases of vaginal yeast infections (vulvovaginal candidiasis). It is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, and treatment of male partners is generally not necessary unless they have symptoms of a yeast infection.

* Herpes is a viral infection caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). While it can be sexually transmitted, the treatment of male partners may not be routinely necessary unless they are also infected or experiencing symptoms of genital herpes.
questions.learning: Trichomoniasis — The male partner should be treated with a single dose of oral metronidazole in cases of recurrent Trichomonas infection. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman develops proximal muscle pain and elevated CK 3 weeks after starting simvastatin. She requires continued lipid-lowering therapy due to recent ACS. Which statin is the best alternative?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pravastatin

Pravastatin is the best alternative because it is hydrophilic, has minimal CYP450 metabolism, and the lowest risk of statin-associated myopathy. In patients who develop myositis or CK elevation on simvastatin but still need aggressive lipid lowering after ACS, switching to pravastatin is recommended.

A. Atorvastatin – Lipophilic and CYP3A4-metabolized; still higher myopathy risk.

B. Rosuvastatin – Potent but can still cause myopathy; not first choice after intolerance.

D. Lovastatin – Lipophilic and CYP3A4-dependent; similar risk as simvastatin.
questions.learning: Pravastatin Pravastatin is the best alternative because it is hydrophilic, has minimal CYP450 metabolism, and the lowest risk of statin-associated myopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents with complaints of progressive loss of vision in the right halves of both eyes. Where is the lesion located in the optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic tract

The patient presenting with progressive visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

Here, vision is lost in the right half of both eyes, which means:

• in the left eye, the nasal visual field is lost, and
• in the right eye, the temporal visual field is lost.

It means left temporal and right nasal fibers are destroyed which leads to right homonymous hemianopia. Anatomically, this can be explained by the fact that each optic tract contains fibers from the ipsilateral temporal half of the retina and the contralateral nasal half of the retina.

Optic tract lesions can occur due to pituitary adenomas (most common), craniopharyngioma, tumors of optic thalamus, large aneurysm of superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries, demyelinating diseases, and infarction.

Other options:

Option B - Lesion at right visual cortex causes left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

Option C - Lesion at optic chiasma causes bitemporal hemianopia.

Option D - Lesion at the right optic nerve causes blindness in the right eye.
questions.learning: Left optic tract — The patient presenting with progressive visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 48-year-old female underwent total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The surgical specimen revealed solid ovarian tumour and histology revealed thecoma-fibroma. Which one of the following is the most appropriate statement regarding this condition?
options: It is always associated with gross ascites
It is derived from germ cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial hyperplasia is often associated

Thecoma-fibroma tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary. Thecomas are estrogen-producing tumors, whereas fibromas are usually hormonally inactive. The estrogen secretion by thecoma can stimulate the endometrium, leading to endometrial hyperplasia, Abnormal uterine bleeding and, occasionally, endometrial carcinoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  20% of such tumours are bilateral: Fibromas and thecomas are usually unilateral (>90%). Bilaterality is uncommon.
• C. It is always associated with gross ascites:

• Ascites is not always present.
• Ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion = Meigs syndrome, which occurs only in a minority of patients.

• D. It is derived from germ cells: Thecoma-fibroma tumors arise from the sex cord-stromal cells, not germ cells.
questions.learning: Endometrial hyperplasia is often associated — Thecoma-fibroma tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors of the ovary. Thecomas are estrogen-producing tumors, whereas fibromas are usually hormonally inactive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with the complaints of chest pain. Which among the following is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Troponin-T

Measurement of troponin is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours.

Troponin T/I:

• Highly specific for MI
• Troponin I is more important than troponin T.
• Troponins will remain elevated longer than creatine kinase (CK), for up to 14 days.
• This makes troponins a superior marker for diagnosing MI in the recent past (late diagnosis).
• Reinfarction: It is now clear that cardiac troponin (cTn) increases rapidly, even if it is from an abnormal baseline in patients with reinfarction.
• Sometimes cTn concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. In this case, the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement

Creatine kinase (CK):

• Less sensitive and specific than troponins
• When cTn is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH):

• Normally, LDH2>LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1>LDH2. This is called flipping of the LDH ratio.
• Current recommendations suggest that LDH no longer has a role in the diagnosis of MI.

Myoglobin:

• Earliest enzyme to increase after MI.
• Not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle.

Heart-type fatty acid-binding protein (H-FABP), which mainly exists in cardiomyocytes, has recently emerged as a potential biomarker, which was found to be sensitive for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. H-FABP as an early marker and cTnI as a late marker would be the ideal combination to cover the complete diagnostic window for AMI

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Bleeding as shown in the image is due to which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bridging veins

The image showing a bleed over the arachnoid layer but under the dura is suggestive of a subdural hemorrhage. Most commonly, it results from the shearing of cortical bridging veins.

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. The causes of SDH include

• trauma
• anticoagulants, antiplatelets
• alcohol abuse
• battered baby syndrome.

Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Other options:

Middle meningeal artery rupture would result in an extradural hemorrhage.

Lenticulostriate artery would lead to an intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

Vertebral artery dissection leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage or sometimes intraparenchymal hemorrhage.

questions.learning: Bridging veins — The image showing a bleed over the arachnoid layer but under the dura is suggestive of a subdural hemorrhage. Most commonly, it results from the shearing of cortical bridging veins.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old conceives on the IUCD. She wants to continue pregnancy. The IUCD threads are visible. What would be the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Remove the IUCD gently

If pregnancy occurs with an IUCD and threads are visible, removal is recommended because the device increases risk of:

| Complication | Reason

| ------------ | ------

| Miscarriage | Intrauterine irritation

| Infection | Foreign body

| Preterm labor | Inflammation

If pregnancy continues with an IUCD in situ, the safest approach is gentle removal if strings are visible. Leaving it increases risks of preterm labor, infection, and miscarriage. Removal slightly increases miscarriage risk but is still preferred.

Removal with Shirodkar hook indicated for CuT when threads are not visible.

| Situation | Management

| --------- | ----------

| Threads visible | Remove IUCD

| Threads not visible | Leave IUCD in situ

Attempting blind removal may cause abortion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The CSF findings in bacterial meningitis would include which of the following?
options: Elevated WBC count with normal glucose
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis is characterized by distinct cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities: elevated protein levels (>100 mg/dL) due to blood-brain barrier disruption and decreased glucose (<40% of blood glucose) because of utilization by bacteria and neutrophils. It also features a high white blood cell count, predominantly polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). Options B and D are incorrect because the glucose level is almost always low in bacterial infections. Option C is the opposite of the typical finding. In contrast, viral meningitis (Option D-like) usually has normal glucose and a lymphocyte predominance. Fungal or tubercular meningitis also has low glucose but typically features lymphocyte predominance rather than the high PMNs seen in bacterial causes. Therefore, the combination of high protein and low glucose is the classic biochemical hallmark of bacterial meningitis

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic consuming alcohol for the last 20 years had his last drink 3 days back. He presents with altered sensorium, disorientation, tremors, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are:

* Altered sensorium with disorientation

* Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations

* Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, and hypertension and sweating

* Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy
Altered sleep-wake cycle

Other options:

Option B: Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by:

* Global confusion

* Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex

* Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait

* Vestibular dysfunction

Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam (intravenously) or chlordiazepoxide (orally every 4 hours) are given. It is also recommended to administer thiamine in patients with alcohol-related disorders to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Option C: Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient:

* Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory

* Anterograde amnesia

* Confabulation

Option D: Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. These patients have a clear sensorium, unlike the patients with delirium tremens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the primary factor responsible for the demographic burden?
questions.explanation: The "demographic burden" typically refers to the socio-economic strain placed on the working-age population (usually 15-64 years) to support the non-working segments. In modern demographic transitions, the most significant and growing factor is the increased old age dependency ratio. As life expectancy increases and birth rates decline (demographic aging), there are more elderly individuals requiring healthcare and pensions relative to the fewer workers available to fund these systems. While an increased young age dependency (Option B) also creates a burden, it is often seen as a temporary "investment" in future productivity. Decreased dependency ratios (Options A and C) actually represent a "demographic dividend" or relief rather than a burden. Therefore, the long-term structural burden associated with an aging population is the primary concern described by this demographic term
questions.learning: The "demographic burden" typically refers to the socio-economic strain placed on the working-age population (usually 15-64 years) to support the non-working segments.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 75-year-old woman presents with a vaginal mass as shown in the accompanying image. After pre-anesthetic assessment, she is found to be unfit for major surgical intervention. What is the most appropriate management procedure recommended for this patient?
questions.explanation: For an elderly patient (75 years old) with advanced pelvic organ prolapse who is deemed medically unfit for major reconstructive surgery, an obliterative procedure is the safest and most effective option. Le Fort’s colpocleisis involves denuding a portion of the anterior and posterior vaginal walls and suturing them together to obliterate the vaginal canal. This provides excellent support for the prolapsed organs with minimal surgical time and low anesthesia risk. Options A, B, and D are "sling" procedures or suspensions used in younger, sexually active patients to preserve vaginal function while correcting prolapse or nulliparous prolapse. Because the patient is unsuitable for major surgery and likely not prioritizing sexual activity, Le Fort's repair is the definitive gold standard. This procedure essentially "closes" the vagina to keep the pelvic organs in place. It requires the presence of the uterus and must include lateral channels for the drainage of cervical secretions
questions.learning: For an elderly patient (75 years old) with advanced pelvic organ prolapse who is deemed medically unfit for major reconstructive surgery, an obliterative procedure is the safest and most effective option.

Correct answer: B. Globin part of hemoglobin

2,3-BPG binds to the globin chains of deoxyhemoglobin in the central cavity between the β-chains.

This stabilizes the T (tense) state, reducing hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and facilitating tissue oxygen delivery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A tympanometry tracing shows a shallow peak occurring at a pressure of 0 daPa, as indicated by the arrow. Based on this tympanometric finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The tympanogram features a shallow peak at normal middle ear pressure (0 daPa), which is diagnostic of a Type As pattern. This indicates a state of reduced compliance or stiffening of the tympano-ossicular system. Common clinical causes include otosclerosis (stapes fixation), tympanosclerosis, or a thickened tympanic membrane. Type A (Option A) has a normal peak height reflecting normal middle ear function. Type B (Option B) is a flat tracing indicating middle ear fluid or a perforation. Type Ad (Option D) shows an extremely high peak (hypercompliance), typically associated with ossicular discontinuity or a very thin tympanic membrane. Because the peak is centered at the correct pressure but is pathologically shallow, Type As is the correct classification for this stiffened system
questions.learning: The tympanogram features a shallow peak at normal middle ear pressure (0 daPa), which is diagnostic of a Type As pattern. This indicates a state of reduced compliance or stiffening of the tympano-ossicular system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient came to the clinic, and the following test was performed, as shown in the image below. Which of the following is being tested here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abduction

The test being performed here is the Trendelenburg test, which is done to check the action of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, which are powerful abductors of the hip supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

A positive Trendelenburg test on the right side indicates a right superior gluteal nerve injury, and vice versa.
When the patient stands on his left foot, there is drooping of the right; this is a positive Trendelenburg test on the left side.

Normally, when the leg is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus on the opposite (unsupported) side exert traction on the hip bone. This results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in an upright position.

If the gluteus medius and minimus are paralysed, the pelvis drops on the contralateral side. This is known as a positive Trendelenburg sign. It is positive in the paralysis of the hip abductors and in developmental dysplasia of the hip. A characteristic lurching gait is seen.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the first step in conducting an immunization survey?
options: Completing the cluster and summary forms
Calculating the total fertility rate of the area
questions.explanation: The standard methodology for assessing immunization coverage in a community is the "30-cluster sampling" technique recommended by the WHO. The first and most critical step in this process is cluster identification. This involves dividing the total population of the study area into smaller geographical units (clusters), such as villages or wards, and selecting 30 of them using a systematic random sampling method based on probability proportional to size (PPS). Option B (Conducting the survey) and Option C (Completing forms) are subsequent operational steps that can only occur after the specific clusters and households have been identified. Option D is unrelated to the specific methodology of an immunization coverage survey. Proper cluster identification ensures that the survey sample is statistically representative of the entire population, allowing for an accurate estimation of the percentage of children who have received their scheduled vaccines. This data is vital for identifying gaps in the health system
questions.learning: The standard methodology for assessing immunization coverage in a community is the "30-cluster sampling" technique recommended by the WHO. The first and most critical step in this process is cluster identification.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a major diagnostic criterion of neuromyelitis optica?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Focal epilepsy

Focal epilepsy is not considered a major diagnostic criterion of neuromyelitis optica (NMO).

Neuromyelitis optica (Devic’s disease) is an aggressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis.

It is associated with a highly specific autoantibody directed against aquaporin-4(AQP-4). AQP-4 is localized to the foot processes of astrocytes in close proximity to endothelial surfaces.

The core clinical characteristics include optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome (unexplained hiccups/ nausea/ vomiting), acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy or acute diencephalic clinical syndrome with Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)-typical diencephalic MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMSOD-typical brain lesions.

Attacks of optic neuritis are bilateral and severe in NMO, whereas in multiple sclerosis (MS) optic neuritis is usually unilateral. Progressive symptoms are not typical of NMO, unlike in MS. CSF findings in NMO show higher pleocytosis, with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, and rare occurrence of oligoclonal bands, distinguishing it from MS.

Acute attacks of NMO are treated with high-dose glucocorticoids. Plasma exchange can be used in acute attacks that do not respond to glucocorticoids.

Drugs used for prophylaxis against relapses include mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, glucocorticoids, and azathioprine. Three monoclonal antibodies approved for attack prevention include eculizumab (terminal complement inhibitor), inebilizumab (B-cell depleter), and satralizumab (IL-6 receptor blocker).

NMO typically presents as a recurrent disease, with a monophasic course observed in less than 10% of patients. Untreated NMO can lead to disability, including respiratory failure, blindness, and limb paralysis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Among the listed laryngeal cartilages, which is least prone to calcification?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages are composed of either hyaline or elastic cartilage, and this histological difference determines their tendency to calcify with age. The thyroid (Option A), cricoid (Option B), and the majority of the arytenoid (Option C) cartilages consist of hyaline cartilage. Hyaline cartilage characteristically undergoes calcification and even ossification as a normal part of the aging process, which can be visible on radiographic imaging. In contrast, the epiglottis, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages are composed of elastic cartilage. Elastic cartilage contains a high density of elastic fibers and does not typically undergo calcification regardless of age. This flexibility is essential for the epiglottis to function as a lid during swallowing. Clinically, understanding this pattern is important because a calcified thyroid cartilage on an X-ray can be mistaken for a foreign body by an inexperienced clinician, whereas the epiglottis remains radiolucent throughout life due to its elastic nature
questions.learning: The laryngeal cartilages are composed of either hyaline or elastic cartilage, and this histological difference determines their tendency to calcify with age.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient falls onto an outstretched hand, and an X-ray shows a fracture of the first metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint with associated subluxation. How is this type of fracture classified?
questions.explanation: The X-ray and clinical description define a Bennett's fracture, which is an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. It typically occurs due to axial loading on a partially flexed thumb, such as from a fall on an outstretched hand. The fracture involves a small fragment of the metacarpal base remaining attached to the volar oblique ligament, while the main metacarpal shaft is subluxed proximally and dorsally by the pull of the abductor pollicis longus (APL) muscle. Scaphoid fractures (Option B) involve the carpal bones and are noted for pain in the anatomical snuffbox. Colle's fracture (Option D) is a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement ("dinner fork" deformity), while Reverse Colle's (Smith's fracture, Option C) involves volar displacement of the distal radius. Because this fracture specifically involves the base of the thumb's metacarpal with subluxation, it is identified as a Bennett's fracture
questions.learning: The X-ray and clinical description define a Bennett's fracture, which is an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. It typically occurs due to axial loading on a partially flexed thumb, such as from a fall on an outstretched hand.

questions.text: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents to the outpatient department with complaints of painful urination and a thick yellow urethral discharge for the past 3 days. He denies any fever, chills, or flank pain. He reports multiple unprotected sexual encounters in the past month. A urethral swab is sent for Gram stain, which shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes. The organism is resistant to penicillins. questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents to the psychiatric outpatient department with inattention at school, hyperactivity (excessive talking and difficulty remaining seated), aggressive behavior toward peers, and poor academic performance. Which drug is indicated for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: The child's symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity (hitting friends, excess talking), and impulsivity (cannot sit still) causing functional impairment in school are classic for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD in children aged 6 years and older is Methylphenidate, a CNS stimulant. It works by increasing the levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex, helping to improve focus and impulse control. Modafinil (Option B) is used for narcolepsy. Atenolol (Option C) is a beta-blocker. Amitriptyline (Option D) is a tricyclic antidepressant; while sometimes used off-label for ADHD, it is never the first-line choice. Management of ADHD also requires behavioral interventions and parent training. Long-term use of stimulants requires monitoring for side effects like suppressed appetite and growth. Methylphenidate remains the gold-standard treatment for pediatric ADHD

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During total mesorectal excision for mid-rectal cancer, the surgeon carefully dissects in the correct avascular planes around the rectum. Which statement regarding the fascial planes is most accurate?
options: Fascia of Denonvilliers lies posterior to the rectum and separates it from the sacrum.
Fascia of Waldeyer lies anterior to the rectum and separates it from the prostate or vagina.
Fascia of Denonvilliers is an important anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs.
Both fasciae are routinely excised along with mesorectum in TME.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fascia of Denonvilliers is an important anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs.

During total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer, precise dissection along embryologic fascial planes ensures oncologic clearance while preserving autonomic nerves.

• Fascia of Denonvilliers lies anterior to the rectum, separating it from the prostate/seminal vesicles in males and vagina in females.

• It forms a key anterior surgical plane in TME and must be carefully identified to avoid injury to genitourinary structures and autonomic nerves.

Key fascial relationships in TME

• Mesorectal fascia (holy plane): Avascular plane surrounding mesorectum used for TME dissection

• Denonvilliers fascia: Anterior plane between rectum and genitourinary organs

• Waldeyer’s fascia: Posterior rectosacral fascia connecting rectum to sacrum

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by a defect in which of the following platelet glycoproteins?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in the GpIb/IX complex on the platelet surface. This complex serves as the primary receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF), mediating the essential step of platelet adhesion to the subendothelial matrix following vascular injury. When this step is impaired, patients develop a defective primary platelet plug. Characteristic findings include a prolonged bleeding time and "giant platelets" on a peripheral smear. Option A (GpIIb/IIIa) is defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which affects platelet aggregation. Option C (GpIa/IIa) binds collagen, and its defects are rare and mild. Option D (GpIV or CD36) is involved in scavenger functions. BSS is specifically distinguished by the failure of platelets to aggregate in response to ristocetin, a defect that is not corrected by adding normal plasma
questions.learning: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in the GpIb/IX complex on the platelet surface.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is transmitted by all the components of blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malaria

Among the options provided, Malaria is the only disease transmitted by all components of blood.

Malaria is primarily spread through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes, which inject sporozoites into the bloodstream but can also be transmitted by transfusion of blood and blood products.

other options:

Option A : Syphilis is primarily transmitted through direct contact with syphilitic sores (chancres), which can occur on the genitals, lips, mouth, or anus during sexual activity.In most cases, transmission via blood transfusion is rare.

Option C:  Filarial parasites are primarily transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. However, they can also be found in the blood of infected individuals, which can potentially transmit the infection through blood transfusion. However, plasma and platelets may not typically harbor filarial parasites unless there's concurrent infection or contamination.

Option D: Toxoplasma is transmitted through various routes, including ingestion of contaminated food or water, contact with infected cat feces, and transplacental transmission from mother to fetus. However, it is not primarily transmitted through blood

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady of 49 kg is in her first trimester. What are her additional calorie requirements in this trimester?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue same diet

The pregnant lady can continue the same diet since there are no additional calorie requirements in the first trimester.

Pregnancy requires an additional 80,000 kcal, mostly during the last 20 weeks. To meet this demand, a caloric increase of 100 to 300 kcal/d is recommended during pregnancy. This greater intake, however, should not be divided equally during the course of pregnancy. The Institute of Medicine (2006) recommends adding 0, 340, and 452 kcal/d to the estimated nonpregnant energy requirements in the first, second, and third trimesters respectively.

Whenever caloric intake is inadequate, protein is metabolized rather than being spared for its vital role in fetal growth and development.
questions.learning: Continue same diet — The pregnant lady can continue the same diet since there are no additional calorie requirements in the first trimester. Pregnancy requires an additional 80,000 kcal, mostly during the last 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Premature aging in Werner syndrome is due to:
options: Increase in length of telomere due to decrease in telomerase activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defect in DNA helicase

Premature aging in Werner syndrome is due to a defect in DNA helicase.

DNA helicase is involved in DNA replication and repair and other functions requiring DNA unwinding. A defect in this enzyme causes rapid accumulation of damaged chromosomes that may mimic the injury that normally accumulates during cellular aging.
questions.learning: Defect in DNA helicase Premature aging in Werner syndrome is due to a defect in DNA helicase. DNA helicase is involved in DNA replication and repair and other functions requiring DNA unwinding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely causative organism of ventilator-associated pneumonia among the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acinetobacter

Among the given options, Acinetobacter species is the most commonly isolated organism in cases of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). VAP develops in a mechanically ventilated patient >48 hours after endotracheal intubation.

The organisms causing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) significantly vary from one hospital to another. However, the organisms that frequently cause VAP in hospital settings are Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter sp., Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and gram-negative rods (Enterobacter species, K. pneumoniae, and Escherichia coli).

Three factors distinguish nosocomial pneumonia from community-acquired pneumonia:

1. Different infectious agent
2. Different antibiotic susceptibility patterns, specifically, a higher incidence of drug resistance
3. Poorer underlying health status of patients putting them at risk for more severe infections

Within 48 hours of admission, 75% of seriously ill hospitalized patients have their upper airway colonized with organisms from the hospital environment. Impaired cellular and mechanical defense mechanisms in the lungs of hospitalized patients raise the risk of infection after aspiration has occurred.

VAP patients may be infected with Acinetobacter species and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Anaerobic organisms (Bacteroides, anaerobic streptococci, Fusobacterium) may also cause pneumonia in the hospitalized patient.
questions.learning: Acinetobacter Among the given options, Acinetobacter species is the most commonly isolated organism in cases of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following with regard to Amino Acids: I. Essential amino acids are those that the body cannot synthesize and they must be obtained from dietary proteins. II. Not just the essential amino acids, non-essential amino acids are also needed by the body for synthesis of tissue proteins. III. Unless a protein contains all the essential amino acids in amounts corresponding to human needs, a protein is said to be biologically incomplete. IV. Animal proteins are rated superior to vegetable proteins. Of the above statements, how many are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All four

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are classified into essential and non-essential amino acids based on the body’s ability to synthesize them. The biological value (BV) of a protein depends on its content of essential amino acids and their proportion relative to human requirements.

• Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
• Non-essential amino acids can be synthesized by the body but are also required for protein synthesis and normal growth.
• A protein lacking one or more essential amino acids in adequate amounts is called a biologically incomplete protein.
• Animal proteins (milk, egg, meat, fish) are complete proteins with high biological value, whereas most vegetable proteins are incomplete.
questions.learning: All four Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are classified into essential and non-essential amino acids based on the body’s ability to synthesize them.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young male patient was given regional block with 0.25% bupivacaine for a minor surgical procedure. Shortly after the injection, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and the pulse was not recordable. Which of the following would be the best course of management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CPR with 20% intralipid

The clinical picture of an unresponsive patient with an absent pulse following bupivacaine administration is most likely due to bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity resulting from accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic. The best course of management in this scenario would be administering CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), along with a 20% intralipid injection.

Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic that is the most cardiotoxic among the local anesthetics. It depresses the rapid phase of depolarization in Purkinje fibers and ventricular muscle due to a decreased availability of fast sodium channels in cardiac membranes. This reduced rate of depolarization depresses myocardial contractility. Hence, bupivacaine is a potent cardio depressant.

Cardio-vascular effects of bupivacaine-induced toxicity are as follows:

* Left ventricular depression

* Atrioventricular heart block

* Ventricular arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation

* Sinus bradycardia can lead to cardiac arrest

Initial management includes immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation as per the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) algorithm.

Following CPR, intralipid therapy is initiated. Its mechanism is explained by the lipid sink theory which states lipophilic drugs (bupivacaine) are absorbed into the lipid emulsion of the plasma, hence, removed from tissues affected by toxicity. Intralipid therapy is administered as :

* 20% IV dose as a rapid bolus (1.5 mL/kg)

* Infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min for 10 min after the patient is hemodynamically stable

Local anesthesia systemic toxicity (LAST) can also affect the central nervous system (CNS), which is more susceptible to local anesthetic action as compared to the cardiovascular system. Dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation are the initial symptoms. Shivering, muscular twitching, and tremors follow. Tonic-clonic seizures occur. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest.

Pearl PF2259: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

The adult cardiac arrest algorithm is based on the AHA guidelines as shown below.

Pearl PF1780: High quality CPR for adults

* Push hard: 5-6cm depth

* Push fast: 100-120/min frequency

* Allow for complete chest recoil

* Minimize interruptions in compressions <10 seconds

* Avoid excessive ventilation

* Rotate compressor every 2 min or earlier if fatigued

* If no advanced airway, 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio

Attempt to improve CPR quality if :

* Quantitative waveform capnography - PETCO2 <10mmHg,

* Intra-arterial pressure - If relaxation phase (diastolic) pressure <20mmHg
questions.learning: CPR with 20% intralipid — The clinical picture of an unresponsive patient with an absent pulse following bupivacaine administration is most likely due to bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity resulting from accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with left knee swelling following a trivial injury. His platelet count and bleeding time are normal. His aPTT is prolonged and factor VIII levels are decreased. Which of the following can be used in the management of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Emicizumab

A child with hemarthrosis, normal platelet count/bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, and low factor VIII has Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency). Emicizumab is a newer therapy used in hemophilia A:

• Bispecific monoclonal antibody
• Bridges factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIII function
• Used for prophylaxis in patients with or without inhibitors
• Reduces frequency of bleeding episodes

Why not others:

B. Voxelotor → sickle cell disease

C. Eculizumab & D. Ravulizumab → complement inhibitors for PNH/aHUS
questions.learning: Emicizumab — A child with hemarthrosis, normal platelet count/bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, and low factor VIII has Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection?

1. Neonates who are asymptomatic at birth have a lesser risk of later sequelae.

2. 20-40% are symptomatic at birth.

3. In developing countries, the rate of transmission of CMV infection to the infant is more common from primary maternal infection than reactivation.

4. Diagnosis by urine specimen at 4 weeks of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3

The true statements regarding CMV infection are statements 1 and 3.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester.

Only 10% (statement 2) of the infected babies are symptomatic. Asymptomatic neonates have lesser chances of having late sequelae (statement 1).

Congenital CMV infection can result from either primary or reactivation infection of the mother. The rate of transmission of infection to the fetus in a mother who has a primary infection is about 30% (statement 3) while in a mother with a non-primary infection, it is 1-2%. However, the total number of infants who have acquired an infection from a mother with a non-primary infection is 3-4 times more than infants who have acquired an infection from mothers with a primary infection.

The clinical manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss.

The investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first three weeks of life (statement 4). After this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection. Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine and/or saliva are more reliable samples than blood.

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness.

questions.learning: 1, 3 The true statements regarding CMV infection are statements 1 and 3. Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 43-year-old woman presented with serous discharge from a single duct of the nipple of her right breast which was sent for evaluation. She is unlikely to be suffering from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fibrocystic disease

Pathological nipple discharge is typically spontaneous, unilateral, and from a single duct. A serous discharge from a single duct is most commonly caused by intraductal papilloma, but it can also occur in duct ectasia and carcinoma. It is uncommon in fibrocystic disease.

Why is A correct?

• A. Fibrocystic disease ✅: Correct (unlikely).

• Usually presents with cyclical breast pain, nodularity, and multiple cysts.
• Nipple discharge, if present, is usually non-spontaneous and from multiple ducts, making single-duct serous discharge uncommon.

About other options:

• B. Intraductal papilloma ❌

• Most common cause of spontaneous unilateral single-duct nipple discharge.
• Discharge is typically serous or blood-stained.

• C. Duct ectasia ❌

• Can present with unilateral nipple discharge, which is often green, brown, or serous, along with nipple retraction and periareolar tenderness.

• D. Carcinoma ❌

• May present with spontaneous unilateral single-duct serous or blood-stained discharge, especially if associated with a breast lump.
questions.learning: Fibrocystic disease Pathological nipple discharge is typically spontaneous, unilateral, and from a single duct. A serous discharge from a single duct is most commonly caused by intraductal papilloma, but it can also occur in duct ectasia and carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 19-year-old otherwise healthy female experiences episodic numbness and tingling of the fingers, precipitated by stress or exposure to cold, with characteristic features shown in the accompanying image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon (Raynaud's disease) is characterized by episodic digital vasospasm, classically triggered by cold temperatures or emotional stress. It typically occurs in young females (late teens to early 20s) who have no underlying connective tissue or systemic disease. The condition involves a symmetric triphasic color change: white (pallor due to ischemia), blue (cyanosis due to deoxygenation), and red (rubor due to reactive hyperemia). The provided image supports this diagnosis by showing the sharp demarcation of pallor in the digits. Secondary Raynaud's phenomenon (Option B) is associated with an underlying autoimmune disorder, such as systemic sclerosis, and usually presents later in life or with systemic symptoms. Cold sores (Option C) are caused by the herpes simplex virus and present with painful vesicles. Scleredema (Option D) involves a distinct thickening of the skin. Therefore, given the demographic and the absence of pre-existing conditions, primary Raynaud's is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon (Raynaud's disease) is characterized by episodic digital vasospasm, classically triggered by cold temperatures or emotional stress.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of feed forward control mechanism?
options: Exercise resulting in heart rate increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exercise resulting in heart rate increase

Exercise resulting in heart rate increase is not an example of feedforward control mechanism. However, thinking about exercise and it resulting in a heart rate increase would be an example of feedforward control mechanism.

Feedforward control is that which makes an anticipatory or adaptive response without a specific stimulus.

Temperature control - Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by the hypothalamus before the changes in environmental temperature changes the core body temperature. Thus, shivering in response to cold environment would be an example of feedforward control.

In the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, the thought of food itself and not food per se produces a gastric secretion.

The cerebellum has a feed-forward inhibition that limits the duration of the excitation produced by any given afferent volley.
questions.learning: Exercise resulting in heart rate increase Exercise resulting in heart rate increase is not an example of feedforward control mechanism. However, thinking about exercise and it resulting in a heart rate increase would be an example of feedforward control…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, which line would PCO2 follow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the alveolar PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, PCO2 would follow line 1.

This concept can be understood in three steps.

Step 1- Effect of CO2 on ventilation, when the alveolar PO2 is kept constant.

When the alveolar PO2 (PaO2) is kept constant, an increased amount of inspired CO2  leads to increase in the ventilation. The relation is a straight line.

The below graph shows the effect of CO2 on ventilation when alveolar PaO2 is kept constant at 100mm Hg.

Step 2. The shift of the above graph when PO2 changes.

When PO2 changes, the relation between the amount of CO2 inhaled and ventilation still remains in a straight line. However, the slopes of the lines change. The slope increases when alveolar PO2 decreases and vice versa. In other words, the lines move towards the left when PO2 decreases. However, the point of intersection of all these lines remains the same.

The below graph shows the relation between inspired CO2 and ventilation when alveolar PO2 is maintained at 40mm Hg, 55mm Hg, and 100 mm Hg. As the alveolar PO2 has decreased, the lines have shifted to the left. But they are all intersecting at the same point on the x-axis.

Step 3. The shift of the above graph when pH changes.

When pH decreases, as in acidosis, the CO2 response curve is similar to the above. The only difference is they are shifted to the left and have different points on the intersection on x- axis.

The below graphs show CO2 response curves when pH is 7.4, 7.3, and PO2 is 40mm Hg, 55mm Hg, and 100mm Hg. The lines have shifted to the left and have a different point of intersection.

In the question image, only line 1 has been shifted to the left and has a different point of intersection on x-axis compared to other lines. Therefore, line 1 is the answer.
questions.learning: 1 If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the alveolar PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, PCO2 would follow line 1. This concept can be understood in three steps.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient reports calf pain that develops after walking a fixed distance, forcing him to stop and rest before he can continue. According to Boyd’s classification of intermittent claudication, this presentation corresponds to which grade?
questions.explanation: The patient describes calf pain occurring after walking a fixed (short) distance and relieved by rest, which is characteristic of intermittent claudication. The key factor in Boyd’s classification is the distance walked before onset of pain. Boyd’s grading: 1. Grade 1: Pain after long distance (>500 m) 2. Grade 2: Pain after moderate distance (200–500 m) 3. Grade 3: Pain after short distance (<200 m) 4. Grade 4: Pain at rest (critical ischemia) In the question, although the exact distance is not mentioned, the phrase “pain after a fixed distance forcing him to stop” typically implies early onset on walking, i.e., short-distance claudication, which corresponds to Grade 3
questions.learning: The patient describes calf pain occurring after walking a fixed (short) distance and relieved by rest, which is characteristic of intermittent claudication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with vault prolapse associated with both cystocele and rectocele. Considering this combination of pelvic organ prolapse, what would be the most appropriate and effective management strategy?
questions.explanation: Pelvic organ prolapse often involves multiple compartments simultaneously. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) represents a defect in the anterior vaginal wall, while a rectocele (rectum prolapse) represents a defect in the posterior wall. To comprehensively repair the pelvic floor in a patient with both these conditions along with vault prolapse, the most optimal surgical approach is to perform both anterior colporrhaphy and posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (Option C). Anterior colporrhaphy (Option A) specifically reinforces the anterior wall to correct the cystocele. Posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (Option B) reinforces the posterior wall and the perineal body to correct the rectocele. A hysterectomy (Option D) addresses uterine prolapse but will not fix the underlying fascial defects of the bladder or rectum on its own. Therefore, a combined multi-compartment repair is necessary to achieve a successful functional and anatomical outcome for the patient
questions.learning: Pelvic organ prolapse often involves multiple compartments simultaneously. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) represents a defect in the anterior vaginal wall, while a rectocele (rectum prolapse) represents a defect in the posterior wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle movements are related to the Abducens nerve?
questions.explanation: The Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI) is purely a motor nerve that innervates a single extraocular muscle: the lateral rectus. The primary function of the lateral rectus muscle is to abduct the eye, moving it laterally away from the midline. The medial rectus (Option B), superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique (Option D) are all innervated by the Oculomotor nerve (CN III). The superior oblique muscle (Option C) is innervated by the Trochlear nerve (CN IV). A classic mnemonic for eye muscle innervation is , where 6 refers to the abducens and 4 to the trochlear. Clinical paralysis of the abducens nerve results in the inability to abduct the affected eye, leading to convergent strabismus (esotropia) and horizontal diplopia (double vision) that worsens when looking toward the side of the affected muscle. This nerve has a long intracranial course, making it susceptible to damage from increased intracranial pressure
questions.learning: The Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI) is purely a motor nerve that innervates a single extraocular muscle: the lateral rectus. The primary function of the lateral rectus muscle is to abduct the eye, moving it laterally away from the midline.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A surgeon returns home from a party after many pegs of alcohol and was called to perform an emergency operation. During the operation, the assisting staff noticed the surgeon's hand shaking and instruments falling. He eventually nicks an artery and the patient collapses. Under which of the following terms will this incident be tried?
options: Civil negligence not amounting to criminal negligence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Criminal negligence

The incident mentioned in the given scenario will be tried under criminal negligence.

Criminal negligence is when a doctor lacks a gross skill or care while treating, which results in serious injury/death of the patient, or when an illegal act is performed by a doctor or when an assaulted person dies. Most cases of criminal negligence occur due to drunkenness or usage of drugs, which leads to impaired efficiency.

Some of the examples are amputation of the wrong finger; leaving an instrument, tube, or sponge in the abdomen; incompetent administration of general anesthetic; and administrating the wrong substance in the eye, leading to visual loss.

The doctor is prosecuted by the police and charged in criminal court, when it is proved that no medical doctor in his ordinary senses would have done it. Contributory negligence cannot be used as a defense in criminal negligence.

Other options:

Option B: Civil negligence occurs as a result of lacking care and skill in the profession. Contributory negligence can be cited as a defense in civil negligence.

Option C: Therapeutic misadventure is a case that causes injury or death to the individual due to an unintentional act by a doctor or hospital. The physician is not liable for the injuries unless some negligence on his part contributed to the occurrence of the injury.

Option D: Dichotomy is a type of unethical act, wherein a physician offers or receives any gift or bonus for referring or procuring any patient for medical or surgical treatment.
questions.learning: Criminal negligence — The incident mentioned in the given scenario will be tried under criminal negligence. Criminal negligence is when a doctor lacks a gross skill or care while treating, which results in serious injury/death of the patient, or when an…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents with frequent headaches. Investigation reveals raised intracranial pressure and the presence of a dural-based tumor. Which of the following histological findings correlate with the diagnosis?
options: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells

The clinical vignette of a dural-based tumor presenting with headaches and raised intracranial pressure is most likely a meningioma and they have psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells on histopathological examination.

Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid.

* Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

* Prior radiation therapy to the head and neck, typically is a risk factor.

* The most common cytogenetic abnormality is the loss of chromosome 22, especially the long arm (22q).

* Meningiomas are a common lesion in the setting of NF2 (multiple sites, especially in association with acoustic neuromas or glial tumors.

* The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated.

* They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura. This form is commonly associated with hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone.

* The lesions may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies.

Psammoma bodies are shown below:

Histological subtypes:

* WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic

* WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical

* Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic

* Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth

* Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma

* Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen

* Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

* Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered.

* Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy.

Option A: Fried egg appearance of cells refers to cells with clear cytoplasm and a nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. Fried egg appearance in pathology are:

* Oligodendroglioma on histopathology

* Hairy cell leukemia on bone marrow biopsy

* Seminoma/Dysgerminoma on light microscopy

* Mycoplasma pneumonia fried egg colonies on Eaton agar

Option B: Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes with arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen can be seen in retinoblastoma.

Option D: In medulloblastoma, tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neurophil can be seen.

Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors

Pilocytic Astrocytomas:

* Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas

* Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.

* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions

* Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions

Medulloblastoma:

* Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells

* Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped

* Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil

Ependymoma:

* Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen

* Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel

Oligodendroglioma:

* Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.

* Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries

Retinoblastoma:

* Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei

* Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen

* Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center

* Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.
questions.learning: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells — The clinical vignette of a dural-based tumor presenting with headaches and raised intracranial pressure is most likely a meningioma and they have psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells on…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, and dizziness upon standing. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. Her mother was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism. On examination, her blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg supine and 80/50 mm Hg standing. Laboratory results reveal the following: Sodium 129 meq/l Potassium 5.9 meq/l Chloride 100 meq/l Bicarbonate 21 meq/l Creatinine 1.4 mg/dl BUN 38mg/dl Which of the following in circulating hormone levels are expected in this patient?
options: Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high
Cortisol normal, Aldosterone low, ADH normal, Norepinephrine normal
Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH normal, Norepinephrine normal
Cortisol high, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cortisol low, Aldosterone low, ADH high, Norepinephrine high

This patient has features of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease).

• Fatigue, weight loss, salt craving
• Orthostatic hypotension
• Hyponatremia (Na⁺ 129 mEq/L)
• Hyperkalemia (K⁺ 5.9 mEq/L)
• Family history of autoimmune disease → suggests autoimmune adrenal destruction

Hormonal pattern in primary adrenal insufficiency:

• ↓ Cortisol → adrenal cortex failure
• ↓ Aldosterone → Na⁺ loss, K⁺ retention, hypotension
• ↑ ADH → due to hypovolemia and cortisol deficiency
• ↑ Norepinephrine → compensatory sympathetic activation to maintain blood pressure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He has a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg. On clinical examination, hyper-resonance is noted on the left side of the chest, and the chest X-ray (shown) reveals corresponding findings. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 2nd ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS
questions.explanation: The patient presents with trauma, hypotension (shock), respiratory distress, and hyper-resonance, which is the classic triad for a Tension Pneumothorax. This is a clinical emergency where air is trapped in the pleural space, shifting the mediastinum and compressing the heart. According to updated ATLS guidelines, the immediate decompression site for an adult is "wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space" (ICS) at the mid-axillary line, immediately "followed by an intercostal drain" (chest tube) at the same level. The 2nd ICS (Option A) was the older recommended site but is now preferred only for children. Aspiration of fluid (Option C) is for pleural effusion, not air. Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition that must be diagnosed and treated clinically before waiting for an X-ray if the patient is unstable
questions.learning: The patient presents with trauma, hypotension (shock), respiratory distress, and hyper-resonance, which is the classic triad for a Tension Pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient complains of neck stiffness and severe headache. The CT image shown below is suggestive of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache with CT revealing blood in the basal cistern points out to the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region (65%), or in the Sylvian fissure (30%).

The modified Fisher scale is a method for grading SAH as seen on non-contrast CT (NCCT). The Hunt and Hess scale describes the severity of SAH and is used as a predictor of survival.

Xanthochromia on CSF is indicative of SAH in case of a negative CT scan.
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage — The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache with CT revealing blood in the basal cistern points out to the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the given image of the placenta previa.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marginal

The picture shown is of the Marginal placenta previa.

Placenta previa is used to describe a placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment. Painless bleeding towards the end of the second trimester or later is characteristic of the condition. It usually occurs without warning and resolves spontaneously only to recur.

There are four types of placenta previa according to the degree of placental expansion to the lower uterine segment.

* Type-I: Low-lying- The lower margin of the placenta reaches the lower uterine segment but not the os. (Option B)

* Type-II: Marginal- The placenta does not cover the internal os but reaches its margin.

* Type-III: Incomplete or partial central- The placenta covers the closed internal os but does not do so when fully dilated. (Option C)

* Type-IV: Complete or central- The placenta covers the internal os even when fully dilated. (Option D)
questions.learning: Marginal — The picture shown is of the Marginal placenta previa. Placenta previa is used to describe a placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with ataxia, ichthyosis, retinitis pigmentosa, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated phytanic acid levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Refsum disease

Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder caused by deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, resulting in defective α-oxidation of phytanic acid. The accumulation of phytanic acid causes the characteristic combination of retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, ichthyosis, hearing loss, and cardiac conduction defects.

Why not the other options?

• A. Zellweger disease: Peroxisome biogenesis disorder presenting in infancy with severe hypotonia, seizures, craniofacial abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and developmental delay.
• C. Adrenoleukodystrophy: X-linked disorder due to impaired peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), causing adrenal insufficiency and progressive demyelination.
• D. Metachromatic leukodystrophy: Caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, leading to sulfatide accumulation with progressive peripheral neuropathy and central demyelination.
questions.learning: Refsum disease Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder caused by deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, resulting in defective α-oxidation of phytanic acid.

questions.text: What is the denominator in infant mortality rate?
questions.explanation:

Infant mortality rate is the ratio of deaths under 1 year of age in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year usually expressed as a rate per 1000 live births.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A married woman dies under unnatural or suspicious circumstances within three years of her marriage. Following this, her father lodges a complaint with the police. Under which legal provision will the inquiry into her death be conducted?
questions.explanation: Under Indian law, specifically Section 176 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrP(C) and the updated Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magistrate-led inquiry is mandatory for the unnatural death of a married woman within seven years of her marriage. This legal provision ensures a thorough and impartial investigation by an Executive or Judicial Magistrate into potential dowry-related violence or foul play. Section 174 CrPC (or 194 BNSS) (Option A) refers to a standard Police Inquest, which is conducted for routine unnatural deaths but is insufficient for this specific high-priority category. Sections 106 and 116 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) (Options C and D) deal with substantive offenses like causing death by negligence or abetment, rather than the procedural rules for conducting an inquest. Therefore, the procedural inquiry must be initiated under the Magisterial mandate of Section 196 BNSS

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is the anaesthesia of choice in a day care dental surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infiltration anesthesia

Infiltration anesthesia is ideal to perform in day care dental procedures as a fast-track procedure.

It has a lesser incidence of complications than regional or general anesthesia. Other anesthetic techniques for hernia repair include intercostal block and ilioinguinal nerve block.

Ambulatory/Outpatient anesthesia employs the use of fast - Track surgical techniques to provide adequate surgical anesthesia and minimize post-operative complications in order to reduce the duration of hospital stay.

Disadvantage of infiltration anesthesia - Short duration of anesthesia even when long-acting local anesthetics like bupivacaine are used. Extended- duration local anesthesia can be produced by encapsulating bupivacaine into a biodegradable carrier.

Regional anesthesia is contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders, those on anticoagulants and with local infections.

Spinal anesthesia has the disadvantage over epidural anesthesia of delayed recovery due to profound motor blockade. Spinal opioids like fentanyl or sufentanil are added to prolong postoperative analgesia and minimize motor block without delaying recovery. But the adverse effects of spinal opioids like nausea, pruritus and postoperative urinary retention are additive.
questions.learning: Infiltration anesthesia Infiltration anesthesia is ideal to perform in day care dental procedures as a fast-track procedure. It has a lesser incidence of complications than regional or general anesthesia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with IHD presents with sudden, severe, generalized abdominal pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, the pulse rate is 118bpm, rhythm is irregularly irregular, BP is 90/60 mmHg. The abdomen appears soft, non-distended, and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following could be a likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute mesenteric ischemia

The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia.

Mesenteric ischemia may be acute or chronic. The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is most likely affected. An embolus is the most common cause of SMA occlusion. Possible sources for SMA emboisation include:

• Left atrium in atrial fibrillation
• Previous history of ischemic heart disease/myocardial infarction
• Vegetations on mitral and aortic valves associated with endocarditis
• An atheromatous plaque from an aortic aneurysm.

Other causes of mesenteric ischemia include:

• Atherosclerosis of mesenteric vessels
• Vasculitides
• Venous thrombosis in factor V Leiden mutation
• Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia due to alterations in splanchnic blood flow.

The most important clue to an early diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain in a patient with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis. The pain is typically in the central abdomen and out of proportion to the physical findings.

Associated clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distension, peritonitis, and the passage of bloody stools.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is angiography, and management is laparotomy. The goal of operative exploration is to resect the compromised bowel and restore blood supply via embolectomy.

Other options:

Option B: A pulsatile abdominal mass is seen in the case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation.

Options A and D: Acute severe pancreatitis and peptic ulcer perforation have no association with atrial fibrillation. They usually present with pain over the upper abdomen associated with guarding and rigidity on examination.
questions.learning: Acute mesenteric ischemia — The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to WHO, which of the following are components of the Human Development Index (HDI)?
options: Life expectancy at birth, literacy and standard of living
Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and standard of living
Infant mortality rate, literacy and standard of living
Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and infant mortality rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Life expectancy at birth, literacy and standard of living

The components of the Human Development Index (HDI) include life expectancy at birth, literacy, and standard of living.

Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of a country's average achievements in three dimensions of human development:

• A long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth
• Knowledge (literacy), as measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling, and
• A decent standard of living, as measured by GNI (gross national income) per capita.

HDI values range from 0 to 1, with 1 as the maximum value.

Note- Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and infant mortality rate are components of the Physical quality of life index (PQLI).
questions.learning: Life expectancy at birth, literacy and standard of living The components of the Human Development Index (HDI) include life expectancy at birth, literacy, and standard of living.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: At what age in women is a DEXA scan done routinely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. At 65 years

Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA scan) is routinely done in women at 65 years of age to screen for osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disorder characterized by abnormally low bone mass, which makes the bone unusually fragile and increases the risk of fractures.

The criteria to screen for osteoporosis according to the national osteoporosis foundation is as follows:

• Females aged 65 years or more
• Males aged 70 years or more
• Post-menopausal females under the age of 65 years with risk factors
• Fracture after the age of 50 years
• Males aged 50-69 with risk factors

A DEXA scan is performed in the above patients to assess bone mineral density, and the results are reported in terms of T-score or Z-score.
