questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is the new online software launched under the national tuberculosis elimination program (NTEP) by the government to monitor TB patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NIKSHAY

NIKSHAY is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients. (The word is a combination of two Hindi words NI and KSHAY, meaning eradication of TB).

Nikshay is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients to monitor the Revised National Tuberculosis Programme (RNTCP). This system stores information about the patient, medical history, diagnosis, co-morbidities and lab reports.

The system has been developed jointly by the Central TB Division of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and National Informatics Centre (NIC) and it was launched by the Government of India in June 2012. This is used by health functionaries at various levels across the country in association with Central TB Division (CTD), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

NIKSHAY covers various aspects of controlling TB using technological innovations.

Apart from web-based technology, SMS services have been used effectively for communication with patients and monitoring the program on a day-to-day basis.

Other options:

Option B: Nikusth is the new online software for monitoring leprosy patients.

Option C: Nischay is a pregnancy test kit.

Option D: Axshya is a project that works to improve access to quality TB care and control through a partnership between the government and civil society.
questions.learning: NIKSHAY NIKSHAY is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients. (The word is a combination of two Hindi words NI and KSHAY, meaning eradication of TB).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents after a fall and is found to have bleeding from the ear on clinical examination. What is the investigation of choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic bleeding from the ear is a clinical hallmark of a temporal bone fracture. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard investigation because it provides the detailed imaging required to detect fine fracture lines, ossicular chain disruption, and otic capsule involvement. A CBC (Option A) helps assess overall trauma status but cannot diagnose bone injuries. MRI (Option B) is excellent for soft-tissue or intracranial injuries but lacks the bony resolution needed to evaluate the petrous bone or ossicles. Standard X-ray (Option D) has poor sensitivity for these complex fractures and is inadequate for visualizing middle ear anatomy. Early HRCT is essential to guide management, preserve hearing function, and prevent complications like CSF otorrhea or facial nerve palsy
questions.learning: Post-traumatic bleeding from the ear is a clinical hallmark of a temporal bone fracture. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the gold standard investigation because it provides the detailed imaging required to detect fine fracture lines,…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Urinary dipstick analysis in a child reveals: • Urine pH 5.0 • Specific gravity 1.025 • Blood negative • Protein 3+ • Glucose negative • Ketones negative • Nitrite negative • Leukocyte esterase negative The child most likely has:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nephrotic syndrome

Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (≥3+ on urine dipstick) with no hematuria and no evidence of urinary tract infection. The dipstick findings of 3+ protein, negative blood, negative leukocyte esterase, and negative nitrite strongly suggest nephrotic syndrome.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nephrotic syndrome ✔️: Heavy isolated proteinuria is the hallmark.
• B. Acute glomerulonephritis ❌: Typically shows hematuria (blood positive/RBCs or RBC casts) with mild-to-moderate proteinuria.
• C. Urinary tract infection ❌: Usually leukocyte esterase and/or nitrite positive, often with pyuria.
• D. Diabetes mellitus ❌: Characterized by glycosuria (± ketonuria in DKA), not isolated heavy proteinuria.
questions.learning: Nephrotic syndrome Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (≥3+ on urine dipstick) with no hematuria and no evidence of urinary tract infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient reports excessive consumption of bajra (pearl millet) roti and subsequently develops symptoms of drowsiness and giddiness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Consumption of Bajra (pearl millet) that has been contaminated with the fungus Claviceps purpurea leads to ergotism. The fungus produces ergot alkaloids which act as potent vasoconstrictors and CNS disruptors, causing symptoms such as giddiness, drowsiness, and tingling sensations. In severe cases, this can progress to gangrene or convulsions. Epidemic Dropsy (Option A) is caused by the adulteration of mustard oil with Argemone oil, presenting with cardiac failure and edema. Botulism (Option C) results from Clostridium botulinum toxin, typically found in improperly canned foods, and causes descending flaccid paralysis. Fusarium toxicity (Option D) is associated with alimentary toxic aleukia and pancytopenia but is not the classic link for Bajra-induced CNS symptoms. Ergotism is historically prevented by removing contaminated grains using a 20% salt solution flotation method

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones play a permissive role in the attainment of puberty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptin

The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin.

It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty. Leptin is a satiety-producing hormone secreted by adipocytes. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure.

Evidence for which is given by:

• Obese ob/ob mice that cannot make leptin are infertile, and their fertility is restored by injections of leptin.
• Leptin treatment also induces precocious puberty in immature female mice.
• However, the way that leptin fits into the overall control of puberty remains to be determined.

Leptin also accelerates GnRH pulsatility in neurons, fastening puberty.
questions.learning: Leptin — The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin. It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the civil negligence case against a doctor who bears the onus of proof?
options: Police not under rank of sub inspector
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patient

In the case of civil negligence, the burden of proof is on the patient.

The question of civil negligence arises when a suit is filed in a civil court:

• By a patient or his/her relatives against the doctor for getting compensation from the doctor if he/she has suffered an injury due to the doctor's negligence.
• By a doctor against the patient or his/her relatives to collect the fees, the payment of which has been refused due to alleged professional negligence by the doctor.

In either case, the patient has to prove that the doctor has committed professional negligence.

To prove negligence, all the following four elements must be present:

• Duty - A duty of care by the doctor must exist.
• Dereliction - The physician must maintain the standard of a 'prudent physician' under similar circumstances. If the physician fails to maintain the standard of care, it is called dereliction.
• Direct causation - The negligent act or omission must directly cause the injury without any intervening cause.
• Damage - The negligent act must cause damage of a type that would have been foreseen by a reasonable physician.
questions.learning: Patient — In the case of civil negligence, the burden of proof is on the patient. The question of civil negligence arises when a suit is filed in a civil court: • By a patient or his/her relatives against the doctor for getting compensation from the doctor…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following antidiabetic drugs is recommended for weight loss in obese patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liraglutide

Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, promotes weight loss by increasing satiety, delaying gastric emptying, and reducing appetite. It is recommended for obese patients with type 2 diabetes, particularly those who would benefit from both glycemic control and weight reduction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glimepiride: Sulfonylurea; causes weight gain due to increased insulin secretion.
• C. Sitagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitor; generally weight neutral.
• D. Insulin: Commonly associated with weight gain.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A body brought for autopsy is cold to touch, shows rigor mortis in all four limbs, and has fixed livor mortis on the back, with no evidence of putrefaction. Based on these findings, what is the estimated time since death?
questions.explanation: 12-24 hours The estimation of the postmortem interval (PMI) relies on the combined findings of algor, rigor, and livor mortis. In this case, the body is cold to the touch, suggesting death occurred more than 8–12 hours ago. Rigor mortis is fully established in all four limbs, a state that typically occurs around 12 hours post-death and lasts up to 24 hours. Livor mortis (postmortem staining) is fixed at the back, which usually indicates a fixation time of 6–12 hours. Most importantly, there are no signs of putrefaction; putrefaction generally begins only after 24–36 hours depending on environmental conditions. Combining these markers, the most accurate estimate for the time since death is 12–24 hours. Option B (6–12 hrs) is less likely because rigor would not be fully established in all limbs. Options C and D are incorrect because putrefaction would likely have started.
questions.learning: 12-24 hours The estimation of the postmortem interval (PMI) relies on the combined findings of algor, rigor, and livor mortis. In this case, the body is cold to the touch, suggesting death occurred more than 8–12 hours ago.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chorioretinitis

Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis.

The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice, and mild thrombocytopenia.

Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation. The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery. The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan.

The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies. IgG can cross the placenta is hence, cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests.

Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission. It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus. Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks.
questions.learning: Chorioretinitis Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis. The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A middle-aged Indian man came to your OPD with the lesion as shown in the image below. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Basal cell carcinoma

The image above shows a central ulcer with raised borders and rolled-out edges (rodent ulcer) suggesting a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing malignant tumor with locally invasive characteristics. It affects the pilosebaceous skin.

Ultraviolet radiation exposure is the strongest predisposing factor. Other risk factors include exposure to arsenic, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and ionizing radiation.

Basal cell carcinoma mainly affects elderly or middle-aged men with excessive skin exposure, commonly in the age group of 40–80 y and in white-skinned people.

Macroscopically, it is categorized as localized and generalized. Nodular, nodulocystic (nodular and nodulocystic together account for 90% of basal cell carcinoma), pigmented, and nevoid are the localized cancers, while superficial multifocal and superficial spreading, infiltrative, and cicatrizing are the generalized types. The nodular type is described as pearly waxy nodules at the margins. A central depression (umbilication) or ulceration and rolled-out edges are characteristic of basal cell carcinoma.

Sites near the eye, nose, and ear and of size >2 cm are considered to be high risk. Direct invasion at these sites can reach the cranium.

Management is by Mohs microscopic surgery. Non-surgical measures, such as the administration of topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod, are useful. Metastasis is extremely rare.

Other Options:

Option A: Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common malignant tumor, seen more commonly in men. Microscopically, the proliferation of irregular masses of squamous epithelium is seen. The image is shown below.

Option C- Lupus vulgaris originates from an underlying focus of tuberculosis, typically in a bone, joint, or lymph node, or maybe from the hematogenous and lymphatic spread. It presents as a slowly enlarging plaque with an elevated border and central atrophy. The edges of the lesion gradually extend in some areas and heal with scarring in others. In India, the buttocks, and trunk are more frequently involved. Apple jelly nodules are demonstrated on diascopy.

Option D: Nevus are aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or dermo-epidermal junction. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.
questions.learning: Basal cell carcinoma — The image above shows a central ulcer with raised borders and rolled-out edges (rodent ulcer) suggesting a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the image, what condition has developed three days after catheterization?
questions.explanation: The image displays extensive necrotic sloughing of the scrotal skin, which is the hallmark of Fournier's gangrene. This is a rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia. While it can be idiopathic, it often follows local trauma or instrumentation, such as catheterization in a high-risk patient (e.g., diabetic). Gas gangrene (Option B) involves muscle necrosis and crepitus, usually in the limbs. Wet gangrene (Option C) is a more general term for infected necrotic tissue. Scrotal hematoma (Option D) would appear as a tense, purple swelling but not as open necrotic sloughing. Fournier's gangrene is a surgical emergency with a high mortality rate. It requires immediate, aggressive surgical debridement of all non-viable tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and intensive supportive care. The goal of surgery is to stop the spread of the polymicrobial infection along the fascial planes. Early recognition of the "dirty" dishwater-fluid and necrotic skin is vital for saving the patient's life
questions.learning: The image displays extensive necrotic sloughing of the scrotal skin, which is the hallmark of Fournier's gangrene. This is a rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy is brought with respiratory symptoms. You suspect an upper respiratory tract infection. No other complication is present. Which radiological investigation is required?
options: CT scan of neck and chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No radiological investigation required

Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are primarily diagnosed clinically and do not require routine imaging in uncomplicated cases. Radiological investigations should be reserved for patients with suspected complications, severe disease, atypical presentations, or an alternative diagnosis.

• An otherwise healthy 12-year-old with uncomplicated URTI does not require any radiological investigation.
• Management is based on clinical assessment and supportive care.

Why not the other options?

• A. Plain chest radiograph: Indicated only if lower respiratory tract involvement (e.g., pneumonia) or complications are suspected.
• B. CT scan of neck and chest: Reserved for suspected deep neck space infections, abscesses, or airway compromise.
• C. HRCT: Used for chronic or diffuse parenchymal lung diseases, not routine URTI evaluation.
questions.learning: No radiological investigation required Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are primarily diagnosed clinically and do not require routine imaging in uncomplicated cases.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young teenage boy with a history of drug abuse had been instilled with a shot of intravenous cocaine at a party. He is rushed to the emergency room by his friends. Some of the symptoms were diaphoresis, headache, and acute coronary spasm. Which of the following symptoms noted would go against the likely diagnosis of cocaine poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bradycardia

Cocaine intoxication presents with tachycardia and not bradycardia. Thus, the presence of bradycardia would go against the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication.

Cocaine is an alkaloid deliriant extracted from Erythroxylum coca.

Acute intoxication with cocaine leads to symptoms spanning 2 stages-

1. Stage of excitement/euphoria - associated with hypervigilance, anxiety, hyperactivity along with hyper-adrenergic signs of mydriasis, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmias.
2. Stage of depression - associated with loss of reflexes, muscle paralysis, circulatory and respiratory failure, and coma.

Chronic intoxication is characterized by toxic delirium and tactile hallucination of bugs (cocaine bugs) or vermin crawling under the skin (formication).

Common complications include cerebrovascular accidents and myocardial ischemia.

Treatment includes intravenous diazepam for controlling seizures. For ventricular arrhythmias, propranolol may be given intravenously. If the patient has psychosis, haloperidol may be given. Treatment of chronic cocaine abuse requires psychiatric support.

Cocaine withdrawal is a triphasic syndrome that presents after the sudden stoppage of chronic cocaine use. The phases are as follows -

1. Crash phase (9 hours - 4 days): Anorexia, depression, excessive craving, hypersomnia, fatigue.
2. Normal mood, anxiety, and anhedonia (4 - 7 days)
3. Extinction phase (7 - 10 days): Absence of withdrawal symptoms but increased susceptibility to relapse.

Treatment for withdrawal includes bromocriptine and amantadine. They are useful in reducing cocaine craving.
questions.learning: Bradycardia Cocaine intoxication presents with tachycardia and not bradycardia. Thus, the presence of bradycardia would go against the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presented with severe watery diarrhea resembling that of rice gruel stool. Damage of which structure is likely to have resulted in this diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zona occludens

The given clinical picture of a patient having rice gruel stools is suggestive of the diagnosis of ‘cholera’. Vibrio cholerae in addition to the cholera toxin (CT) produces some additional toxins such as,

• Zonula occludens toxin, which alters the intestinal permeability by acting on intestinal epithelial cell tight junctions (which are also called zonula occludens)
• Accessory cholera enterotoxin.

Zonula occludens:

• Also known as tight junctions
• Characteristically surround the apical margins of the cells in epithelia such as the intestinal mucosa, the walls of the renal tubules, and the choroid plexus.
• Also important to the endothelial barrier function and endothelium-dependent vasodilation.
• Made up of ridges- half from one cell and a half from another cell- which adhere so strongly that there is no space between the cells.
• Three families of transmembrane proteins are involved:

1. Occludin
2. Junctional adhesion molecule
3. Claudins

• Paracellular pathway - these tight junctions permit the passage of ions, solutes, and intracellular signaling molecules in between adjacent cells.

Other options:

B) Gap junctions:

• The gap between the two cells in these types of junctions is about 4nm.
• These junctions are formed by units called connexons, which are present in the membrane of each cell.
• Each connexon is made up of six protein subunits called connexins.
• They permit substances to pass between the cells, without entering the ECF.
• The pore diameter is around 0.8 to 1.4  nm, which permits the passage of ions, sugars, amino acids, and other solutes which weigh up to 1000 Da.
• They also permit rapid propagation of electrical activity from cell to cell, as well as the exchange of various chemical messengers and intracellular signaling molecules.

C) Adherent junctions:

• Adherent junctions or Zonula adherens is a continuous structure on the basal side of the zonula occludens.
• It contains cadherins.

D) Hemidesmosomes:

• They look like half-desmosomes.
• They attach cells to the underlying basal lamina and are connected intracellularly to intermediate filaments.
• They contain integrins.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Cadaveric spasm is seen in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Traumatic asphyxia

Cadaveric spasm is an instantaneous stiffening of a group of voluntary muscles at the moment of death, without passing through primary relaxation.

• Occurs in sudden, violent deaths with intense emotion or physical activity
• Commonly involves hands gripping objects (weapon, weeds, etc.)
• Helps reconstruct circumstances at time of death

Common situations where seen:

• Suicidal firearm injuries → weapon tightly held
• Drowning → weeds/mud grasped in hands
• Electrocution → object firmly held due to tetanic contraction

Why not traumatic asphyxia:

• Death is gradual due to compression of chest
• Lacks sudden intense neuromuscular activity required for cadaveric spasm

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme serves as the rate-limiting step in the heme synthesis pathway?
questions.explanation: The synthesis of heme is a complex pathway occurring partly in the mitochondria and partly in the cytosol. The rate-limiting and primary regulatory step of the entire pathway is the first step: the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase. This enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) as a cofactor and is inhibited by the end-product, heme (feedback inhibition). HMB synthase (Option A) is the enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria. ALA dehydratase (Option B) and Ferrochelatase (Option D) are enzymes later in the pathway that are highly sensitive to lead inhibition but are not the primary rate-limiting steps under normal physiological conditions. Proper regulation of ALA synthase is essential to ensure that heme production matches the body's requirements for hemoglobin and other hemoproteins while preventing the accumulation of toxic porphyrin intermediates
questions.learning: The synthesis of heme is a complex pathway occurring partly in the mitochondria and partly in the cytosol. The rate-limiting and primary regulatory step of the entire pathway is the first step: the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with rectal prolapse underwent surgery. The postoperative image is given below. Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thiersch wiring

The postoperative image shows a purse-string suture which is suggestive of Thiersch wiring for rectal prolapse.

In Thiersch's wiring, a steel wire or a silastic/nylon tape is placed around the anal canal. It is rarely done now due to post-operative problems like chronic perineal sepsis, anal stenosis, and obstructed defecation.

Rectal prolapse is of two types:

1. Partial rectal prolapse - only the mucosal layer of the rectum is prolapsed. It is seen in children and is managed by digital repositioning. If there is a recurrence, then Theirsch's wiring or sclerotherapy is performed.
2. Complete rectal prolapse - all the layers of the rectum are involved. It is seen in adults due to the weakening of the pelvic floor. It is managed by using the following approaches:

1. The perineal approach - easy to perform, and has fewer complications but a high recurrence rate. It is preferred in elderly patients with comorbidities. The surgeries done include:

1. Thiersch's wiring
2. Delorme's mucosectomy - In this procedure, the rectal mucosa is stripped circumferentially from the rectum over the length of the prolapse. The underlying muscle is plicated with a series of sutures. The excess rectal mucosa is excised and a mucosal anastomosis is performed.
3. Altemeier's recto sigmoidectomy (option D) - In this procedure, full-thickness resection of the prolapsed rectum is performed, incorporating any associated colonic prolapse. Restoration of colorectal continuity can be performed by hand-sewn/stapled anastomosis. This is the procedure of choice in patients presenting with incarcerated and strangulated prolapse.

2. The abdominal approach - It is difficult to perform and has more complications, but a lower recurrence rate. The surgeries done include:

1. Ripstein's procedure - It involves the placement of a prosthetic mesh around the mobilized rectum, with the attachment of the mesh to the presacral fascia below the sacral promontory.
2. Well's procedure (option B) - It involves posterior rectopexy.

Other options:

Option A: Stapled hemorroidopexy is used in the treatment of internal hemorrhoids, where a circular stapling device is used to excise a cylinder of mucosa and submucosa and simultaneously staple the mucosal ends together.
questions.learning: Thiersch wiring — The postoperative image shows a purse-string suture which is suggestive of Thiersch wiring for rectal prolapse. In Thiersch's wiring, a steel wire or a silastic/nylon tape is placed around the anal canal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Anterior most air cells of anterior ethmoidal sinus are known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Agger nasi

Agger nasi is the anterior-most air cells of anterior ethmoid air cells. When enlarged it may cause mechanical obstruction to frontal sinus drainage.

Other options:

Option A: Bulla ethmoidalis is the largest air cell in the ethmoidal air sinus. It is situated behind the uncinate process and forms the posterior boundary of hiatus semilunaris through which the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain.

The image below shows the ethmoidal bulla:

Option B: Onodi cell is formed from posterior ethmoidal air cell. The optic nerve lies in its lateral wall and can be injured while operating in the cells.

The image below shows Onodi air cell:

Option D: Haller cells are formed from either anterior or posterior ethmoid air cells. They present in relation to the floor of the orbit and roof of the maxillary sinus, enlargement may prevent drainage of the maxillary sinus.

The image below shows Haller cell:
questions.learning: Agger nasi Agger nasi is the anterior-most air cells of anterior ethmoid air cells. When enlarged it may cause mechanical obstruction to frontal sinus drainage.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presented with the following findings on her face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acne vulgaris

The age of the patient and the presence of papules and pustules with an erythematous base on the face are suggestive of acne vulgaris.

Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit. It is commonly seen in teenagers and young adults.

Comedonal lesions are the earliest lesions of acne. They represent the keratin plugs of the pilosebaceous duct and are non-inflammatory.

When the keratin plug is inside the follicle, it is called a closed comedone/whitehead.
When the keratin plug in the pilosebaceous unit is exposed to the environment, it gets oxidized by the air and turns black, known as open comedones/blackheads.
Inflammatory changes lead to the formation of papules, which may become pustules that rupture superficially or else spread deeper and form cystic lesions.

Management is directed at minimizing inflammation, decreasing keratin production, antibiotics, and antiandrogens to diminish sebum production.

The FDA has recently approved the drug Clascoterone, an androgen receptor inhibitor for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients aged 12 years and older.

Other options:

Option A: Acne rosacea or Rosacea is predominantly a disease with onset in middle‐aged adults (30–50 years old) and involves the convexities of the face.

Option C: Eczema presents more over the flexures and extremities from early adulthood. Features of pruritus and excoriations are predominant.

Option D: Tinea faciei is a fungal infection of the face and presents with a scaly lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45 y/o male patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. A CT scan reveals multiple appendices epiploicae, particularly prominent in the sigmoid colon. Which of the following statements regarding the anatomy of the large intestine is false?
options: The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae.
The sigmoid colon, which is S-shaped, leads directly into the rectum.
The total length of the large intestine in adults ranges from 1 to 1.5 meters.
Appendices epiploicae are more common in the distal colon.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae.

Appendices epiploicae are fat-filled peritoneal pouches attached to the outer surface of the colon. Key anatomical features:

• They are most numerous in the transverse and sigmoid colon.
• They are rare or absent in the cecum, appendix, and rectum.
• They can become inflamed, leading to epiploic appendagitis, which may mimic appendicitis or diverticulitis.

Large intestine facts:

• Length: about 1–1.5 meters in adults.
• Sigmoid colon: S-shaped and continues into the rectum.
• Appendices epiploicae are more common in the distal colon, especially the sigmoid colon.

Therefore, the false statement is that the cecum is a common site for appendices epiploicae.
questions.learning: The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae. Appendices epiploicae are fat-filled peritoneal pouches attached to the outer surface of the colon.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought with progressive pallor, recurrent infections, and failure to thrive. On examination, the child has hypopigmented skin and sparse, light-colored hair. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia and neutropenia. Which of the following micronutrient deficiencies best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copper

The combination of anemia + neutropenia + hypopigmentation of skin and hair is characteristic of copper deficiency. Copper is a cofactor for several important enzymes:

• Ceruloplasmin → involved in iron metabolism (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺)
• Cytochrome c oxidase → energy production
• Tyrosinase → melanin synthesis

Pathophysiology:

• ↓ Ceruloplasmin → impaired iron mobilization → anemia
• Impaired immune function → neutropenia
• ↓ Tyrosinase activity → ↓ melanin → hypopigmentation

Clinical associations:

• Malnutrition
• Excess zinc intake (interferes with copper absorption)
• Menkes disease (genetic copper deficiency)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Zinc: Causes dermatitis, delayed wound healing
• Selenium: Cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease)
• Iron: Causes anemia only (no neutropenia or hypopigmentation)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is used to measure fetal anemia?
options: Peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery (MCA)
questions.explanation: The measurement of Peak Systolic Velocity in the fetal Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA-PSV) is the non-invasive gold standard for detecting fetal anemia. In anemic states, blood viscosity decreases, which leads to a compensatory increase in the velocity of blood flow through the MCA. This is measured using Doppler ultrasonography and compared to normative values. Umbilical artery Doppler (Option A) is primarily used to assess placental insufficiency rather than anemia. While cord blood sampling (Option B) can directly measure hemoglobin levels, it is highly invasive and carries significant procedural risks. Chorionic villus sampling (Option C) is utilized for genetic testing in the first trimester, not for evaluating anemia. Therefore, MCA-PSV is the preferred first-line screening tool for monitoring pregnancies at risk of Rh isoimmunization or other causes of fetal red cell depletion

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the subsequent colonoscopy findings is indicative of a highly malignant condition?
questions.explanation: In colonic pathology, the number and morphology of polyps are critical indicators of malignant potential. Finding "multiple flat polyps (about 100)" is highly suggestive of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). FAP is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by the development of hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Without a total proctocolectomy, the risk of these polyps progressing to colorectal carcinoma is virtually 100% by the fourth decade of life. A single pedunculated polyp (Option B) has a much lower risk of malignancy, as the stalk provides a margin of safety during endoscopic removal. Multiple pedunculated polyps (Option C) increase the overall risk but do not carry the same systemic certainty of malignancy as a polyposis syndrome. A solitary flat polyp (Option D), also known as a sessile or non-polypoid lesion, has a higher risk than a pedunculated one but is less significant than a diffuse field of polyposis. Thus, the quantity and genetic implication of Option A represent the most malignant scenario
questions.learning: In colonic pathology, the number and morphology of polyps are critical indicators of malignant potential. Finding "multiple flat polyps (about 100)" is highly suggestive of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male whose staple diet primarily consisted of only maize presents with diarrhea, dementia, and photosensitive dermatitis in sun-exposed areas. Which vitamin is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Maize contains niacin in bound form and is unavailable for absorption. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

* Diarrhea

* Dermatitis

* Dementia

Casal’s necklace pattern classically seen in pellagra is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar.

Pellagra occurs despite an adequate intake of tryptophan & niacin in the case of

* Carcinoid syndrome as tryptophan will be used up in the production of serotonin

* Hartnup disease due to a defect in the tryptophan transporter resulting in intestinal malabsorption and failure of renal reabsorption.

Niacin significantly decreases concentrations of all apoB-containing lipoproteins like VLDL, IDL, LDL, and lipoprotein a. It also increases HDL cholesterol.

Niacin toxicity occurs when it is taken in excess quantity for the treatment of hyperlipidemia and manifests as

* Prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing

* Glucose intolerance

* Fulminant hepatitis (the most serious complication)

* Hyperuricemia

* Macular edema and macular cysts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old man sustains a fracture of the neck of the fibula following a road traffic accident. A few days later, he develops foot drop with weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot. Sensory examination reveals loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral aspect of the leg. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, making it the most commonly injured nerve in fibular neck fractures. Injury results in paralysis of both the deep and superficial peroneal nerves. The patient has the classical features of common peroneal nerve injury:

• Fracture of the neck of the fibula (common site of injury)
• Foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior compartment (loss of dorsiflexion)
• Weak eversion due to paralysis of the lateral compartment
• Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral aspect of the leg

Why not the other options?

• A. Tibial nerve: Injury causes loss of plantar flexion, inability to stand on tiptoes, and sensory loss over the sole of the foot, not foot drop.
• B. Superficial peroneal nerve: Causes weak eversion and sensory loss over most of the dorsum of the foot, but dorsiflexion is preserved.
• C. Deep peroneal nerve: Causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion and sensory loss limited to the first dorsal web space, while eversion is largely preserved.
questions.learning: Common peroneal nerve — The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, making it the most commonly injured nerve in fibular neck fractures.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with a three-day history of persistent fever, malaise, and splinter hemorrhages. Echocardiography shows valvular vegetations suggestive of endocarditis. Blood cultures reveal alpha-hemolytic cocci in chains that are resistant to optochin and bile. Which bacterium is most likely causing his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with subacute Infective Endocarditis, characterized by valvular vegetations and peripheral markers like splinter hemorrhages . The microbiology results are definitive: alpha-hemolytic cocci in chains that are resistant to optochin and bile identify the organism as a member of the Viridans group Streptococci, of which Streptococcus sanguis is a primary member. Streptococcus pneumoniae is also alpha-hemolytic but is sensitive to optochin and bile. Mycoplasma (Option A) lacks a cell wall and would not show these Gram-stain/culture features. Enterococcus (Option C) is usually gamma or alpha-hemolytic but is bile-esculin positive (meaning it grows in bile). Streptococcus agalactiae (Option D) is beta-hemolytic. Viridans group organisms like S. sanguis are part of the normal oral flora and are the most common cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures. Therefore, Option B is the correct pathogen

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The cover–uncover test is commonly used to assess ocular alignment disorders. Which of the following conditions cannot be detected using this test?
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is a reduction in vision that occurs because the brain favors one eye over the other during early development. While it can be caused by strabismus, the cover-uncover test itself is used only to detect ocular deviations, not to diagnose amblyopia. Latent squint or heterophoria (Option A) is detected by the uncover test, as the eye moves to refixate only when the cover is removed. Manifest squint or heterotopia (Option B) is identified by the cover test, where the eye under the paddle remains still while the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation. Lateral nystagmus (Option C) refers to involuntary rhythmic eye movements; although the cover-uncover test is not the primary diagnostic tool, it can sometimes exacerbate or reveal these movements. The cover-uncover test is a fundamental part of the pediatric ophthalmic exam for identifying horizontal and vertical strabismus

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who works as a teacher presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a teacher—a professional voice user prone to vocal abuse—presenting with chronic hoarseness is the classic scenario for Vocal nodules (Singer’s or Screamer’s nodules). These are small, symmetrical, whitish callosities that typically develop at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the vocal cords, which is the point of maximum vibration. A vocal polyp (Option A) is usually unilateral and often results from a single traumatic vocal event. A vocal cyst (Option B) is also typically unilateral and deeper within the cord tissue. Reinke's oedema (Option D) involves a diffuse swelling of the vocal cords, most commonly seen in middle-aged female smokers. Management of vocal nodules is initially conservative, focusing on intensive voice therapy to correct vocal habits. Surgical excision (microlaryngoscopy) is only reserved for mature, large nodules that do not respond to voice rest and therapy. This diagnosis is a foundational "spotter" in ENT clinics
questions.learning: The clinical history of a teacher—a professional voice user prone to vocal abuse—presenting with chronic hoarseness is the classic scenario for Vocal nodules (Singer’s or Screamer’s nodules).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common site for tubal ligation and the reason for ligation at this site?
options: Ampulla; as it has more circular muscles than longitudinal muscles
Ampulla; as it is the widest part
Isthmus; as it has uniform muscle thickness
Isthmus; as it is the narrowest part
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isthmus; as it has uniform muscle thickness

The most common site for tubal ligation is the isthmus of the fallopian tube due to its uniform muscle thickness, which facilitates effective occlusion.

The isthmus, being a narrow segment closest to the uterine wall, provides an ideal location for surgical intervention. This site ensures a more reliable and efficient ligation, minimizing the risk of complications and maximizing the success rate of the procedure. The uniformity of the muscle layer at this location allows for a consistent occlusion technique. Common procedures for tubal ligation at this site include the Pomeroy method, where a loop of the tube is tied and excised, and other techniques like the Falope ring or the electrocoagulation method.

While the ampulla, which has a larger-diameter segment lateral to the isthmus, is also a part of the fallopian tube, it is less frequently chosen for tubal ligation. Additionally, ligation at the isthmus allows for the possibility of future reversal, should the patient desire to conceive again, making it a favourable choice for women considering sterilization.

The fallopian tube consists of three layers: the mesosalpinx, an outer mesothelial layer serving as visceral peritoneum; the myosalpinx, which has an inner circular smooth muscle layer for pressure during contractions and an outer longitudinal layer for tube movement; and the endosalpinx, an inner columnar epithelium with ciliated and secretory cells, featuring longitudinal folds. Together, these layers transport the ovum efficiently toward the uterine cavity.

Note: The interstitial portion of the fallopian tube is the narrowest segment, located within the uterine wall, and it forms the tubal ostia that opens into the endometrial cavity.
questions.learning: Isthmus; as it has uniform muscle thickness — The most common site for tubal ligation is the isthmus of the fallopian tube due to its uniform muscle thickness, which facilitates effective occlusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are metabolic causes of splenic enlargement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amyloid and Gaucher’s disease

Splenomegaly has numerous causes and is commonly classified into infectious, hematological, congestive, neoplastic, inflammatory, and metabolic/storage disorders. Metabolic causes are mainly due to lysosomal storage diseases and abnormal protein deposition, leading to accumulation of substances within the spleen.

• Amyloidosis causes splenomegaly due to extracellular deposition of amyloid protein.
• Gaucher’s disease (β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency) is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and classically presents with massive splenomegaly.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rickets and Still’s disease:

• Rickets is a metabolic bone disease and does not cause splenomegaly.
• Still’s disease is an inflammatory disorder and may cause splenomegaly, but it is not a metabolic disease.

• C. Porphyria and Felty’s syndrome:

• Porphyria is a metabolic disorder but splenomegaly is uncommon.
• Felty’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), not metabolic.

• D. Myelofibrosis and Weil’s disease:

• Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
• Weil’s disease is severe leptospirosis (infectious).
questions.learning: Amyloid and Gaucher’s disease Splenomegaly has numerous causes and is commonly classified into infectious, hematological, congestive, neoplastic, inflammatory, and metabolic/storage disorders.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old factory worker presents to the emergency department with headache, vomiting, and blurred vision after consuming locally prepared alcohol. What is the treatment of choice for methanol poisoning?
questions.explanation: Methanol poisoning is a medical emergency that occurs after ingesting tainted illicit alcohol. The toxicity is not caused by methanol itself but by its metabolite, formic acid, which causes severe metabolic acidosis and irreversible damage to the optic nerve (blurred vision). The treatment of choice (antidote) is Fomepizole. Fomepizole is a potent competitive inhibitor of the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase; it prevents the conversion of methanol into its toxic metabolites, allowing the parent methanol to be safely excreted. If fomepizole is unavailable, intravenous ethanol can be used as an alternative. Flumazenil (Option B) is the antidote for benzodiazepines. N-acetyl cysteine (Option C) is for acetaminophen overdose. Naloxone (Option D) is for opioid toxicity. Along with the antidote, patients often require aggressive administration of sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis and urgent hemodialysis to rapidly remove methanol and formic acid from the blood. Rapid intervention is essential to prevent permanent blindness and death
questions.learning: Methanol poisoning is a medical emergency that occurs after ingesting tainted illicit alcohol. The toxicity is not caused by methanol itself but by its metabolite, formic acid, which causes severe metabolic acidosis and irreversible damage to the optic…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following hormones is the major product of the fetal adrenal glands?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DHEA

The major steroid products of the fetal adrenal gland are DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) and DHEA-S.

They serve as important substrates for estrogen synthesis in the placenta.

The fetal-adrenal-placental axis is vital for normal childbirth. Placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulates the fetal adrenal gland to produce DHEA-S and cortisol. Cortisol further stimulates the production of placental CRH, creating a positive feedback loop that enhances adrenal steroid hormone production.

The steroid products released by the fetal adrenal gland have effects on the placenta and membranes. These effects contribute to transforming the myometrium from a quiescent to a contractile state.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal recessive condition in which cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland is affected. Cortisol deficiency increases the secretion of ACTH, which leads to adrenocortical hyperplasia and overproduction of intermediate metabolites.
questions.learning: DHEA — The major steroid products of the fetal adrenal gland are DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) and DHEA-S. They serve as important substrates for estrogen synthesis in the placenta.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 20 per second

The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period. It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction.

In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second.
Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds.

In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves.
Hence, the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds.

Substituting the value in the formula, we get:
Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100/5 = 20/sec.

Tetanization:

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

• by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
• by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

• Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
• Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.
questions.learning: 20 per second The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second. Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient underwent a left submandibular gland excision during which the hypoglossal nerve was injured. Which of the following deficits would be seen in this case?
options: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side
Deviated tongue to the same side
Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deviated tongue to the same side

A hypoglossal nerve injury would damage all muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus resulting in deviation of the tongue to the same side. Since, the left hypoglossal nerve is injured in the above scenario, the tongue will deviate to the left side.

Hypoglossal nerve injury:

* Ipsilateral tongue atrophy

* Paralysis of all muscles except palatoglossus resulting in ipsilateral deviation of the tongue on protrusion

* Paralysis of geniohyoid and thyrohyoid resulting in deviation of larynx to the contralateral side.
questions.learning: Deviated tongue to the same side — A hypoglossal nerve injury would damage all muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus resulting in deviation of the tongue to the same side.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A female presented with burning micturition and symptoms of Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Which of the following fluoroquinolones is least likely to be effective?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Moxifloxacin

Moxifloxacin does not accumulate significantly in urine and is not approved for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin, and Levofloxacin can be used in UTIs caused by susceptible organisms.
questions.learning: Moxifloxacin Moxifloxacin does not accumulate significantly in urine and is not approved for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs). Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin, and Levofloxacin can be used in UTIs caused by susceptible organisms.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which is the false statement among the following for the condition given in the picture?
options: Retention cyst of major salivary glands
Most common site is lower lip
Retention cyst of minor salivary glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retention cyst of major salivary glands

The image shows a mucocele of the lower lip and it is a retention cyst of the minor salivary glands of the lip.

Mucocele:

* The most common site of mucocele in the oral cavity is the lower lip.

* It is a retention cyst of the minor salivary glands of the lip.

* The lesions appear as a soft and cystic mass of bluish color.

* Treatment is surgical excision.

Note:

If the ducts of any salivary gland become obstructed they can develop a retention cyst. If such cysts occur due to the obstruction in the sublingual salivary gland, it is called a ranula. A ranula usually presents as a large, tense, bluish swelling on the floor of the mouth to one side on the midline.
questions.learning: Retention cyst of major salivary glands — The image shows a mucocele of the lower lip and it is a retention cyst of the minor salivary glands of the lip.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 64-year-old woman was brought by her son, during a cataract outreach camp. She gives a history of trauma to her left eye, one year back and a complete loss of vision in that eye since then. Her left eye image is given below. What is the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoplasty

The above image shows a dense white opacity which results due to the scarring of more than half of the stroma. It is characteristic of Leucomatous corneal opacity  and the treatment of choice is keratoplasty.

Depending on the density, corneal opacities are graded as nebula, macula and leucoma.

* Nebular corneal opacity (fog or mist):

* Hard-to-see corneal scar, due to superficial scars involving Bowman's layer and superficial stroma.

* Slit-lamp detection is required.

* A thin, diffuse nebula covering the pupillary area interferes more with vision than the localised leucoma away from the pupillary area. Nebula produces more discomfort due to blurred image (irregular astigmatism).

* Macular corneal opacity:

* Semi-dense opacity that can be seen with proper illumination.

* Due to scarring involving about half the corneal stroma.

* Leucomatous corneal opacity (leucoma simplex):

* White scar that is easily seen just by looking at the eye.

* Due to scarring of more than half of the stroma

* Adherent leucoma:

* It results when healing occurs after perforation of the cornea with incarceration of iris

Secondary changes in corneal opacity which may be seen in long-standing cases include hyaline degeneration, calcareous degeneration, pigmentation and atheromatous ulceration.

Treatment:

* Keratoplasty is the treatment of choice in leucomatous corneal opacities.

* Optical iridectomy may be performed in cases with central adherent leucomas

* Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) performed with excimer laser is useful only in superficial (nebular) corneal opacities.

* Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in patients with corneal opacities, who have lost their vision or who do not expect to recover it. It improves cosmetic appearance by altering the white colour of the opacity and blending it to normal eye colour.
questions.learning: Keratoplasty — The above image shows a dense white opacity which results due to the scarring of more than half of the stroma. It is characteristic of Leucomatous corneal opacity and the treatment of choice is keratoplasty.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A person is kept in a dark room for a prolonged period. Which of the following is correct regarding the physiology of dark adaptation (night vision)? 1. Conversion of retinal pigment to vitamin A 2. Increase in pupillary size 3. Increased sensitivity to light 4. Conversion of retinal and opsin to photosensitive pigment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3 and 4

Dark adaptation is the process by which the eye becomes progressively more sensitive to low levels of illumination after entering a dark environment. It is primarily mediated by rod photoreceptors through regeneration of rhodopsin (visual purple).

During dark adaptation:

• Pupillary dilatation (mydriasis) increases the amount of light entering the eye.
• Regeneration of rhodopsin occurs by recombination of 11-cis retinal with opsin, increasing rod sensitivity.
• Sensitivity to light progressively increases, allowing vision in dim light.

Why is A correct?

• 2. Increase in pupillary size
• 3. Increased sensitivity to light
• 4. Conversion of retinal and opsin to photosensitive pigment (rhodopsin)

Why is 1 incorrect?

• Retinal is derived from vitamin A (retinol), not converted into vitamin A. During dark adaptation, vitamin A is converted to 11-cis retinal, which combines with opsin to regenerate rhodopsin.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Dark adaptation is the process by which the eye becomes progressively more sensitive to low levels of illumination after entering a dark environment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The finger-nose test is done to check the integrity of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cerebellum

The finger-nose test is done to assess cerebellar function.

Coordination in the upper limb is tested by finger-nose test. The patient is asked to touch his nose with the index finger of one hand. Then he is asked to touch the examiner's index finger. He is asked to do this multiple times, while the examiner keeps moving his index finger from place to place. It is important to ensure that the patient has to stretch his upper limb to reach the examiner's finger, so that the coordination can be assessed over the full range of motion of the upper limb.

Lower limb coordination is tested by heel-shin test. The test is done with the patient lying down on a bed. They are asked to put the heel of one leg onto the shin of the other leg, just below the knee. They are then asked to run the heel down the front of the shin till the dorsum of the foot. Patients with cerebellar lesions will have a tremor when trying to place the heel on the shin, and will be unable to accurately run the heel down the entire length of the shin.

The functioning of the posterior column tracts (option B) is assessed by Romberg's test. While performing Romberg's test, the patient is asked to stand with his feet close together, initially with his eyes open. If the patient is able to maintain their balance with the eyes open, they are asked to close their eyes. If they lose their balance and sway or fall with their eyes closed, the test is said to be positive. The examiner needs to be prepared to support the patient in case they are about to fall.

Patients with disorders of the posterior column tracts will have impaired proprioception, and will have a positive Romberg's test. If the patient has dizziness or a tendency to fall even with the eyes open, then the lesion is likely to be in the vestibular system or cerebellum, and other relevant tests should be performed.
questions.learning: Cerebellum — The finger-nose test is done to assess cerebellar function. Coordination in the upper limb is tested by finger-nose test.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 49-year-old man presenting with flu-like symptoms, a rash involving the palms and soles, and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy on examination?
questions.explanation: The constellation of flu-like constitutional symptoms, generalized maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, and characteristic epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of Secondary Syphilis. This stage of infection, caused by Treponema pallidum, occurs weeks to months after the resolution of the primary chancre. Epitrochlear lymph node enlargement is highly suggestive of this condition. Primary syphilis (Option A) is characterized by a painless, solitary chancre at the site of inoculation, usually without a systemic rash. Endemic diseases (Option C) refer to localized disease patterns and are not a specific diagnosis for these clinical signs. Steven-Johnson Syndrome (Option D) is a severe hypersensitivity reaction characterized by painful, necrotic skin sloughing and mucosal involvement, usually triggered by drugs, which is inconsistent with this non-painful palm/sole rash. Diagnosis should be confirmed with non-treponemal tests like VDRL or RPR followed by specific treponemal assays. Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G remains the first-line therapeutic intervention
questions.learning: The constellation of flu-like constitutional symptoms, generalized maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, and characteristic epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of Secondary Syphilis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: High-ceiling diuretics are used in the treatment of all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary hypertension

High-ceiling diuretics or loop diuretics are used to treat pulmonary edema and are not used in pulmonary hypertension.

They act by inhibiting the Na+-K+-2Cl- symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle resulting in increased excretion of sodium, potassium, and chloride.

* Their diuretic property helps in removing the excess fluid in hepatic, renal, and cardiac diseases. Their vasodilatory and diuretic action cause natriuresis reduces left ventricular filling pressures and thereby rapidly relieve pulmonary edema.
s helpful for the quick relief of symptoms in LVF and acute pulmonary edema. They are also used for the treatment of chronic CHF.

* Loop diuretics can be used as an adjunct to mannitol in cerebral edema. The osmotic effect of mannitol can be prolonged by the use of a loop diuretic. They preferentially excrete water over solute and maintain blood-brain osmotic gradient established by mannitol.

Pulmonary artery hypertension is a condition where there is increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Since nitric oxide is an important regulator of pulmonary vascular resistance, PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil, vardenafil, or tadalafil are primarily used in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with loss of the right visual field in both eyes while central (macular) vision is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A right-sided field defect in both eyes (right homonymous hemianopia) with central vision intact is characteristic of Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing. This condition typically results from a lesion in the contralateral (left) primary visual cortex, often following a stroke in the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory. Macular sparing occurs because the macular representation in the visual cortex has a dual blood supply from both the PCA and the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Heteronymous hemianopia (Option B) involves different sides of the visual field being lost (e.g., bitemporal), which is not the case here. An optic chiasm lesion (Option C) classically causes bitemporal hemianopia due to crossing nasal fibers. An optic tract lesion (Option D) causes a complete homonymous hemianopia but usually does not demonstrate macular sparing because it occurs before the cortical level of dual blood supply. This finding is key for cortical localization
questions.learning: A right-sided field defect in both eyes (right homonymous hemianopia) with central vision intact is characteristic of Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 3-year-old male is brought into the OPD by his mother. She complains that his left eyelid is constantly drooping. Physical examination reveals that the eyeball is abducted and depressed in its primary position. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3rd nerve palsy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (3rd nerve palsy).

In primary gaze, the patient's left eye has deviated down and out. There is also profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle. Due to the involvement of the superior rectus and medial rectus, elevation and adduction will be impaired. Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles. All of these findings indicate left oculomotor nerve palsy.

The signs of left oculomotor nerve palsy are summarised in the image attached below.

In trochlear nerve palsy (4th nerve palsy), the superior oblique is affected, causing:

* The weakness of depression: Mainly seen when the eye is adducted (depression during abducted position is a function of the Inferior rectus)

* Weakness of abduction

* Failure of intorsion: cause of diplopia.

In abducens nerve palsy (6th nerve palsy), the lateral rectus is affected. Due to the involvement of only the lateral rectus, abduction will be impaired.

In facial nerve palsy (7th nerve palsy), there is facial weakness.
questions.learning: 3rd nerve palsy The clinical scenario is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (3rd nerve palsy). In primary gaze, the patient's left eye has deviated down and out.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to the casualty after a road traffic accident. A lacerated wound of 4x1 cm, which is bone-deep, is noted over the scalp of the forehead. Which of the following is the correct mechanism of this lacerated wound?
options: Impact of a semi sharp-edged object
Overstretching of skin and subcutaneous tissue
Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone

The description of the wound given in the question suggests a split laceration and the mechanism is the tissue being crushed between the underlying bone (i.e. skull) and the weapon.

A laceration is a tear or a split in the skin, mucous membrane, muscle, or any internal organ produced by blunt force. The margins are irregular and may show minute tears and bruising. Tears that are seen at the ends, diverging away from the main laceration are called swallowtails. In skin lacerations, usually one of the margins overhangs the other. This helps in assessing the direction of the force.

Classification of a laceration:

• Split laceration (incised-like laceration): It occurs when the skin is crushed between two hard objects. For example, during a fall, the scalp gets crushed between the skull from inside and hard ground outside. This results in a wound, which usually mimics an incised one unless examined closely.

• Incised-looking lacerated wound is a wound with the linear splitting of the tissue caused by blunt force. It is seen where the skin overlies an area of the bone where there is scanty underlying subcutaneous tissue such as the scalp, forehead, shin, etc.

• Avulsed laceration: A lesion where the skin separates or peels off by tearing from the underlying tissues. An avulsion is a laceration produced by a shearing force delivered at an acute angle to tear off a portion of a traumatized surface or viscus from its attachments. It may overhang the wound. It is also called flaying. This is common in road traffic accidents. (Option A)
• Tears: Tearing of skin and subcutaneous tissue can occur from localized impact by or against irregular or semi-sharp objects. It may be due to blows by broken glass, or a fall on a rough projected object. (Option B)
• Stretch laceration: It occurs due to the over-stretching of the skin, beyond its elasticity. This is seen in wounds produced from running over by a motor vehicle, and when a fracture produces a sudden deformity of the bone. (Option C)
• Cut laceration: Injury by a heavy sharp-edged instrument. For example, cut from ax, chopper, etc

The image shows a split laceration which is incised looking laceration.
questions.learning: Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone — The description of the wound given in the question suggests a split laceration and the mechanism is the tissue being crushed between the underlying bone (i.e. skull) and the weapon.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An elderly man presents with skeletal deformities, including bowing of the legs, and requires crutches for ambulation. Several other individuals from the same village exhibit similar features. Given this geographic clustering, what is the most appropriate next step in the investigation?
options: Collect and analyze water samples for fluoride content
questions.explanation: The presence of a cluster of cases involving bowed legs and skeletal abnormalities in a single village strongly suggests an environmental or endemic cause. This presentation is characteristic of endemic skeletal fluorosis, which is caused by the long-term ingestion of groundwater with a fluoride concentration exceeding 1.5 mg/L. Therefore, the immediate priority is analyzing the local water supply. While Checking Vitamin D (Option A) or Calcium (Option B) might detect individual cases of rickets or osteomalacia, these nutritional deficiencies do not typically occur in sudden geographic clusters. A PTH assay (Option C) investigates endocrine disorders like hyperparathyroidism, which is also an individual-level condition. Since endemic fluorosis is common in various parts of India and presents with progressive joint stiffness and bony overgrowth, water testing is the logical public health response
questions.learning: The presence of a cluster of cases involving bowed legs and skeletal abnormalities in a single village strongly suggests an environmental or endemic cause.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A nerve conduction study is being conducted, as shown in the image. Electrodes are positioned near the wrist, and stimulation is used to evaluate motor and sensory function. Which nerve is most likely being monitored in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulnar nerve

In the given scenario, the ulnar nerve is being monitored. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve. This assesses the contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle to monitor neuromuscular activity.

The procedure shown in the image is known as electromyography (EMG). It is the process of recording changes in muscle electric potential using surface or needle electrodes. An EMG test examines the electrical signals produced by muscles both at rest and while in use. A healthy muscle at rest does not emit any electrical signals. A damaged muscle may show electrical activity while at rest or in activity.

In order to avoid postoperative residual curarisation, an acceleromyograph can be used for neuromuscular monitoring during general anaesthesia with neuromuscular-blocking drugs.

In the image given below: (A) Placement of electrodes for physiological measurement of conduction of the ulnar nerve, based on standard surface Ag-AgCl electrodes applied differentially (21 mm centre-to-centre spacing) located along the ulnar nerve track. Centre distance: 18 cm between 5 and 4, all others 8 cm apart; (B) photo showing the location of the ulnar nerve track and the digiti minimi abductor muscle as well as the labelling of recording and triggering points.
questions.learning: Ulnar nerve — In the given scenario, the ulnar nerve is being monitored. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperglycemia

Hyperglycemia does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis. Instead, hypoglycemia stimulates catecholamine synthesis.

Catecholamine synthesis is primarily stimulated by various physiological stressors and factors that activate the sympathetic nervous system, such as physical exertion(exercise), changes in posture, or certain external stimuli like smoking.

Other options:

Option B: Smoking stimulates catecholamine release through the activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which increases catecholamines like adrenaline and norepinephrine.

Option C: When a person stands up, it can lead to orthostatic hypotension, which triggers the release of catecholamines to help increase blood pressure and maintain adequate perfusion.

Option D: Exercise stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and increases catecholamine production to support increased heart rate, blood pressure, and metabolic demands.
questions.learning: Hyperglycemia Hyperglycemia does not stimulate catecholamine synthesis. Instead, hypoglycemia stimulates catecholamine synthesis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the immunological abnormality that is seen with the lack of CD40 in B cells is?
options: Total lack of natural killer cells
Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM
Inability of neutrophils to fight against infections
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells leads to Hyper IgM syndrome. A decrease in IgG and an increase in IgM is seen in this syndrome.

The patients most often have loss-of-function mutations involving either CD40 or activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a DNA-editing enzyme expressed in B cells that are required for Ig class switching and affinity maturation.

The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to antigens, is unaffected, accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies. Hence, the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome.

The serum of the patients has normal or elevated levels of IgM but no IgA or IgE and extremely low levels of IgG. Clinical features are recurrent pyogenic infections because of low levels of opsonizing IgG antibodies. They are highly susceptible to pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.
questions.learning: Decrease in IgG and increase in IgM — The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells leads to Hyper IgM syndrome. A decrease in IgG and an increase in IgM is seen in this syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mother came back home to see her child suffering from difficulty breathing. The child had contact with rotenone while trying to bathe their pet. The child was taken to the emergency department and she later passed away. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes was the likely cause of her death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NADH-Q oxidoreductase

In the given clinical vignette, inhibition of NADH-Q oxidoreductase by rotenone was the likely cause of breathlessness, followed by death in this child.

Rotenone inhibits complex I, thereby inhibiting the respiratory chain, so electrons cannot be transferred to oxygen. This halts ATP production, leading to an energy deficit in the cells, eventually causing cell death. The ETC constitutes four enzyme complexes:

• Complex I: NADH-Q oxidoreductase
• Complex II: Succinate-Q reductase
• Complex III: Q-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
• Complex IV: cytochrome c oxidase

Components of complex I are FMN and Fe-S complex. NADH-Q oxidoreductase catalyses the transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q, along with the transfer of four H+ across the membrane.
questions.learning: NADH-Q oxidoreductase — In the given clinical vignette, inhibition of NADH-Q oxidoreductase by rotenone was the likely cause of breathlessness, followed by death in this child.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following tests will be positive in the urine of a patient who has undergone prolonged starvation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only 3

Only test 3, which is Rothera's test for ketone bodies in the urine will be positive in the urine of a patient with prolonged starving.

Urine tests

Test 1 - Benedict’s test for reducing sugars

Test 2 - Heat and acetic acid test for presence of albumin

Test 3 - Rothera’s test for ketone bodies

In case of prolonged starvation,

1. After a meal till about 2 hours later, maintenance of blood glucose is primarily from the diet. During this time, hepatic glycogen stores are getting replenished.
2. As dietary blood glucose levels start to decline, glucagon secretion increases and insulin secretion decreases, resulting in rapid mobilisation of hepatic glycogen stores.
3. If there is fasting for a longer period of time, hepatic glycogen stores cannot maintain blood glucose levels. 12 hours after the last meal, gluconeogenesis becomes the primary source of blood glucose, since most of the hepatic glycogen would have depleted. If an individual continues fasting, gluconeogenesis continues to be the main source.
4. However, over the first few days of fasting, ketogenesis happens. This is when the concentration of acetyl CoA from fatty acid oxidation exceeds the oxidative capacity of the TCA cycle. Also, ketogenesis releases CoA, ensuring its availability for continued fatty acid oxidation. Water-soluble ketone bodies are used as fuel by most tissues, including the brain during fasting. It also reduces the need for gluconeogenesis from amino acid carbon skeletons, thus preserving essential protein in the body.

Therefore, during prolonged fasting, the levels of ketone bodies in the body rise and subsequently begin to be eliminated in urine. Hence, in starvation ketosis, Rothera's test will be positive, but Benedict's test will be negative.

Both Benedict's and Rothera's tests will be positive in diabetic ketoacidosis. (Option 1)
