questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following does not exhibit the Koebner's phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Koebner’s phenomenon, also known as the "isomorphic response," refers to the development of new skin lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of local trauma or injury. Classic examples of skin diseases that exhibit this phenomenon include Vitiligo (Option A), Psoriasis (Option B), and Lichen planus (Option C). Herpes (Option D) is a viral infection; while trauma can reactivate a latent virus (triggering a cold sore), it does not follow the definitive clinical definition of Koebner’s phenomenon, which specifically describes the linear induction of chronic dermatoses by trauma. Other conditions showing Koebner’s include warts and molluscum contagiosum (due to autoinoculation). Because Herpes is an acute, localized viral process rather than a trauma-induced distribution of a chronic dermatosis, it is the correct "not" choice. Recognizing this phenomenon is useful for clinicians when assessing the distribution of lesions
questions.learning: Koebner’s phenomenon, also known as the "isomorphic response," refers to the development of new skin lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of local trauma or injury.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are functions of the gall bladder? I. Reservoir for bile II. Production of bile III. Secretion of mucus IV. Concentration of bile Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

The gallbladder is a storage and concentrating organ for bile. It does not produce bile; bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver. The gallbladder modifies bile by absorbing water and electrolytes and secreting mucus, which protects the mucosa and facilitates bile flow.

The normal functions of the gallbladder include:

• I. Reservoir for bile: Stores approximately 30–60 mL of bile between meals.
• III. Secretion of mucus: Mucus protects the gallbladder mucosa and lubricates bile flow.
• IV. Concentration of bile: The gallbladder absorbs water, sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, concentrating bile 5–10 times.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Production of bile: Bile is produced by hepatocytes in the liver, not by the gallbladder.
questions.learning: I, III and IV — The gallbladder is a storage and concentrating organ for bile. It does not produce bile; bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the hospital with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor. The radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute laryngotracheobronchitis

The diagnosis in this child with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor is acute laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The x-ray finding is the 'steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months to 6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and low-grade fever.

Management:

• Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to the rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.
• Dexamethasone is administered by the least invasive route (Oral > IV > IM ) for all the grades of croup.
• Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

Antibiotics are not indicated in acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Other options:

Option A: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency presenting in children with a rapidly progressive course of fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and respiratory obstruction, followed by a toxic appearance and drooling. The neck is hyperextended and stridor is a late finding. Radiography shows a classic thumb sign.

Option C: Foreign body aspiration initially presents with a paroxysm of cough, choking, and gagging, accompanied by new-onset wheezing and asymmetric breath sounds.

Option D: Laryngomalacia is a congenital laryngeal anomaly presenting in children with low-pitched inspiratory stridor exacerbated by exertion.
questions.learning: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis — The diagnosis in this child with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor is acute laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which method would be most effective for presenting statistical data to highlight the importance of routine antenatal care to a small, uneducated village during a rural health posting?
questions.explanation: When communicating health statistics to a population with low literacy levels, such as an uneducated rural village, visual simplicity is paramount. A pictogram (Option A) is the most effective method because it uses easily recognizable symbols or pictures to represent data, making complex concepts intuitive and engaging. For example, a picture of a mother can represent ten pregnant women, allowing villagers to quickly grasp ratios without needing advanced numeracy. Line diagrams (Option B) are better for showing trends over time but require an understanding of X-Y coordinates. Histograms (Option C) are used to show frequency distributions of continuous data and can appear cluttered and confusing to those unfamiliar with statistical charts. Frequency polygons (Option D) are even more abstract, using lines to connect midpoints of intervals. Therefore, the pictogram's ability to simplify data into relatable imagery makes it the gold standard for community health education in underserved rural settings where traditional literacy is limited
questions.learning: When communicating health statistics to a population with low literacy levels, such as an uneducated rural village, visual simplicity is paramount. A pictogram (Option A) is the most effective method because it uses easily recognizable symbols or pictures…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about breastmilk jaundice?
options: Breastfeeding need not be stopped for the treatment
Most of the children require phototherapy
Exclusive breastfeeding with a total bilirubin of more than 10mg/dl after 3-4 weeks of birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Most of the children require phototherapy

Most of the children suffering from breastmilk jaundice do not require phototherapy.

Breastmilk jaundice is due to significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Option D), after the 7th day and may last for 2–3 weeks. This may be caused by the breast milk that might contain β-glucuronidase, which deconjugates intestinal bilirubin and promotes its absorption and other inhibitors of glucuronyl transferase. Persistently high bilirubin levels may require changing from breast milk to infant formula for 24–48 h and/or treatment with phototherapy, without cessation of breastfeeding. (Option A)

Most cases of breast milk jaundice are mild and self-limiting, and phototherapy is required only in rare severe cases where bilirubin levels are significantly elevated. (Option B)

Breast milk jaundice is typically observed in exclusively breastfed infants, often with elevated bilirubin (>10mg/dl) levels persisting beyond the neonatal period (after 3-4 weeks of birth). (Option C)
questions.learning: Most of the children require phototherapy Most of the children suffering from breastmilk jaundice do not require phototherapy. Breastmilk jaundice is due to significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Option D), after the 7th day and may last for 2–3 weeks.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn born to a diabetic mother develops symptoms 24 hours after birth, and blood glucose estimation shows a level below 35 mg/ dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.explanation: In a symptomatic neonate with blood glucose <35 mg/dL, immediate intravenous correction is required to prevent seizures and permanent neurological injury. The standard treatment is an IV bolus of 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg), followed by a continuous glucose infusion. It is essential to recheck the glucose within 20–30 minutes to confirm stabilization. Infants of diabetic mothers are at exceptionally high risk for this condition due to fetal hyperinsulinism. Hartmann solution (Option A) does not contain glucose and is ineffective. Waiting to recheck glucose without intervention (Option B) is dangerous in a symptomatic baby. Starting oral feeds (Option D) is only appropriate for mild, asymptomatic hypoglycemia. Therefore, immediate IV glucose is the mandatory life-saving intervention
questions.learning: In a symptomatic neonate with blood glucose <35 mg/dL, immediate intravenous correction is required to prevent seizures and permanent neurological injury.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the following natural history of disease flowchart, point A to C is called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lead time

Lead time is the period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the usual time of diagnosis (point C).

Screening time is the time difference between the first point of diagnosis and the critical point of diagnosis.

Diagnosis of a disease before the critical point has a good outcome and reduces the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred.

Screening must be done in conditions where there is a considerable time lag between the onset of disease and the usual time of diagnosis. That is conditions with a long lead time.

Generation time is defined as the interval of time between the onset of infection by a host and the maximal infectivity of that host.
questions.learning: Lead time Lead time is the period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the usual time of diagnosis (point C). Screening time is the time difference between the first point of diagnosis and the critical point of diagnosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-month-old child with a history of multiple blood transfusions presents with hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, normal MCH and MCHC, and a peripheral smear showing hypochromic, microcytic red cells. Which diagnostic test should be performed next to determine the cause of this anemia?
questions.explanation: The combination of severe anemia (Hb 6.3), microcytosis (MCV 70), and a history of multiple blood transfusions in an infant is highly suspicious for a hemoglobinopathy, specifically Beta-thalassemia major. The most appropriate and definitive next step in the diagnostic workup is Hemoglobin (Hb) electrophoresis (Option D) . This test will identify the abnormal hemoglobin patterns, such as an absence of HbA and elevated levels of HbF and HbA2. Serum iron (Option A) would be elevated in thalassemia and is used to rule out iron deficiency. Direct Coombs' test (Option B) is used for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which typically presents with a normocytic/macrocytic pattern. The osmotic fragility test (Option C) is diagnostic for hereditary spherocytosis, which shows spherocytes rather than the microcytic hypochromic cells described. Therefore, Hb electrophoresis is the definitive tool to confirm the underlying genetic defect in hemoglobin synthesis
questions.learning: The combination of severe anemia (Hb 6.3), microcytosis (MCV 70), and a history of multiple blood transfusions in an infant is highly suspicious for a hemoglobinopathy, specifically Beta-thalassemia major.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which gas is commonly used in pneumoperitoneum, which involves inflating the abdominal cavity during laparoscopic surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carbondioxide

The correct gas used in pneumoperitoneum is carbon dioxide. Pneumoperitoneum is a technique used in laparoscopic or minimally invasive surgery to create a working space within the abdominal cavity.

CO2 is the preferred gas for this purpose due to several reasons:

*

Non-Flammable: CO2 is non-flammable, making it safer to use in surgical procedures where electrical equipment is in close proximity.

*

Minimal Absorption: CO2 is minimally absorbed by the body, which means it can be introduced into the abdominal cavity without causing significant physiological changes.

*

Rapid Absorption: CO2 is quickly absorbed into the bloodstream and can be eliminated through respiration after the procedure, reducing the risk of post-operative complications.

*

Low Cost: CO2 is readily available and cost-effective.

Other Options:

* Oxygen is not used for pneumoperitoneum due to its flammable nature. In the presence of electrical equipment and surgical tools, using oxygen would pose a significant fire hazard.

* Nitrous oxide is not commonly used for pneumoperitoneum because it is a greenhouse gas and has poor absorption characteristics. It can lead to increased intra-abdominal pressure and potential complications.

* Nitrogen is not typically used for pneumoperitoneum because it is also a non-absorbable gas. This means it would remain in the body after the surgery, potentially causing discomfort and complications.
questions.learning: Carbondioxide — The correct gas used in pneumoperitoneum is carbon dioxide. Pneumoperitoneum is a technique used in laparoscopic or minimally invasive surgery to create a working space within the abdominal cavity.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted among nursing staff to find out time taken in different aspects of patient care viz., bed preparation, monitoring of vitals, attending doctor's rounds, blood sampling, drug administration. Which management technique would be applied for the analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Work sampling

Work sampling is a management technique used to analyze how time is distributed among various activities by observing workers at random intervals.

It is particularly useful for studying nursing activities such as bed preparation, vitals monitoring, drug administration, and assisting in rounds.

Work Sampling is a management technique used to determine how workers spend their time on different activities.

Instead of continuously timing every task, the observer records random observations of what activity is being performed at specific moments.

Unlike CPM or systems analysis, work sampling focuses on time utilization patterns, not process flow or project scheduling.

| Critical Path Method | Used for project scheduling and planning

| Input–Output Analysis | Evaluates relationship between resources and output

| Systems Analysis | Examines entire system performance

| Work Sampling | Used to analyze distribution of workers’ time across activities

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the treatment of choice for a 4-year-old boy presenting with generalized edema, urine analysis showing 4+ proteinuria, and a urine protein–creatinine ratio of 3?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Nephrotic Syndrome, characterized by massive proteinuria and generalized edema. In children, approximately 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases are due to Minimal Change Disease, which is highly responsive to corticosteroids. The preferred initial treatment is oral Prednisolone (Option A) given at a dose of for 6 weeks, followed by a tapering course. Cyclophosphamide (Option B), Levamisole (Option C), and Cyclosporine (Option D) are second-line immunosuppressive agents reserved for patients who are "steroid-resistant," "steroid-dependent," or "frequent relapsers" . Starting these agents as the initial treatment would be inappropriate given the high likelihood of steroid responsiveness in a 4-year-old. Complete remission (disappearance of proteinuria) is usually achieved within the first few weeks of Prednisolone therapy. Therefore, corticosteroids remain the cornerstone and gold standard for the first-line management of childhood nephrotic syndrome
questions.learning: The patient presents with Nephrotic Syndrome, characterized by massive proteinuria and generalized edema. In children, approximately 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases are due to Minimal Change Disease, which is highly responsive to corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old individual was involved in a motorcycle accident and presents with the following clinical or imaging findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical photograph shows the affected limb in a position of abduction and external rotation, which is pathognomonic for an anterior hip dislocation. This injury typically occurs during high-energy trauma, such as a bike accident, when a force is applied to an abducted leg. In contrast, posterior hip dislocation (Option B) is much more common (dashboard injury) and presents with the opposite deformity: flexion, adduction, and internal rotation. Superior hip dislocation (Option C) is extremely rare and usually associated with extensive pelvic fractures. Option D is incorrect as the clinical presentation for anterior and posterior dislocations is mutually exclusive due to the different positions of the femoral head. Therefore, the visible external rotation and abduction in this patient definitively identify the dislocation as anterior
questions.learning: The clinical photograph shows the affected limb in a position of abduction and external rotation, which is pathognomonic for an anterior hip dislocation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: Consider the following statements for diagnosing ventricular aneurysm in a patient with recent myocardial infarction: I. Paradoxical impulse on chest wall II. Persistent ST elevation on ECG III. Unusual bulge from cardiac silhouette on X-ray IV. Presence of pulsus paradoxus Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and III

A left ventricular (LV) aneurysm is a late mechanical complication of a transmural myocardial infarction, usually developing 2 weeks to several months after MI. It results from thinning and outward bulging of the infarcted ventricular wall, leading to a dyskinetic, scarred segment.

Why is C correct?

The following findings are characteristic of a ventricular aneurysm:

• I. Paradoxical precordial impulse: Due to dyskinetic outward bulging of the aneurysm during systole.
• II. Persistent ST-segment elevation on ECG: A classic ECG finding that persists weeks after MI without reinfarction.
• III. Bulge in the cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray: Suggests aneurysmal dilatation of the left ventricle.

IV. Pulsus paradoxus is not a feature of ventricular aneurysm. It is classically seen in:

• Cardiac tamponade
• Constrictive pericarditis (occasionally)
• Severe bronchial asthma/COPD
questions.learning: I, II and III — A left ventricular (LV) aneurysm is a late mechanical complication of a transmural myocardial infarction, usually developing 2 weeks to several months after MI.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child was brought to the emergency with drooling and choking following ingestion of a foreign body. Based on the given X-ray, what object was most likely swallowed by the child?
options: Cap of a cool drink bottle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Button battery

The presence of a halo sign or double ring sign is indicative of the foreign body being a button battery. Furthermore, the presence of irregularities along the periphery of the battery indicates the possibility of corrosion.

Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal.

Button batteries, in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies, which must be expediently removed because they can cause:

• Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time
• Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours

Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge. Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The growth and differentiation of primordial follicles is under the control of which hormone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FSH

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) promotes the growth and differentiation of ovarian follicles, particularly from the preantral/antral stages onward.

• A. LH: Acts mainly on theca cells and is important for androgen production and ovulation.
• B. FSH — Correct: Stimulates follicular growth and granulosa-cell proliferation, and promotes aromatization of androgens to estrogen.
• C. Growth hormone: Has supportive metabolic effects but is not the primary regulator of follicular development.
• D. Progesterone: Predominantly acts after ovulation during the luteal phase

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a bluish, translucent swelling under her tongue. She describes it as cystic, with visible veins on the surface. On examination, the swelling transilluminates, indicating a fluid-filled structure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a bluish, translucent, cystic swelling located specifically under the tongue on the floor of the mouth is highly characteristic of a ranula. A ranula is a type of mucocele that arises from the sublingual salivary gland due to ductal obstruction or trauma, leading to mucus extravasation into the surrounding tissues. Its characteristic "frog-belly" appearance and positive transillumination confirm its fluid-filled nature. In contrast, a dermoid cyst (Option B) typically presents as a midline swelling that is doughy on palpation and does not transilluminate. A thyroglossal cyst (Option C) is a midline neck mass that moves with tongue protrusion and is not located sublingually. A sublingual tumor (Option D) would typically be firm, non-translucent, and solid rather than cystic. Therefore, the anatomical location and classic physical signs documented in this 28-year-old patient definitively point toward a ranula as the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a bluish, translucent, cystic swelling located specifically under the tongue on the floor of the mouth is highly characteristic of a ranula.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Arrange the following in order of being most to least resistant:
options: Spores > Prions > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus
Prions > Spores > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus
Mycobacterium > Naked Virus > Spores > Enveloped virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prions > Spores > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus

Microorganisms vary in their resistance to sterilization and disinfectants. The order from most resistant to least resistant is:

Prions > Bacterial spores > Mycobacteria > Naked (non-enveloped) viruses > Enveloped viruses

• Prions are most resistant because they are misfolded proteins without nucleic acids, resistant to heat, radiation, and many disinfectants.
• Bacterial spores (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) resist heat and chemicals due to thick protective coats and low metabolic activity.
• Mycobacteria are moderately resistant because of their lipid-rich mycolic acid cell wall.
• Naked viruses are more resistant than enveloped viruses since they lack a fragile lipid envelope.
• Enveloped viruses are least resistant because their lipid envelope is easily destroyed by detergents, alcohol, and drying.
questions.learning: Prions > Spores > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus Microorganisms vary in their resistance to sterilization and disinfectants. The order from most resistant to least resistant is: Prions > Bacterial spores > Mycobacteria > Naked…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with altered sensation in the extremities and impaired coordination. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, but the accommodation reflex is intact. Which condition is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of absent pupillary light reaction in the presence of a preserved accommodation reaction is known as light-near dissociation. This specific sign is classically called the Argyll Robertson pupil. It is the pathognomonic ocular hallmark of late-stage Neurosyphilis (Tabes Dorsalis), which also explains the patient's symptoms of altered sensation and coordination (sensory ataxia). The lesion is thought to involve the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain, sparing the more ventral fibers involved in the near reflex. Horner's syndrome (Option B) presents with miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis, but the light reflex remains intact. Papilledema (Option C) involves bilateral optic disc swelling due to increased intracranial pressure. Optic Neuritis (Option D) causes sudden vision loss and a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD), but both the light and near reflexes are typically impacted relative to the visual deficit. Diagnosis of neurosyphilis is confirmed by positive CSF-VDRL testing. Early treatment with intravenous penicillin is mandatory to halt neurological progression
questions.learning: The clinical combination of absent pupillary light reaction in the presence of a preserved accommodation reaction is known as light-near dissociation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose 6-phosphatase

Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is glucose 6-phosphatase.

A decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is seen in fasting state, in which there is the activation of gluconeogenesis and inhibition of glycolysis.

Among the given options, only glucose 6-phosphatase is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis and therefore is activated. The enzymes mentioned as other options are irreversible enzymes of glycolysis and are inhibited in the fasting state.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which segment of the nephron has the lowest osmolality in the absence of the ADH hormone?
options: Descending limb of the Loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cortical collecting duct

In the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), the cortical collecting duct has the lowest osmolality.

As filtrate moves through the nephron, it changes concentration. Initially, in the proximal tubule, water and solutes are reabsorbed in equal proportions, keeping the filtrate isotonic (~300 mOsm/L). In the loop of Henle, water is removed in the descending limb, increasing osmolality, while solutes are actively reabsorbed in the ascending limb, diluting the filtrate to ~100 mOsm/L by the time it reaches the early distal convoluted tubule.

In the absence of ADH, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts remain impermeable to water, preventing reabsorption. As a result, in the cortical collecting duct, additional solutes such as sodium and chloride are reabsorbed without water, leading to further dilution of the tubular fluid.

This makes the cortical collecting duct the segment with the lowest osmolality, often reaching values as low as 50–75 mOsm/L, before the filtrate moves into the medullary collecting duct and is excreted as dilute urine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which clinical test is being shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Cottle's test, which is used to evaluate the patency of the nasal valve. It involves pulling the patient's cheek laterally while they breathe in through the nose. If the nasal airway improves significantly upon pulling the cheek, the test is positive, indicating nasal valve collapse as a cause of obstruction. Epley's maneuver (Option A) is used to treat Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The Heimlich maneuver (Option B) is used to clear an obstructed airway. Trotter's method (Option D) is a posture used to control epistaxis (leaning forward and pinching the nose). Cottle's test is a simple, non-invasive diagnostic maneuver that helps surgeons determine if a patient with nasal obstruction requires specific correction of the internal nasal valve. Therefore, the visual of lateral cheek traction during respiration uniquely identifies this clinical test

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The subcostal line corresponds to which vertebrae level?
questions.explanation: The subcostal line (or subcostal plane) is a transverse anatomical plane used to divide the abdomen into nine regions. It is defined as the horizontal line connecting the lowest points of the costal margins, which typically correspond to the 10th costal cartilages. This plane passes through the body of the L3 vertebra. It should not be confused with the transpyloric plane (Option B), which passes through the L1 vertebra and marks the pylorus of the stomach. The T12 level (Option A) corresponds to the origin of the celiac trunk and the esophageal hiatus. The L2 level (Option C) is the site where the spinal cord typically ends (conus medullaris) and the renal arteries originate. The subcostal plane at L3 serves as an important landmark for the third part of the duodenum and the lower borders of the kidneys. Understanding these vertebral levels is essential for accurate physical examination and the interpretation of cross-sectional abdominal imaging in clinical practice

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Arrange the steps of the Disaster cycle in sequence.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation

The disaster cycle describes the continuous sequence of activities before and after a disaster. It begins with disaster impact, followed by response involving rescue and relief measures. It is a continuous cycle used in disaster preparedness programs such as those coordinated by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA).

This is succeeded by rehabilitation and recovery, and finally mitigation, which aims to reduce the impact of future disasters through preparedness and risk reduction.

Expanded version of the same: Impact- Response- Rehabilitation-Reconstruction-Development-Prevention-Mitigation-Preparedness

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man who was on crutches now presents with tingling and paraesthesia on the medial side of the arm, forearm, and hand. Which structure is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

A person with the use of crutches, tingling and paraesthesia along the medial side of the arm, forearm, and hand is suggestive of brachial plexus injury(shown as A), specifically lower brachial plexus injury, and is called Klumpke’s palsy.

* Klumpke’s palsy is caused by lower brachial plexus injury.

* Most lower plexus injuries are from penetrating wounds, difficult births, falling on an outstretched arm, and trauma from crutches.

* There are usually motor and sensory deficits involving C8 and T1 with or without C7 dysfunction.

* In case of an avulsing injury, Horner’s syndrome may be associated with this condition.

* There is paralysis of the flexors of the wrist and fingers.

* The sensory deficit is along the medial aspect of the arm, forearm, and hand.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman who underwent dilatation and curettage for molar pregnancy 6 months ago presents with persistent symptoms of abdominal pain and distention. On further evaluation, the beta-hCG levels were persistently elevated and cannonball foci were found on the chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

A woman with a history of dilatation & curettage for molar pregnancy complaining of abdominal pain, distention, cannonball foci, and persistently elevated beta HCG levels is likely having Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

Based on the mentioned features in the question stem, the diagnosis is low risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) of stage III.

Gestational trophoblastic diseases are histologically is divided into:

Hydatiform mole
Non-molar trophoblastic neoplasms

Villi absent

• Complete hydatidiform mole
• Partial hydatidiform mole

-

• Placental site trophoblastic tumor
• Epithelioid trophoblastic
tumor

They typically develop along with or after a molar pregnancy. Rarely, it may develop after live birth, miscarriage, or medical termination of pregnancy.

Risk factors for malignant change are:

* Molar pregnancy -

* partial moles - 1-5% risk

* complete moles - 15-20% risk

* Patient's age ≥ 40 years or <20 years

* Parity ≥3

* Serum β hCG >1,00,000 IU/mL

* Uterine size >20 weeks

* Previous history of molar pregnancy

* Large theca lutein cysts >6 cm in diameter

Treatment of GTN:

* Low-risk GTN (FIGO Stages I-III: score <7): Single-agent chemotherapy with methotrexate (MTX) or Dactinomycin (less commonly used).

* 50 mg MTX is given IM on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 with folinic acid on alternate days.

* High-risk GTN (FIGO Stages II-III: score >7 and Stage IV): Multiple agent chemotherapies, with or without adjuvant surgery or radiotherapy. The preferred multiple agent chemotherapy regime is the EMACO regime:

* Etoposide

* Methotrexate

* Dactinomycin (actinomycin D)

* Cyclophosphamide

* Vincristine (Oncovin)

questions.text:
Which of the following are causes of neonatal seizures ?

1. Hyponatremia
2. Hypomagnesemia
3. Hypocalcemia
4. Hypernatremia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3, and 4

All of the above-given options, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypernatremia are causes of neonatal seizures.

The causes of neonatal seizure according to the age of presentation are summarised in the table below:

Hypocalcemia

Hypoglycemia Hypomagnesemia

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is the most common cause. Metabolic disorders cause neonatal seizures commonly. Hypoglycemia is the most common metabolic cause of neonatal seizures.

Neonatal seizures may be of different types - subtle, tonic, clonic, spasms, and myoclonic.

Subtle seizures are the most common type of neonatal seizures. They involve movements like transient eye deviations, nystagmus, blinking, mouthing, cycling, and apnea, and are more common in premature infants.

Tonic seizures are characterized by increased muscle tension, either focal (sustained posturing of a single limb) or generalized (bilateral tonic limb extensions or flexions of the upper limbs with tonic extension of the lower limbs and trunk). They can not be provoked by stimulation or suppressed by restraint.

Clonic seizures involve repetitive contractions of muscle groups. Spasms are sudden generalized jerks associated with brief discharges.

Myoclonic seizures are the least common type of neonatal seizures and are rapid jerks (<50 msec) without rhythmicity.

Electroencephalogram (EEG) is the preferred diagnostic investigation for seizures, while MRI is the recommended neuroimaging modality for etiological evaluation. Phenobarbital is the drug of choice for treatment. In term neonates, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is the most common cause of seizures, while intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is more prevalent in preterm neonates.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, headache, photophobia, and neck rigidity for the last 2 days. He had undergone a heart transplant one year back and is on immunomodulatory drugs. A lumbar puncture was taken in view of meningitis which showed reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils. On microscopy, differential motility was seen, non-motile at 37 degrees and tumbling motility at 25 degrees. What is the most likely organism causing this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Listeria

The clinical scenario and LP findings are suggestive of meningitis. Differential motility with risk factors of immunosuppression suggests a Listeria infection.

Risk factors for Listeria meningitis include:

* Age>50

* Diabetes

* Chronic illness

* Malignancy

* Immunosuppressive therapy

Listeria monocytogenes shows slow tumbling motility when grown at 25 °C.

But at 37°C, it is non-motile because the peritrichous flagella are produced by the bacillus optimally between 20°C and 30°C. This is known as differential motility as motility pattern changes with a change in temperature.

Listeria moves from cell-to-cell using host cell actin framework.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which radiographic view is considered best for optimal visualization of the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation: The "Water’s view" (occipitomental projection) is the standard radiographic projection used for the "optimal visualization of the maxillary sinuses". By tilting the patient’s head back, the dense petrous ridges are projected below the maxillary antra, providing a clear view of any air-fluid levels or mucosal thickening. Towne’s view (Option B) is used primarily for the occipital bone and the foramen magnum. Law’s view (Option C) and Stenvers view (Option D) are specialized projections used for imaging the "mastoid air cells" and the "petrous temporal bone" (internal auditory canal), respectively. While CT scans have largely replaced plain films for detailed sinus evaluation, Water’s view remains a useful, cost-effective initial screening tool for acute sinusitis. Radiologists look for opacification of the normally air-filled sinuses to confirm the presence of inflammatory disease. Accurate positioning is essential to ensure the sinuses are not obscured by the skull base

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young lady presented to the ENT OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. Rinne test and fistula test were positive. She had refused treatment then and currently came with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. On examination, the fistula test was negative. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. False negative

The given clinical scenario indicates severe sensorineural hearing loss as a consequence of untreated suppurative labyrinthitis and Rinne's test is a false negative in this case.

Initially, the patient had a positive fistula test, which implies that the labyrinth is still functioning. Rinne's test is positive which could be due to normal hearing or sensorineural hearing loss.

Currently, the patient has a negative fistula test which implies that the labyrinth is dead. This is an example of severe sensorineural hearing loss and here, Rinne test is a false negative.

If intermittent pressure applied to the external ear produces vertigo and nystagmus, it is a positive fistula test. The pressure changes in the external ear are transmitted to the labyrinth. This is suggestive of abnormal communication between the middle ear and the inner ear.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presented with biliary colic. The intern has administered an analgesic, following which the pain got aggravated. Which of the following could be responsible for the aggravation of the patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Morphine

Morphine is the analgesic which could be responsible for the aggravation of the patient's symptoms.

It causes constriction of the sphincter of Oddi causing an increase in fluid pressure in the common bile duct and gall bladder.

Note: Pethidine causes lesser spasm of the sphincter of Oddi and can be used in biliary colic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Enzyme deficient in Gaucher disease:
questions.explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, following an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. It is caused by a definitive deficiency in the enzyme Beta-glucocerebrosidase (Option B). This deficiency leads to the accumulation of glucocerebroside within the lysosomes of macrophages, creating the characteristic "Gaucher cells" with a "wrinkled tissue paper" appearance. Beta-galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Option A) is the cause of Krabbe disease. Glucose-6-phosphate (Option C) is a metabolic intermediate in glycolysis, and its phosphatase is deficient in Von Gierke's disease. Alpha-glucocerebrosidase is not the standard enzyme involved. Clinically, Gaucher disease presents with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and bone crises. Therefore, because the specific metabolic block at the level of glucocerebroside breakdown defines this syndrome, Beta-glucocerebrosidase is the correct enzyme. Treatment involves enzyme replacement therapy to clear the accumulated lipids and manage symptoms
questions.learning: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, following an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. It is caused by a definitive deficiency in the enzyme Beta-glucocerebrosidase (Option B).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy comes with complaints of right ear pain, difficulty in opening the mouth, painful swallowing, and fever. The oral cavity examination reveals the following. The external facial examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Quinsy

The given clinical scenario describes a child with fever, otalgia, trismus, and odynophagia with a normal external facial examination. The oral cavity shows congested and edematous tonsil and tonsillar pillars with edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. These findings are highly suggestive of quinsy (peritonsillar abscess).

It is the collection of pus in the peritonsillar space between the fibrous capsule of the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both aerobic and anaerobic organisms are seen.

Patient presents with fever, unilateral throat pain, odynophagia, hot potato voice, torticollis, foul breath, referred otalgia through glossopharyngeal nerve and trismus due to spasm of pterygoid muscles.

Oral cavity examination may show congested and edematous tonsils, pillars, and soft palate on the involved side. Edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. Pus may be seen on the tonsillar region. Jugulodigastric lymph nodes may be enlarged.

The management of quinsy is by antibiotics and incision and drainage to drain the abscess followed by interval tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks later.

Rare complications seen are parapharyngeal abscess, edema of the larynx, septicemia, lung abscess, or jugular vein thrombosis.

Other options:

Option A: Pharyngitis presents with fever, throat pain, enlarged tonsils, and lymphoid follicles on the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Option B: Parotid abscess occurs due to the suppuration of parotid space. It presents with swelling, redness, firmness, and tenderness in the parotid area and at the angle of the mandible. It is usually unilateral, but bilateral abscesses can occur. Due to the thick capsule, fluctuation is often difficult to elicit.

Option C: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the spleen. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis

The super scan appearance is due to increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis.

Diffuse osteoblastic metastatic diseases such as carcinoma breast and prostate carcinoma lead to a generalized increase in the skeletal uptake relative to soft tissue and absent or faint renal activity on a bone scan. This is known as a super scan. It may also be seen in generalized bone diseases such as hyperparathyroidism.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the maximum number of occupants allowed in a two-room house to prevent overcrowding?
questions.explanation: The public health standards for housing define overcrowding based on the number of rooms and the floor area relative to the number of occupants. According to standard Indian health guidelines (based on the Model Building Bye-laws), the accepted occupancy limit to prevent overcrowding in a two-room house is 3 people (Option B). Option A (2 people) is the limit for a one-room house. Option C (4 people) would typically require 2.5 to 3 rooms depending on the specific age of the occupants (children count as half). Option D (5 people) is excessive for two standard rooms. Overcrowding is a significant risk factor for the transmission of infectious diseases, particularly respiratory infections like TB and meningitis. Therefore, for the purpose of housing and health standards, 3 people is the definitive maximum capacity for a two-room dwelling

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A mother notices a swelling in the abdomen of her 3-year-old child while bathing him. He had a history of hematuria two weeks back which resolved spontaneously. On examination, a right-sided reniform ballotable mass was found. What all investigations will you do?

1. CECT
2. PET-CT
3. 24-hour urinary VMA
4. FNAC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, and 3

The clinical features of hematuria and a ballotable renal mass in a 3-year-old child are suggestive of Wilms tumor (Nephroblastoma). CECT abdomen is used to identify the extent of the tumor, integrity of the other kidney, and metastasis. Wilms tumor is metabolically active and can concentrate fluorodeoxyglucose therefore PET/CT is also helpful to identify regional spread and metastatic lesions. A biopsy is discouraged as it may lead to disease upstaging. 24-hour urinary vanillyl mandelic acid is measured to exclude neuroblastoma, which is an important differential diagnosis of Wilms tumor.

Wilms tumor is the most common primary malignant renal tumor in children, typically affecting children less than 5 years. After neuroblastoma, it is the second most common malignant abdominal tumor in childhood. It most commonly presents as an asymptomatic abdominal mass.  Other findings include hypertension, abdominal pain, gross painless hematuria, and constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss.

Imaging studies done to diagnose Wilms tumor include plain radiography, USG, and CT of the abdomen to demonstrate the renal mass. USG with doppler study of renal veins is useful in the evaluation of collecting system and to look for tumor thrombi in renal veins and inferior vena cava. A chest CT is done preoperatively to screen for pulmonary metastasis. A positron emission tomography (PET) scan is useful in identifying regional spread and metastatic lesions. A biopsy is discouraged in this condition as it results in disease upstaging, and is considered only in cases of unusual presentation or imaging.

Neuroblastoma is an important differential diagnosis to consider, as it can present similarly to Wilms tumor. It is usually seen in preschool-aged children and commonly presents as a palpable abdominal mass. The retroperitoneum is the most common site for this tumor. Therefore, it is essential to test for elevated vanillyl mandelic acid (VMA) in the urine in this patient to rule out neuroblastoma.

Children's oncology group (previously known as National Wilms Tumor study group) staging system for Wilms tumor:

Stage I
Tumour confined to the kidney and completely resected with negative lymph nodes.

Stage II
Tumour extends beyond the kidney but is completely resected with negative margins and lymph nodes.

Stage III
Residual tumour present following surgery confined to the abdomen, including gross or microscopic tumour.

Stage IV
Hematogenous metastases (lung, liver, bone, brain, etc.) or lymph node metastases outside the abdominopelvic region.

Stage V
Metastasis to opposite kidney (bilateral renal involvement).

Treatment: Surgery and chemotherapy, with or without radiotherapy, are the mainstays of treatment.

• Radical nephrectomy is the standard surgical procedure done. Routine sampling of the para-aortic, hilar, and paracaval lymph nodes should be done.
• Nephron-sparing nephrectomy is done for children with bilateral disease or with a solitary kidney. Preoperative chemotherapy can be used in these cases to induce tumor shrinkage.
• The classical chemotherapy includes vincristine and dactinomycin with the addition of Adriamycin(Doxorubicin).
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 3 The clinical features of hematuria and a ballotable renal mass in a 3-year-old child are suggestive of Wilms tumor (Nephroblastoma). CECT abdomen is used to identify the extent of the tumor, integrity of the other kidney, and metastasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient's plasma has high levels of interferon beta. He most likely has an infection due to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Virus

Interferon-beta is secreted during infection due to viruses.

Interferons are classified as cytokines. Interferons are non-toxic, non-antigenic and species-specific molecules. They are inactivated by proteases. They are stable at pH over 2-10, except INF-γ (labile at pH 2) and are non-dialysable and non-sedimentable.

There are three types of interferons - α, β and γ. IFN-α or leukocyte interferon is produced by leucocytes. It has antiviral activity, is immunoregulaotry and antiproliferative. IFN-β or fibroblast interferon is produced by fibroblasts and epithelial cells. It has antiviral activity and is thus increased in viral infections. It enhances MHC class 1 and NK cell activity. IFN-γ or immune interferon is produced by T-lymphocytes, NK cells . It activates macrophages, increases neutrophil function, enhances both MHC class 1 and class II expression and has anti-proliferative (anti-tumour) functions.
questions.learning: Virus Interferon-beta is secreted during infection due to viruses. Interferons are classified as cytokines.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following anaesthetic agents act on NMDA receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ketamine

Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that inhibits NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors resulting in a decrease in excitatory stimulation by glutamate in the brain. It is a strong analgesic and amnestic agent.

On the cardiovascular system, it directly has a cardio-depressive effect and indirectly stimulates it by activating the sympathetic system and inhibiting the vagus nerve. It predominantly shows a stimulatory effect hence causing tachycardia, increased cardiac output, and increased systemic and pulmonary hypertension.

On the respiratory system, it has a bronchodilator effect on bronchial smooth muscles. It increases salivary secretion and bronchial secretion. It also acts on other systems and increases the intracranial and intraocular pressures.

Uses:

* Ketamine is the intravenous agent of choice for patients with shock, low cardiac output states, and reactive airway diseases.

* It is also used in patients with congenital heart diseases, especially with right-to-left shunts

* Perioperative analgesia

Ketamine should be avoided in patients with a history of seizures, psychiatric illness, or vascular aneurysms. It is also contraindicated in open-eye injuries and eye surgeries.

Adverse effects:

* Hallucination is the most common side effect of ketamine.

* Emergence reaction (vivid dreaming, illusion, etc)

* Increases brain oxygen consumption and metabolic rate leading to increased intracranial tension.

Other options:

Option A: Propofol facilitates the inhibitory neurotransmission by action on GABA-A receptors. It has a rapid onset of action (within 15 sec). Induction dose is usually 1-2 mg/ kg and the maintenance dose is 100-200 µg/ kg/ min. Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion and appears as a milky white liquid. It has antiemetic properties which help reduce post-operative nausea and vomiting.

Option C: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine that facilitates GABA-A receptors' action by increasing the frequency of opening of GABA-mediated chloride channels. It is used in treating seizures and is used in daycare surgeries as an induction agent due to its short half-life.

Option D: Thiopentone sodium belongs to the barbiturate group which acts on the GABA-A receptors. This site is separate from the GABA-A site to which benzodiazepines bind. They potentiate the action of GABA in increasing the duration of openings of chloride-specific ion channels.
questions.learning: Ketamine Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that inhibits NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors resulting in a decrease in excitatory stimulation by glutamate in the brain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for wound infection? 1. Malnutrition 2. Poor perfusion 3. Antibodies 4. Foreign body material Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Surgical site infection (SSI) develops when bacterial contamination overcomes host defense mechanisms. The risk depends on host factors (e.g., nutrition, tissue perfusion, immune status) and local wound factors (e.g., foreign bodies, dead tissue). Optimizing these factors before and after surgery reduces the incidence of wound infection.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Malnutrition ✅

• Protein-calorie malnutrition impairs collagen synthesis, immune function, and wound healing, increasing the risk of infection.

• 2. Poor perfusion ✅

• Reduced tissue oxygenation decreases delivery of immune cells and antibiotics to the wound, predisposing to infection.

• 3. Antibodies ❌

• Antibodies are protective against infection and are not a risk factor.

• 4. Foreign body material ✅

• Foreign materials (e.g., sutures, prostheses, retained debris) facilitate bacterial adherence and biofilm formation, markedly increasing infection risk.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Surgical site infection (SSI) develops when bacterial contamination overcomes host defense mechanisms. The risk depends on host factors (e.g., nutrition, tissue perfusion, immune status) and local wound factors (e.g., foreign bodies, dead tissue).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: By which mechanism does gene repair occur when mediated by CRISPR-Cas9?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-homologous end joining

Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the major mechanism used by CRISPR-Cas9 for gene repair.

The CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) are clustered palindromic sequences found in many bacteria. It is a form of acquired immunity to infection by bacteriophages which complements the system of restriction endonucleases and methylases. CRISPR uses RNA-based targeting to bring the Cas9 endonuclease to foreign (or any complementary) DNA. Within bacteria this CRISPR-RNA-Cas9 complex then degrades and inactivates the targeted DNA.

The CRISPR system has been adapted for use in eukaryotic cells for gene deletion, gene editing and even modulation of gene transcription.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who presents with recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis after excessive alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis (vomiting blood) shortly after heavy alcohol use is pathognomonic for Mallory-Weiss syndrome. This condition involves non-transmural mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction, caused by the sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure during forceful retching. Esophageal carcinoma (Option B) typically presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss in older adults rather than acute alcohol-related hematemesis. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a motility disorder characterized by a "bird's beak" appearance on barium swallow and chronic difficulty swallowing. Boerhaave's syndrome (Option D) is a much more severe condition involving transmural rupture of the esophagus, often presenting with excruciating chest pain, shock, and subcutaneous emphysema rather than simple hematemesis. Most Mallory-Weiss tears are self-limiting and heal within a few days with supportive care, though severe bleeding may require endoscopic intervention. Therefore, based on the specific temporal relationship with alcohol and vomiting, Mallory-Weiss is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical history of recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis (vomiting blood) shortly after heavy alcohol use is pathognomonic for Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the WHO, what percentage of immunization coverage is needed for eradication of measles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 96%

According to the WHO, eradication of measles requires achieving an immunization coverage of at least 96% of children under 1 year of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the qSOFA score components?
questions.explanation: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a bedside tool designed to identify patients outside of the ICU who are at high risk for poor outcomes due to suspected sepsis. It consists of exactly three clinical components: Respiratory rate breaths per minute (Option A) Altered mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale ) (Option C) Systolic blood pressure mmHg (Option D) LDH (Option B) is NOT a component of the qSOFA score. While lactate is an important biomarker used in the full SOFA score and in defining septic shock, the qSOFA was specifically created to rely solely on physical exam findings and vital signs, requiring no laboratory tests at all for its calculation. A score of indicates a higher risk of prolonged ICU stay or in-hospital mortality. Therefore, LDH is the correct "except" choice as it is a laboratory value
questions.learning: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a bedside tool designed to identify patients outside of the ICU who are at high risk for poor outcomes due to suspected sepsis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: ICER is a unit for which of the following economic analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cost effectiveness

ICER is a unit for Cost-effectiveness.

Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis (ICER) is a difference in cost/difference in effectiveness. Effectiveness is usually measured in Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs), which reflect both the quality and quantity of life.

The Cost-effectiveness analysis measures the costs and outcomes of different interventions and calculates the cost-effectiveness ratio. The benefits of the health care system are expressed in terms of results achieved (Eg, the number of lives saved or the number of days free from disease). This is a more promising tool in the health field than cost-benefit analysis. However, in many cases, it is not possible to use cost-effective analysis.

Other options:

Option B: Cost-benefit analysis: Here, the economic benefits of any program are compared with the cost of the program. The benefits are expressed in monetary terms (whereas in cost-effectiveness analysis, it is expressed in terms of results achieved)to identify whether it is economically sound and to select the best one from several alternate programs. The main drawback of this technique is that the benefits of a particular program in the health field cannot always be expressed in monetary terms. Usually, the benefits are expressed in terms of births or deaths prevented or illnesses avoided or overcome.

Option C: Cost-utility: compares the cost of a program to the health improvement it provides.

Option D: Cost margin: the difference between a product's revenues and how much it costs to make.
questions.learning: Cost effectiveness ICER is a unit for Cost-effectiveness. Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis (ICER) is a difference in cost/difference in effectiveness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic female who was treated with steroids and remdevisir for COVID now presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is a non-contagious fungal disease most commonly caused by Rhizopus oryzae that is acquired through the inhalation of fungal spores from air. It may occur during COVID infection or after a few weeks (usually around the 3rd week) of recovery from it. Reasons for increase in mucormycosis cases in COVID patients are:

* Uncontrolled hyperglycemia due to any reason. COVID per se has a tendency to worsen diabetes and also precipitate diabetes in previously normal individuals.

* Misuse and irrational use of steroids. Steroid overuse can cause new-onset diabetes.

* Leucopenia associated with COVID

* Prolonged ICU stay, unhygienic humidifiers, and irrational use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

* Pre-existing comorbidities such as hematological malignancies, use of immunosuppressants, and solid organ transplantation.

A high index of suspicion is required for the early diagnosis of mucormycosis. Checklist of sentinel signs/ symptoms of mucormycosis to be monitored in patients admitted with COVID-19 are:

* Relatively early disease (Nose and sinuses):

* Headache and nasal obstruction (especially if severe or persistent and not responding to medications)

* Nasal crusting, brownish or blood-tinged nasal discharge

* Facial pain, pain over sinuses

* Paraesthesia/ loss of sensation over half of the face

* Discoloration of the skin or localized facial puffiness

* Loosening of teeth, discoloration, ulceration, or eschar over the palate

* Moderately advanced disease (Eye/orbital involvement):

* Eye swelling or redness, eye pain

* Double vision, drooping of the eyelid, blurring, and loss of vision.

* Very advanced disease (Intracranial involvement):

* Involvement of cranial nerves II-VI suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis

* Signs of MCA thrombosis

Diagnosis:

* KOH mount and microscopy

* Histopathology of debrided tissue shows presence of ribbon-like aseptate hyphae (5-15 µ thick) branching at right angles.

* Culture can be done but treatment should be started on clinical suspicion.

* CT of sinuses, CT chest for suspected pulmonary involvement ( presence of more than 10 nodules, reverse halo sign are highly suggestive of mucor), and MRI brain to look for the extent of intracranial involvement.

Management:

* Treatment of co-morbid illness and strict glycemic control.

* Anti-fungal therapy started early on high clinical suspicion even prior to microbiological confirmation can reduce mortality. Treatment involves a combination of surgical debridement and antifungal therapy.

* Liposomal Amphotericin B (5-10mg/kg) is the drug of choice and has to be continued for 3-6 weeks. It should be diluted in 5% dextrose and is incompatible with normal saline and Ringer lactate. Step-down therapy to be done with oral posaconazole or isavuconazole. Renal function must be monitored during the entire treatment period.

* Early surgical debridement after stabilization of systemic illness and ensuring facilities for post-surgical care and ventilation.

Other options:

Option A: Invasive aspergillosis leads to the formation of black or greyish membrane in the nasal mucosa. The maxillary sinus may contain a fungus ball containing semisolid cheesy-white or blackish material.

Option C: Foreign body nose presents with foul-smelling unilateral discharge.

Option D: Rhinosporidiosis is a granulomatous condition caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and presents with nasal discharge, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction by a polypoidal mass.
questions.learning: Mucormycosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a non-contagious fungal disease most commonly caused by Rhizopus oryzae that is acquired through the inhalation of fungal spores from air.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person dies suddenly while their family is abroad, and the viscera is preserved during autopsy. Which substances can still be detected in the visceral organs even if the person did not consume them immediately before death?
questions.explanation: Alcohol (ethanol) is unique because it can be detected in viscera even if not consumed before death. This is due to postmortem production of alcohol by bacterial fermentation. After death, microorganisms such as Clostridium and Candida act on carbohydrates present in body tissues, leading to the formation of ethanol. This process is more common in decomposed bodies and can result in detectable alcohol levels despite no premortem intake. Therefore, the presence of alcohol in viscera must be interpreted carefully in forensic analysis, distinguishing between ante-mortem ingestion and post-mortem formation. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Morphine: Rapidly metabolized and can only be detected if taken before death. (B) Aconite: Unstable and decomposes quickly postmortem, making detection difficult unless recently ingested. (C) Arsenic: A cumulative poison but not produced postmortem; it is detectable only if consumed during life. Thus, only alcohol can appear in viscera without prior ingestion, making option (D) correct
questions.learning: Alcohol (ethanol) is unique because it can be detected in viscera even if not consumed before death. This is due to postmortem production of alcohol by bacterial fermentation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is true about gall bladder carcinoma?
options: Palpable abdominal lump is the earliest sign
Clinical presentation of gall stones can be distinguished from gall bladder cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Median survival is 6 months

Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that is seen in the elderly. It is associated with a poor prognosis and median survival is less than 6 months.

Gallbladder carcinoma is indistinguishable from cholecystitis or cholelithiasis (option C). It is usually diagnosed when patients undergo cholecystectomy for gallstones. Its clinical features include right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Jaundice, palpable mass, and anorexia are late features (options A and B). CA 19-9 is elevated in the carcinoma gallbladder and is used for monitoring.

The preoperative diagnosis is often made on ultrasonography and followed up by a CT scan or MRI/ Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

A percutaneous biopsy under radiological guidance is done for pathological examination. PET scanning helps in detecting metastatic disease.

In select cases, a laparoscopic examination is useful in staging the disease. Laparoscopy can also detect peritoneal or liver metastases. The most important prognostic factor is the depth of invasion (T-stage).
questions.learning: Median survival is 6 months Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that is seen in the elderly. It is associated with a poor prognosis and median survival is less than 6 months.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustained burns involving 25% of his body while on duty. He later developed infections and related complications. Under the ESI Act, which of the following benefits is he entitled to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended Sickness benefit

The patient developed a long-term complication (infections after burns) due to a serious condition, and under the ESI Act, such chronic or prolonged illnesses fall under the category of extended sickness benefit.

Extended sickness benefit covers those with more than 20% burns with infection or complication. Leave is given up to a maximum period of two years. The diseases for which extended sickness benefits are applied are TB, leprosy, empyema, HIV, malignancies, plegias, etc. During this period, 80 per cent of the wages are paid.

ESI act was amended to provide cash and medical benefits to employees during sickness, maternity, and employment injury. People with monthly earnings up to 21,000 are covered under this scheme. Cash benefits are made through branches and cash offices. The medical benefits are made available through ESI dispensaries, clinics, hospitals, etc. The benefits provided to the insured persons are:

* Medical benefits - Complete medical care is provided to the insured person and his/ her family members.

* Sickness benefits - include a periodic cash payment for 91 days to the insured sick person. 70% of the average daily wages is given as the daily rate if the person is under medical treatment.

* Enhanced sickness benefit - includes 14 days of leave given for tubectomy and 7 days of leave for vasectomy. The amount payable is equal to the full wages.

* Maternity benefits - cash payments equal to full wages are paid to the insured person for up to 26 weeks in cases of pregnancy.

* Disablement benefit - cash payment and free medical treatment are given for temporary or permanent disablements and occupational diseases.

* Dependant's benefit - if an employment injury causes the death of the insured person, the dependants are eligible for periodic payments.

* Funeral expenses of Rs 15000 are payable to the dependants.

* Rehabilitation allowance - the insured person and the family members continue to get medical treatment after permanent disablement and retirement.
questions.learning: Extended Sickness benefit — The patient developed a long-term complication (infections after burns) due to a serious condition, and under the ESI Act, such chronic or prolonged illnesses fall under the category of extended sickness benefit.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 47-year-old man with a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia with a blood type O negative blood group presents to the transplant clinic to discuss proceeding with an allogeneic stem cell transplant. Which of the following would be an optimal donor?
options: His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is otherwise healthy and is blood type O+
An HLA identical matched unrelated donor who is blood type O–
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is otherwise healthy and is blood type O+

In the case of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), allogeneic stem cell transplants are the treatment of choice. His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is blood type O positive would be the best choice.

Other options:

Option A: An identical twin brother would not be the donor of choice. The therapeutic benefit of stem cell transplant in hematological malignancies is due to the graft-versus-leukemia (GvL). Donor T lymphocytes attack malignant hematopoietic stem cells of the recipient that remain after high-dose chemotherapy. Despite having a low rate of graft versus host disease (GvHD), stem cells from an identical twin do not have a desirable degree of GvL effect, leading to higher rates of recurrence post-transplant.

Option B: Autologous (umbilical cord transplant) is not recommended as higher rates of relapse have been reported.

Option D: An HLA identical sibling is preferred over an unrelated HLA identical donor because there is a greater chance of matching for minor histocompatibility complex (mHC). This reduces the risk of GvHD. ABO compatibility is also important to consider, but a minor ABO mismatch (Rh mismatch) doesn't have any impact on hemolysis, graft-versus-host disease, or survival.
questions.learning: His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is otherwise healthy and is blood type O+ In the case of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), allogeneic stem cell transplants are the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child shows hyperflexible fingers and can touch the dorsum of the hand with an extended wrist. The child also demonstrates the sign shown in the image. On cardiac auscultation, a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is heard after the first heart sound. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This clinical vignette is a classic "pattern recognition" question for medical exams, combining dermatological, musculoskeletal, and cardiac findings. Key Clinical Features from the Prompt: 1. Gorlin Sign (Image): The child touching the tip of the nose with the tongue is known as the Gorlin sign. It is present in approximately 50% of EDS patients due to a hypermobile tongue/frenulum (but only 10% of the normal population). 2. Joint Hypermobility: Touching the dorsum of the hand with an extended wrist is a clear indicator of systemic joint hyperlaxity (a key component of the Beighton Score). 3. Cardiac Auscultation: A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is the classic description of Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP), which is frequently associated with connective tissue disorders like EDS. Why the other options are wrong: (B) Marfan's syndrome: While Marfan's also features hypermobility and MVP, the Gorlin sign is highly characteristic of EDS. Marfan's typically presents with tall stature, arachnodactyly (long fingers), and ectopia lentis (upward lens dislocation), which are not mentioned here. (C) Loeys-Dietz syndrome: This involves aggressive arterial aneurysms and a bifid uvula or hypertelorism. While it is a connective tissue disorder, it doesn't classically present with the Gorlin sign. (D) Osteogenesis imperfecta: This is characterized by blue sclera, multiple bone fractures, and hearing loss. While there is some joint laxity, the core skeletal and ocular features are missing from this case
questions.learning: This clinical vignette is a classic "pattern recognition" question for medical exams, combining dermatological, musculoskeletal, and cardiac findings.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Defect at the level of the optic chiasma will result in which of the following visual field defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bitemporal hemianopia

Lesions at the level of the optic chiasma cause bitemporal hemianopia.

The Nasal fibers of each retina decussate at the optic chiasma. Hence, a lesion at this level affects the temporal quadrants of both eyes.

The optic chiasma lies directly above the tuberculum and diaphragma sellae & is affected in

• Pituitary adenoma
• Craniopharyngioma
• Meningioma
• Gliomas
• Multiple sclerosis, sarcoidosis

Option A: Central scotoma is seen in lesions affecting the optic disc (intraocular part of optic nerve) such as ethambutol toxic neuropathy, macular degeneration and lesions of visual cortex with bilateral homonymous macular defects.

Option C: Binasal hemianopia is seen in lesions affecting bilateral lateral chiasma where the temporal fibers of both the retina continue forward without crossing. This affects vision in the nasal quadrants of both eyes.
questions.learning: Bitemporal hemianopia Lesions at the level of the optic chiasma cause bitemporal hemianopia. The Nasal fibers of each retina decussate at the optic chiasma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Match the following with the nerve supply of external ear:
options: A - Auriculotemporal nerve; B - Greater auricular nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve
A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve
A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Facial and Vagus nerve; C - Auriculotemporal nerve
A - Facial and Vagus nerve; B - Greater auricular nerve; C - Auriculotemporal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve

The correctly matched option regarding the nerve supply of the pinna is option B: A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve.

The nerve supply of the pinna is provided by the following:

• Greater auricular nerve (A) supplies most of the medial surface of the pinna and the posterior part of the lateral surface.
• Lesser occipital nerve supplies the upper part of the medial surface.
• Auriculotemporal nerve  (B) supplies the tragal area and crus helix.
• Arnold's nerve (C) i.e. the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X) supplies the concha and the corresponding area on the medial surface.
• Facial nerve (CN VII) (C) which is distributed along with Arnold's nerve also supplies the concha and the retro auricular groove.

The nerve supply has been demonstrated in the image below.
