questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Serum β-hCG is markedly elevated. Endometrial biopsy shows nuclear enlargement with hyperchromasia, loss of nuclear polarity, and intraluminal papillary projections of glandular epithelium. No chorionic villi are identified in the curettage specimen. Which of the following statements about this finding is most accurate?
options: Presence of this reaction on curettage confirms intrauterine pregnancy
Absence of this reaction excludes ectopic pregnancy
This reaction can mimic clear cell carcinoma of the endometrium histologically
This reaction is driven by rising FSH levels in early pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. This reaction can mimic clear cell carcinoma of the endometrium histologically

This patient demonstrates the Arias-Stella reaction, a benign hypersecretory change of the endometrium caused by exposure to high levels of β-hCG and progesterone during pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy and gestational trophoblastic disease.

Histologic features include:

• Nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia
• Loss of nuclear polarity
• Cytoplasmic vacuolization
• Papillary glandular projections

Because these atypical changes can appear markedly pleomorphic, the Arias-Stella reaction may mimic clear cell carcinoma histologically.

Important concepts:

• Presence of Arias-Stella reaction indicates exposure to pregnancy-related hormones but does not confirm intrauterine pregnancy
• It may occur in ectopic pregnancy
• Absence of chorionic villi in curettage raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or trophoblastic disease
• The reaction is hormonally driven primarily by β-hCG/progesterone effects, not FSH
questions.learning: This reaction can mimic clear cell carcinoma of the endometrium histologically This patient demonstrates the Arias-Stella reaction, a benign hypersecretory change of the endometrium caused by exposure to high levels of β-hCG and progesterone during…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 66-year-old man presents with urinary symptoms, back pain, elevated PSA, radiolucent pelvic bone lesions on X-ray, and enlarged lower abdominal lymph nodes on MRI, suggestive of advanced prostate cancer with bone metastases and nodal involvement. Which medication is indicated for treatment in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, characterized by elevated PSA and osteoblastic bone lesions. The mainstay of management for advanced disease is Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) to lower testosterone levels. Goserelin (Option C) is a Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) agonist used for this purpose. It initially causes a surge in LH and FSH, followed by downregulation of the pituitary receptors, which effectively leads to chemical castration. Anastrozole (Option A) is an aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer. Desogestrel (Option B) is a progestogen used for female contraception. Oxandrolone (Option D) is an anabolic steroid which would be contraindicated in prostate cancer as it could stimulate tumor growth. Therefore, Goserelin is the correct pharmacological choice for suppressing the hormonal drive of the malignancy. ADT often provides significant symptomatic relief and can stabilize metastatic bone disease in elderly patients with prostate adenocarcinoma. Consequently, Goserelin is a standard component of systemic treatment protocols for these patients
questions.learning: The patient presents with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, characterized by elevated PSA and osteoblastic bone lesions. The mainstay of management for advanced disease is Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) to lower testosterone levels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue. Laboratory investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 5.9 g/dL, increased red cell distribution width (RDW) and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), along with low serum ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The laboratory findings are diagnostic for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The patient has severe anemia (Hb 5.9) characterized by increased Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW), which indicates anisocytosis (variation in cell size). The biochemical hallmark of IDA is low Ferritin (depleted iron stores) and increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC), as the body tries to increase iron uptake. Sideroblastic anemia (Option A) would show increased ferritin and decreased TIBC. Megaloblastic anemia (Option C) is macrocystic and unrelated to these specific iron parameters. Hemolytic anemia (Option D) usually presents with increased bilirubin and reticulocytes. IDA is the most common cause of anemia worldwide, often due to nutritional deficiency or chronic blood loss (e.g., from hookworms or GI malignancy). Management involves identifying the source of loss and oral iron supplementation. Recognizing the specific pattern of low ferritin and high TIBC is critical for medical licensing examinations
questions.learning: The laboratory findings are diagnostic for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The patient has severe anemia (Hb 5.9) characterized by increased Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW), which indicates anisocytosis (variation in cell size).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old patient was brought to the casualty ward with high fever and pain abdomen. He had a history of bloody diarrhea for several months. His past history was negative for long-term medications and previous surgeries. The abdominal X-ray image obtained is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxic megacolon

The clinical scenario and the radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon.

Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. Abdominal radiography shows transverse or right colonic dilation of >6 cm and loss of haustrations. It is usually associated with ulcerative colitis as indicated by history of chronic bloody diarrhoea.

It can be triggered by electrolyte imbalance and narcotics which interfere with gut motility. Features of secondary bacterial infecton and sepsis may be present. It can be complicated by intestinal perforation.

It usually resolves with supportive treatment (correcting electrolyte imbalance, fluids, and bowel rest) and medical therapy which includes glucocorticoids, anti-inflammatory drugs, and antibiotics. However, an urgent colectomy is indicated in patients who do not show signs of improvement.

Indications for urgent surgery include:

• Frank intraperitoneal peritonitis, secondary to perforation
• Life-threatening hemorrhage or increasing transfusion requirements
• Worsening systemic toxicity
• Worsening colonic dilatation

Other options:

Option B: Volvulus occurs when the air-filled segment of the colon twists around the mesentery. The sigmoid colon is the most commonly involved part of the large intestine (90%). The patient can present with abdominal distension, nausea and vomiting. X-ray abdomen shows a bent inner tube or coffee bean appearance.

Option C: Ogilvie syndrome, also known as colonic pseudo-obstruction is a functional disorder with colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction. It occurs commonly in hospitalized patients and is associated with narcotics, bed rest and comorbid disease. X-ray shows dilatation of the colon (predominantly transverse colon) with absent mechanical obstruction.

Option D: Pneumatosis intestinalis is the presence of gas within the bowel wall seen in any part of the GI tract but most commonly in the jejunum. It is a pathognomic feature of necrotizing enterocolitis. X-ray of the abdomen will show intramural gas in the bowel.
questions.learning: Toxic megacolon — The clinical scenario and the radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon. Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient is suffering from a rare disease with mitochondrial inheritance. This can be inherited from which of the following members?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mother

Diseases with mitochondrial inheritance are inherited exclusively from the affected mother.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

* Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.

* Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.

* 80% of mitochondrial DNA codes for mitochondrial RNA, and therefore most mitochondrial DNA mutations lead to functional problems, which may be manifested as muscle disorders.

Examples include: Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes (MELAS), Leigh Syndrome

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old girl is brought with breast development and pubic hair noticed by her mother over the past 3 months. She also has irregular café-au-lait macules on her trunk and a history of a pathological fracture of the femur. Her LH and FSH levels are found to be suppressed. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?
options: This is the most common cause of precocious puberty in girls and is gonadotropin dependent
The precocious puberty is driven by autonomous ovarian estrogen secretion and LH/FSH are expectedly low
Hypothalamic hamartoma is the most common cause of this specific syndrome
This condition involves monostotic fibrous dysplasia as its skeletal manifestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The precocious puberty is driven by autonomous ovarian estrogen secretion and LH/FSH are expectedly low

The clinical triad of precocious puberty + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait macules is diagnostic of McCune-Albright Syndrome.

McCune-Albright Syndrome features:

• Precocious puberty due to ↑ estrogen (autonomous ovarian secretion)
• Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (not monostotic)
• Café-au-lait macules
• LH and FSH are suppressed.

The suppressed gonadotropins confirm peripheral precocious puberty. Idiopathic is the most common cause for precocious puberty in girls overall, but it is gonadotropin dependent (elevated LH/FSH).
questions.learning: The precocious puberty is driven by autonomous ovarian estrogen secretion and LH/FSH are expectedly low The clinical triad of precocious puberty + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait macules is diagnostic of McCune-Albright Syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure primarily facilitates the pronation and supination movements of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Supination and pronation are the unique rotational movements of the forearm where the radius rotates around the ulna. These movements occur specifically at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints, which are classified as pivot (trochoid) joints. In a pivot joint, a rounded bone rotates within a ring formed by another bone and a ligament. A saddle joint (Option B), such as the first carpometacarpal joint, allows for flexion, extension, and opposition but not rotation. An ellipsoid joint (Option C), like the wrist joint, allows for biaxial movement but lacks independent rotation. A ball and socket joint (Option D), such as the shoulder or hip, is multiaxial but is not the specific joint type responsible for the distinct forearm rotation between the radius and ulna. Thus, the anatomical design of the pivot joint at the radioulnar articulation is the primary structure enabling pronation and supination
questions.learning: Supination and pronation are the unique rotational movements of the forearm where the radius rotates around the ulna. These movements occur specifically at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints, which are classified as pivot (trochoid) joints.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with a recent history of travel to Africa presents with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations identify an infecting organism that possesses a unique ability to adhere to vascular endothelium, enabling sequestration within blood vessels and thereby evading splenic clearance. What is this phenomenon known as?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of travel to Africa, fever, and neurological deficits (Cerebral Malaria) combined with the blood smear point to Plasmodium falciparum infection. A unique and lethal property of P. falciparum is cytoadherence. This occurs when the parasite expresses proteins (like PfEMP-1) on the surface of infected red blood cells (iRBCs), forming "knobs." These knobs bind to endothelial receptors (like ICAM-1 or CD36) in capillary beds. This sequestration prevents the iRBCs from passing through the spleen, where they would be cleared by macrophages. Rosetting (Option A) is the adherence of iRBCs to uninfected RBCs, which also contributes to microvascular obstruction. Agglutination (Option B) is a general term for cell clumping. Schizogony (Option D) is the asexual reproductive phase within the host. Sequestration in the brain leads to the confusion and coma seen in cerebral malaria. Understanding these mechanical properties of the parasite is critical for managing severe malaria and predicting its multisystem complications
questions.learning: The clinical history of travel to Africa, fever, and neurological deficits (Cerebral Malaria) combined with the blood smear point to Plasmodium falciparum infection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a stab wound over the right chest. The supine X-ray image of the patient is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right hemothorax

The history of stab injury to the right chest and the X-ray showing opacity of the right hemithorax, with a slight tracheal deviation towards the opposite side, indicates a diagnosis of right hemothorax.

In a plain chest radiograph, it's difficult to differentiate an acute hemothorax from other collections of pleural fluid as they are indistinguishable. As blood clots, it often leads to localisation, occasionally forming a fibrin body. Pleural thickening and calcification are acknowledged as potential consequences.

The following are the findings commonly seen in a case of hemothorax:

• Blunting of Costophrenic Angle: Hemothorax results in the accumulation of blood in the pleural cavity, causing the lung to collapse partially. This can lead to the blunting or obliteration of the costophrenic angle on the affected side.
• Increased Opacity: The presence of blood in the pleural space leads to increased opacity or density in the affected hemithorax. This can manifest as a homogenous shadowing that obscures the lung markings.
• Mediastinal Shift: Depending on the volume of blood in the pleural cavity, there may be a mediastinal shift towards the opposite side. However, in mild to moderate hemothorax, this may not be readily apparent on supine X-rays.
• Air-Fluid Level: In cases where there is concurrent pneumothorax (air in the pleural cavity), an air-fluid level may be visible, with the blood layering dependently and the air layer superiorly.
• Unilateral Findings: The abnormalities will typically be limited to one side of the chest, corresponding to the side of the hemothorax.

In cases of suspected hemothorax, a lateral decubitus or chest X-ray in erect position may be more sensitive for detection. Additionally, other imaging modalities such as ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) scans can provide more detailed information about the presence and extent of a hemothorax.

Other options:

The following image is characteristic of a pneumothorax (left-sided) with radiolucency over the left lung, lung collapse, and mediastinal shift on x-ray.

The given radiograph is a case of diaphragmatic hernia that shows elevation of the left hemidiaphragmatic line along with the bowel loops and stomach seen in the pleural cavity.

The following is an image of a right-sided pulmonary contusion post-blunt chest trauma. Note the increased opacity just below the horizontal fissure.
questions.learning: Right hemothorax — The history of stab injury to the right chest and the X-ray showing opacity of the right hemithorax, with a slight tracheal deviation towards the opposite side, indicates a diagnosis of right hemothorax.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village in Assam, a man is seen walking with the aid of a stick and has genu valgum. Several other villagers exhibit similar clinical features. What is the most probable underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: The occurrence of genu valgum (knock-knees) in clusters within a specific geographic region like Assam is a hallmark of endemic skeletal fluorosis. This condition is caused by the chronic ingestion of high levels of fluoride, typically found in contaminated drinking water. Elevated fluoride leads to increased bone density (osteosclerosis) but results in brittle bones, joint stiffness, and severe limb deformities that impair walking. Calcium deficiency (Option A) and Vitamin D deficiency (Option D) cause bone pain and rickets/osteomalacia but are less likely to present in localized regional clusters with these specific joint deformities. Vitamin C deficiency (Option B) causes scurvy, which presents with hemorrhage and impaired collagen synthesis rather than genu valgum. Prevention through water defluoridation is the primary strategy for managing this public health issue

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a painless, mobile, rubbery mass in her left breast. Histopathological examination of the lesion is shown in the provided image. Based on the clinical features and histological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a "mobile, rubbery mass" (often called a "breast mouse") in a young woman is classic for a fibroadenoma. Histologically, it is a biphasic tumor consisting of both proliferating connective tissue (stroma) and glandular epithelium. The glands are often compressed into slit-like spaces by the overgrowing stroma, creating the "intracanalicular" or "pericanalicular" patterns seen in the image. Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option A) would show nests of malignant cells with significant atypia invading the stroma. Phyllodes tumors (Option C) are also biphasic but show much higher stromal cellularity and characteristic "leaf-like" projections. Lobular carcinoma in-situ (Option D) shows small, uniform cells filling the acini without stromal invasion. Fibroadenomas are benign and do not increase the risk of cancer significantly. They are estrogen-sensitive and may enlarge during pregnancy or regress after menopause. Management typically involves reassurance or simple excision if the lesion is growing or causing patient anxiety
questions.learning: The clinical description of a "mobile, rubbery mass" (often called a "breast mouse") in a young woman is classic for a fibroadenoma. Histologically, it is a biphasic tumor consisting of both proliferating connective tissue (stroma) and glandular epithelium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: An individual is in an environment of a temperature of 47°C. What is the mechanism of heat loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sweating

The mechanism of heat loss in the given case where the surrounding temperatures are higher than the body temperature is sweating.

Different methods of heat loss:

• Radiation is heat loss in the form of infrared rays.
• Conduction is heat loss that occurs by direct contact with an object.
• Convection is heat loss resulting from air movement.

When the temperature of the surroundings is more than that of the skin, the body gains heat by both radiation and conduction. Under these conditions, the heat can be lost from the body only by evaporation or sweating.

When the body temperature is greater than the temperature of the surroundings, heat can be lost by radiation and conduction.
questions.learning: Sweating — The mechanism of heat loss in the given case where the surrounding temperatures are higher than the body temperature is sweating. Different methods of heat loss: • Radiation is heat loss in the form of infrared rays. • Conduction is heat loss…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis of the lesion that developed in a patient six months after undergoing cardiac surgery, as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a firm, raised, and thick scar that has grown well beyond the original boundaries of the surgical incision. This "outgrowth" beyond the initial wound margin is the defining characteristic of a Keloid (Option C). A hypertrophic scar (Option A) may be thick and raised but stays within the limits of the original incision and often regresses over time. An atrophic scar (Option B) is depressed below the skin surface, often seen after acne or chickenpox. A contracture (Option D) is a permanent shortening of skin and underlying tissue that restricts joint movement. Keloids result from an overgrowth of collagen (specifically Type III) during the healing process and are more common in darker skin types and on the sternum. They can be itchy or painful and are notoriously difficult to treat, often requiring intralesional steroids, silicone sheeting, or pressure therapy
questions.learning: The image depicts a firm, raised, and thick scar that has grown well beyond the original boundaries of the surgical incision. This "outgrowth" beyond the initial wound margin is the defining characteristic of a Keloid (Option C).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following clotting factors would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Factor 2

Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy.

Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues. This is done by the enzyme γ-glutamyl carboxylase with the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor.

This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue. This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. This enzyme is inhibited by warfarin.

Hence, warfarin indirectly inhibits the γ-carboxylation of vitamin K dependent clotting factors - Factors II, VII, IX, X by directly inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase. Thus leading to decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in these factors.
questions.learning: Factor 2 Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy. Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child is diagnosed with Gaucher's disease. Which statements are true? 1. Deficiency of sphingomyelinase 2. Deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase 3. Presence of foam cells 4. Crumpled tissue-paper cytoplasm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 4

Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase, leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages.

• Enzyme deficiency: β-glucocerebrosidase → impaired breakdown of glucocerebroside
• Affected cells: macrophages in liver, spleen, bone marrow
• Characteristic histology: macrophages with “crumpled tissue-paper” cytoplasm due to accumulated lipid

These macrophages are called Gaucher cells.

Why other statements are incorrect:

• Deficiency of sphingomyelinase → seen in Niemann–Pick disease, not Gaucher disease.
• Foam cells → typically described in Niemann–Pick disease due to sphingomyelin accumulation.
questions.learning: 2 and 4 Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase, leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages. • Enzyme deficiency: β-glucocerebrosidase → impaired breakdown of glucocerebroside…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 49-year-old well-off businesswoman presents with irregular, heavy bleeding. Her mother tells her this is normal at her age, but she seeks medical advice. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TVS

Abnormal Uterine Bleeding is common in perimenopausal women due to hormonal imbalance but must always be evaluated to rule out pathology.

Common causes are classified using the PALM-COEIN system.

| Structural causes | Non-structural causes

| ----------------- | ---------------------

| P – Polyp | C – Coagulopathy

| A – Adenomyosis | O – Ovulatory dysfunction

| L – Leiomyoma | E – Endometrial

| M – Malignancy | I – Iatrogenic

| | N – Not classified

In perimenopausal women (40+ years) with heavy bleeding: irregular cycles may be normal but heavy bleeding always requires evaluation with endometrial sampling to exclude malignancy, hyperplasia, and structural lesions before considering any treatment options. TVS is needed to see any structural cause and endometrial thickness.
questions.learning: TVS Abnormal Uterine Bleeding is common in perimenopausal women due to hormonal imbalance but must always be evaluated to rule out pathology. Common causes are classified using the PALM-COEIN system. | Structural causes | Non-structural causes |…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the given ECG.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Torsades de pointes

The given ECG shows broad QRS tachycardia with changing QRS morphology with every beat. The most likely diagnosis in this case is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or Torsades de pointes.

The causes of torsades de pointes include congenital long QT syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia), certain drugs, cardiac conditions like myocardial infarction and myocarditis, and endocrine disorders like hypothyroidism and pheochromocytoma.

Other options:

Ventricular fibrillation (option B) shows a completely disorganized rhythm with no identifiable waves on ECG, as shown in the image below.

Atrial flutter (option C) shows sawtooth appearance of the P-waves. This is due to rapid and successive atrial depolarization. The arrhythmia usually originates in the area of the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium. The ECG given below depicts atrial flutter, with the sawtooth P-waves most apparent in leads V1 and V2.

Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (option D) shows wide QRS complex tachycardia but with the same QRS morphology in each beat. It occurs most commonly due to structural heart diseases (cardiomyopathy, or scarring after myocardial infarction). The patients are at high risk for sudden cardiac death. The ECG given below shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
questions.learning: Torsades de pointes — The given ECG shows broad QRS tachycardia with changing QRS morphology with every beat. The most likely diagnosis in this case is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or Torsades de pointes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. On evaluation, a diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome is made. Which cranial nerves are compressed in this condition?
questions.explanation: Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. These include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Compression leads to total ophthalmoplegia (inability to move the eye) and ptosis. The maxillary nerve (V2) (Option B) is not affected because it passes through the foramen rotundum. The optic nerve (CN II) (Options C and D) is also spared because it enters the orbit through the separate optic canal. Thus, any syndrome resulting in extraocular muscle paralysis along with sensory loss in the forehead (V1) but sparing vision (CN II) and the mid-face (V2) specifically localizes to the superior orbital fissure
questions.learning: Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), caretakers are advised to return immediately to a health facility if: 1. Any sick child is not able to drink or breastfeed. 2. Fast breathing or difficult breathing, in a child who has no pneumonia. 3. Blood in stool, in a child with diarrhoea. 4. Conjunctivitis in a child with measles. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) strategy emphasizes caregiver counselling to recognize danger signs that require immediate return to a health facility. Early identification of these warning signs helps reduce morbidity and mortality from common childhood illnesses.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Any sick child is not able to drink or breastfeed. ✅

• This is a general danger sign requiring urgent medical evaluation.

• 2. Fast breathing or difficult breathing\, in a child who has no pneumonia. ✅

• Development of fast or difficult breathing after initial assessment may indicate progression to pneumonia and requires immediate reassessment.

• 3. Blood in stool\, in a child with diarrhoea. ✅

• Suggests dysentery (Shigella until proven otherwise) and requires prompt medical attention.

• 4. Conjunctivitis in a child with measles. ❌

• Conjunctivitis is a common feature of measles and, by itself, is not an indication for immediate return unless associated with severe eye complications (e.g., corneal clouding).
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) strategy emphasizes caregiver counselling to recognize danger signs that require immediate return to a health facility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Enalapril, an Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to its severe teratogenic effects. It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which is vital for fetal renal development. Exposure, particularly in the second and third trimesters, can cause fetal renal dysgenesis, leading to oligohydramnios and Potter sequence (lung hypoplasia and limb deformities). Methyldopa (Option A) is a preferred, safe choice for chronic hypertension in pregnancy. Labetalol (Option B) is commonly used for preeclampsia and hypertensive emergencies. Nifedipine (Option D) is a calcium channel blocker that is also considered safe for managing pregnancy-associated hypertension. Other ACE inhibitor risks include hypocalvaria (skull hypoplasia) and neonatal renal failure. Therefore, ACE inhibitors must be discontinued immediately when pregnancy is planned or confirmed to protect the fetus
questions.learning: Enalapril, an Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to its severe teratogenic effects. It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which is vital for fetal renal development.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman sustains a perineal tear during childbirth. Examination shows involvement of less than 50% of the external anal sphincter. According to the classification of perineal tears, how should this injury be described?
questions.explanation: Perineal tears are classified by the depth of tissue involvement. A Grade 3a tear involves less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter (EAS). Grade 2 (Option A) involves only the perineal muscles but spares the anal sphincter entirely. Grade 3b (Option B) involves more than 50% of the EAS thickness. Grade 4 (Option D) is the most severe, involving the entire anal sphincter complex (both external and internal) and the anal epithelium (mucosa). Proper identification is crucial because Grade 3 and 4 tears require specialized surgical repair to prevent future fecal incontinence. Given the specific clinical finding of <50% EAS involvement, Grade 3a is the only correct classification
questions.learning: Perineal tears are classified by the depth of tissue involvement. A Grade 3a tear involves less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter (EAS).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Microanuerysms are seen in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic retinopathy

Among the following microaneurysms are seen in diabetic retinopathy.

Microaneurysms are localized, saccular outpouchings of the capillary wall that are formed either by focal dilatation of the capillary wall where pericytes are absent or by fusion of two arms of a capillary loop.

* Most develop in the inner capillary plexus (inner nuclear layer), frequently adjacent to areas of capillary non-perfusion.

* Loss of pericytes may also lead to endothelial cell proliferation with the formation of ‘cellular’ microaneurysms.

* Microaneurysms may leak plasma constituents into the retina as a result of a breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier or may thrombose.

* They tend to be the earliest sign of DR.

Stages and fundus picture in diabetic retinopathy:

Non-proliferative/ Background Diabetic Retinopathy:

* Microaneurysms

* Dot and Blot hemorrhages

* Exudates

Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (indicates progressive retinal ischemia):

* Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities

* Venous changes (such as beading)

* Cotton wool spots

* Deep retinal hemorrhages

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy:

* NeoVascularization of the Optic Disc (NVD)

* NeoVascularization Elsewhere in the periphery of the fundus (NVE)

Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease:

* Tractional retinal detachment

* Vitreous hemorrhage

* Neovascular glaucoma

Pearl PF1636: Early treatment diabetic retinopathy study (ETDRS) classification

Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR):

* Mild NPDR

* At least one microaneurysm must be present

* Moderate NPDR

* Microaneurysms/intraretinal hemorrhage in 2 or 3 quadrants

* Early mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA)

* Hard exudates and cotton-wool spots may or may not be present

* Severe NPDR - any one of the following (4-2-1 rule)

* 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages

* 2 quadrants of venous beading

* 1 quadrant of IRMA changes

* Very severe NPDR - any two of the following (4-2-1)

* 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages

* 2 quadrants of venous beading

* 1 quadrant of IRMA changes

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR):

* PDR without high-risk characteristics (Early PDR)

* Early neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)

* PDR with high-risk characteristics as follows

* NVD < 1/4 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) or preretinal hemorrhage (PRH)

* NVD 1/4 to 1/3 of disc area with or without VH or PRH

* NVE > 1/2 disc area with VH or PRH

Clinically significant macular edema: 1 of the following 3 criteria are present on slit-lamp examination with 90D lens

* Thickening of the retina at or within 500 micron of the center of the fovea.

* Hard exudates at or within 500 micron of the centre of fovea associated with adjacent retinal thickening.

* Development of a zone of retinal thickening one disc diameter or larger in size. At least a part of this should be within one disc diameter of the foveal center.

Advanced diabetic eye disease:

* Persistent vitreous hemorrhage

* Tractional retinal detachment

* Neovascular glaucoma

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The given diagram shows the steps in bacterial cell wall formation. Identify the site of action of beta-lactam antibiotics.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Beta lactams act on step 4 in the given image.

Mechanism of action of beta-lactams: They are the cell wall synthesis inhibitor. The β-lactam antibiotics inhibit this last step in peptidoglycan synthesis. They inhibit the enzyme transpeptidase which is required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan chain. Transpeptidases cleave the terminal D-alanine of the peptide chains and form cross-linkages between them. This cross-linking provides rigidity and stability to the cell wall.

Transpeptidases and other related proteins constitute penicillin-binding proteins(PBP) and, are located in the bacterial cell membrane. β-lactam antibiotics are bactericidal. This is because bacterias swell and burst due to deficient cell walls when they divide in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics. Penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, and carbapenems are examples of β-lactam antibiotics.

Gram-positive bacteria are more susceptible to β-lactam antibiotics than gram-negative because their cell wall is almost entirely made of peptidoglycan.

Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics develops due to the production of the beta-lactamase enzyme and the development of altered penicillin-binding proteins like in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). β-lactamases inactivate β-lactam antibiotics by opening the β-lactam ring. This could be overcome by using drugs that inhibit this enzyme. Examples of β-lactamase inhibitors are clavulanic acid, sulbactam, and tazobactam.

Other options:

Option A: Fosfomycin inhibits step 1 in the image. It inhibits the cytoplasmic enzyme enol pyruvate transferase that catalyses the initial step in the bacterial cell wall and hence cell wall synthesis. It is used for the treatment of urinary tract infections.

Option B: Bacitracin inhibits step 2 in the image. It is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor that interferes with dephosphorylation in the cycling of the lipid carrier which transfers peptidoglycan subunits to the growing cell wall. It is only given for topical application because of its severe nephrotoxicity when given systemically.

Option C: Vancomycin inhibits step 3 in the image. It binds to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the newly formed peptidoglycan pentapeptide. This prevents further elongation of the peptidoglycan and its cross-linking. It is used against MRSA and Clostridium difficile infection. Redman syndrome due to histamine release following infusion is an important side effect.

Note: The FDA has approved the use of cefepime-enmetazobactam, a combination of a fourth-generation cephalosporin and beta-lactamase inhibitor for use in complicated UTIs (including pyelonephritis).
questions.learning: 4 Beta lactams act on step 4 in the given image. Mechanism of action of beta-lactams: They are the cell wall synthesis inhibitor.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The toughness of bacterial cell walls is due to:
questions.explanation: The structural integrity and toughness of the bacterial cell wall are primarily derived from the peptidoglycan layer (murein). This mesh-like polymer provides the rigidity necessary to maintain cell shape and protect the bacterium from osmotic lysis. In Gram-positive bacteria, this layer is thick (up to 100 layers), whereas in Gram-negative bacteria, it is significantly thinner. Regarding the distractors, teichoic acid (Option A) is found only in Gram-positive cell walls and contributes to stability and ion transport but does not provide primary structural strength. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) (Option C) are components of the outer membrane (Option D) found only in Gram-negative bacteria. While the outer membrane acts as a protective barrier against toxic substances, the physical "toughness" and resistance to pressure are functions of the underlying peptidoglycan. Therefore, peptidoglycan is the essential molecule responsible for the mechanical strength of the bacterial cell wall
questions.learning: The structural integrity and toughness of the bacterial cell wall are primarily derived from the peptidoglycan layer (murein). This mesh-like polymer provides the rigidity necessary to maintain cell shape and protect the bacterium from osmotic lysis.

Correct answer: B. Lanz incision

* Rutherford–Morrison incision : oblique muscle cutting incision with its lower end over McBurney’s point and extending obliquely upwards and laterally as necessary(Shown on the left side in the image for the sake of clarity)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a splenectomy for a 40-year-old patient with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), the surgeon must ensure the complete removal of all splenic tissue, including accessory spleens, to prevent symptom recurrence. Accessory spleens are commonly found in specific anatomical locations. Where is the most likely site the surgeon should search for an accessory spleen during the operation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Splenic hilum and mesentry

The splenic hilum and mesentery represent the most common location for accessory spleens.

An accessory spleen, a supernumerary spleen, a splenule, or a splenunculus refers to splenic tissue found outside the normal spleen.

Incomplete fusion of mesenchymal buds during development results in the formation of accessory spleens.

Most of the accessory spleens are observed in the splenic hilum, the site at which blood vessels enter the spleen. Other sites are:

* Tail of the pancreas

* Gastrosplenic ligament

* Lienorenal ligament

* Stomach wall

* Intestinal wall

* Greater omentum

* Mesentery

* Pelvis

* Scrotum

Accessory spleens are of importance during procedures like splenectomies and imaging studies.

In a therapeutic splenectomy, it is necessary to remove all accessory splenic tissue for resolution of symptoms failing which symptoms will continue because an accessory spleen is a functional splenic tissue. Conditions that tend to necessitate this sort of management are hemolytic anemia and chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Accessory spleens are also relevant when evaluating the results of imaging studies; for example, when a patient undergoes a CT scan, accessory spleens can appear similar to lymph nodes or even a neoplastic growth.
questions.learning: Splenic hilum and mesentry — The splenic hilum and mesentery represent the most common location for accessory spleens. An accessory spleen, a supernumerary spleen, a splenule, or a splenunculus refers to splenic tissue found outside the normal spleen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the postnatal remnant of the distal umbilical artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial umbilical ligament

The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta. After birth, the distal portions of the umbilical arteries obliterate and form the medial umbilical ligaments, which are seen as fibrous cords on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

In contrast, the proximal portions remain patent and persist as the superior vesical arteries, supplying the urinary bladder.

| Fetal Structure | Postnatal Remnant

| --------------- | -----------------

| Distal umbilical artery | Medial umbilical ligament

| Proximal umbilical artery | Superior vesical artery

| Umbilical vein | Ligamentum teres hepatis

| Ductus arteriosus | Ligamentum arteriosum

| Urachus | Median umbilical ligament

| Ductus venosus | Ligamentum venosum

Why Not the Other Options?

• Ligamentum teres → Remnant of the umbilical vein.
• Superior vesical artery → Remnant of the proximal, not distal, umbilical artery.
• Ligamentum arteriosum → Remnant of the ductus arteriosus.
questions.learning: Medial umbilical ligament — The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta. After birth, the distal portions of the umbilical arteries obliterate and form the medial umbilical ligaments, which are seen as fibrous cords on…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following are components responsible for the countercurrent mechanism in the kidney except _____.
options: Sodium outflow in thick ascending limb
Water outflow in thin descending limb
Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb
Flow of tubular fluid from PCT to DCT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb

Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism.

The loop of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:

1. High permeability of the thin descending limb to water ( via aquaporin-1)
2. Active transport of Na+ and Cl- from the thick ascending limb
3. Inflow of tubular fluid from proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule.

Note: The thin ascending limbs of juxtamedullary nephrons are permeable to Na+ and Cl- and hence do contribute passively to countercurrent multiplication. However, among the options provided, Option C is the best answer as the other options are directly responsible for the countercurrent mechanism.
questions.learning: Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism. The loop of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are features of otitis media with effusion EXCEPT?
options: Most cases have Ad type of curve on tympanometry and a conductive hearing loss
Resolves on its own after the symptoms subside
Usually occurs after an episode of common cold, but can occur de-novo
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most cases have Ad type of curve on tympanometry and a conductive hearing loss

Type B tympanometry curve is obtained in otitis media with effusion.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

• Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
• Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus
• Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.
• Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media:

• Rinne negative (BC>AC).
• Weber - lateralized towards the worse ear
• Audiogram - AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present
• Impedance audiometry - flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side)

B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media.

Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve, this results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below:

Note: Tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging swelling near the wrist joint over the past three months. Based on the X-ray findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays an expansile, multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance. The lesion extends right up to the subchondral bone (articular surface). These are pathognomonic radiological features of Osteoclastoma, also known as a Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) (Option C). GCT is typically seen in young adults (ages 20–40) and is locally aggressive. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) presents with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Osteosarcoma (Option B) would show a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and a Codman’s triangle. Osteochondroma (Option D) appears as a bony outgrowth on a stalk (exostosis). Therefore, the subarticular location and soap-bubble morphology confirm Osteoclastoma as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The X-ray displays an expansile, multi-loculated lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal radius, classically described as having a "soap-bubble" appearance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma comes for her chemotherapy treatment. She has had multiple complaints of nausea and vomiting during her previous treatment visits. Which of the following is used to prevent chemotherapy-induced emesis and vomiting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Palonosetron

Palonosetron is used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

Palonosetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist that blocks serotonin in vagal terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). It has a higher receptor affinity as compared to the first-generation 5HT3 antagonists making it more potent. It is also useful in delayed emesis associated with chemotherapy due to its long half-life.

During chemotherapy, there is cell lysis and 5HT(serotonin) is released from the gut mucosa. The released serotonin acts on the 5HT3 receptors and activates the vagal afferents in the gut that carry the emetogenic impulses to the nucleus tractus solitarius and chemoreceptor trigger zone. The selective blockade of 5HT3 receptors reduces the emetogenic impulses.

It is used in combination with netupitant in acute and delayed nausea and vomiting. Netupitant is an NK1 receptor antagonist. It augments the effects of palonosetron. This combination is particularly anti-emetogenic when given along with dexamethasone.

Other options:

Option A: Metoclopramide is a 5HT4 agonist and D2 blocker and is used as an antiemetic agent.

Option B: Ropinirole is an antiparkinsonian drug that is a dopamine agonist and is also the drug of choice for restless leg syndrome.

Option C: Domperidone is not used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
questions.learning: Palonosetron Palonosetron is used in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Palonosetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist that blocks serotonin in vagal terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The fourth heart sound is caused by:
options: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves
Vibrations in the ventricular wall during systole
Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular filling

The fourth heart sound is caused by ventricular filling.

A fourth sound is heard immediately before the first sound when atrial pressure is high or the ventricle is stiff in conditions such as ventricular hypertrophy. It is due to ventricular filling and is rarely heard in normal adults.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with progressive dyspnea and weight loss. Examination reveals a barrel-shaped chest and decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Pulmonary function testing is performed. Which of the following spirometry and lung volume findings are most consistent with emphysema?
options: ↓ FEV₁, ↑ FEV₁/FVC, normal TLC, normal RV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↓ FEV₁, ↓ FEV₁/FVC, ↑ TLC, ↑ RV

Emphysema is an obstructive lung disease characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil, leading to air trapping and lung hyperinflation.

Pulmonary function test findings:

• ↓ FEV₁ due to airway obstruction
• ↓ FEV₁/FVC ratio (<70%) indicating obstructive pattern
• ↑ Total lung capacity (TLC) from hyperinflation
• ↑ Residual volume (RV) due to air trapping

Patients often have progressive dyspnea, barrel-shaped chest, and decreased breath sounds, especially with a long smoking history.
questions.learning: ↓ FEV₁, ↓ FEV₁/FVC, ↑ TLC, ↑ RV Emphysema is an obstructive lung disease characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil, leading to air trapping and lung hyperinflation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man developed generalized muscle spasm with arching of his back as shown in the image, a few days after sustaining a puncture wound to his leg. The toxin responsible for this type of abnormal posturing acts by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Presynaptic inhibition of GABA and glycine release
Cleavage of SNARE proteins, preventing Ach release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Presynaptic inhibition of GABA and glycine release

The toxin responsible for the abnormal posturing shown in the image is tetanospasmin produced by Clostridium tetani. It acts by causing presynaptic inhibition of GABA and glycine release.

Tetanospasmin, after secretion by the bacterium is cleaved into two peptides linked by a disulphide bond. The larger peptide diffuses to terminals of neurons and migrates by the retrograde axonal transport system to the spinal cord and brainstem. It diffuses to the glycinergic interneurons and GABA secreting neurons there. The smaller peptide degrades synaptobrevin and blocks the release of the inhibitory glycine and GABA. This results in hyperreflexia, muscle spasms, and spastic paralysis. Even small amounts of the toxin can be lethal.

The incubation period of C. tetani ranges from 4-5 days up to 3 weeks. Muscle spasms usually involve the area of injury first and then the muscles of the jaw causing trismus or lockjaw. Gradually, other voluntary muscles become involved, resulting in tonic spasms. Any external stimulus can precipitate a tetanic generalized muscle spasm. The patient is conscious but may be in pain. Death usually results from respiratory paralysis.

Other options: Proteolysis of target SNARE proteins in the neurons inhibits the release of Ach at the synapse - this is the mechanism of action of Botulinum toxin.
questions.learning: Presynaptic inhibition of GABA and glycine release — The toxin responsible for the abnormal posturing shown in the image is tetanospasmin produced by Clostridium tetani.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A male patient presents with hydrophobia, tearing, and altered sensorium after a dog bite. You suspect rabies in this patient and take corneal scrapings to confirm the same. What test is performed to obtain the most accurate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reverse transcription-PCR for virus

Detection of rabies virus RNA by RT-PCR(reverse transcriptase -polymerase chain reaction) on corneal scrapings is highly sensitive and specific.

This technique can detect viruses in fresh saliva samples, CSF, skin, and brain tissues. RT-PCR with genetic sequencing can distinguish among rabies variants, permitting identification of the probable source of an infection.

Clinical stages of rabies:

PHASE
TYPICAL DURATION
SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS

Incubation period
20-90 Days
None

Prodrome
2-10 days
Fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, paresthesia

Acute neurologic disease

Encephalitic/Furious rabies (80%)
2-7 days
Anxiety, Agitation, Hyperactivity, hallucinations, hydrophobia, autonomic dysfunction

Paralytic /dumb rabies (20%)
2-10 days
Flaccid paralysis in limbs progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis.

Coma, death
0-14 days
(14 Days of encephalitic rabies and 30 days of paralytic rabies)

Laboratory diagnosis of rabies is performed by the following methods:

* Antigen detection - Direct immunofluorescence (IF) from specimens of

* Skin biopsy from the nape of the neck including hair follicles. Rabies antigen is present in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles. It is the most sensitive and specific test.

* Corneal smears were previously used. They are not used anymore as they are of low diagnostic yield.

* Viral isolation- Intracerebral inoculation in mice can be attempted from the brain, CSF, and saliva

* Antibody demonstration from serum and CSF

* Viral RNA detection by RT-PCR

* Postmortem examination of brain tissue samples- demonstration of Negri bodies

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is operated when its size is greater than __________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5.5 cm

An asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in an otherwise fit patient should be considered for repair if >5.5 cm  in diameter (measured by ultrasonography). The annual incidence of rupture rises from 1% or less in aneurysms that are <5.5 cm in diameter to a significant level of nearly 25%, in those that are 7 cm  in diameter.

As open elective surgery (transabdominal) carries a 5% mortality rate, the balance is in favor of elective operation once the maximum diameter is >5.5 cm.

6 monthly follow-up ultrasonographic assessment is indicated for asymptomatic aneurysms <5.5cm in diameter.
questions.learning: 5.5 cm An asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in an otherwise fit patient should be considered for repair if >5.5 cm in diameter (measured by ultrasonography).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs reduces mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metoprolol

Metoprolol reduces mortality in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

The drugs which reduce mortality in patients with HFrEF are :

* Beta-blockers block β1 receptors and prevent ventricular remodeling promoted by the stimulated RAAS and sympathetic system. Metoprolol and bisoprolol are selective for the β1 receptor, and carvedilol also blocks the β2 and α1 receptors, leading to vasodilation. Adverse effects include fluid retention, worsening HFrEF, fatigue, bradycardia or heart block, and hypotension.

* ACE inhibitors- Enalapril and lisinopril also reduce mortality. ACE inhibitors decrease peripheral resistance and reduce the load on the failing myocardium by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Hereby, preventing vasoconstriction and causing relaxation of the vasculature.

* Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)-  They inhibit the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) by blocking the binding of angiotensin II to its receptor, which in turn leads to vasodilation and prevents the release of aldosterone. They are found to reduce mortality and morbidity in HFrEF cases.

* Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)- Sacubitril/valsartan is a novel therapy that has been approved in July 2015 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for patients with HFrEF. Sacubitril/valsartan consists of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the ARB valsartan.

* Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like Spironolactone and Eplerenone are also known to decrease the mortality risk.

Diuretics like furosemide and torsemide are not found to reduce mortality or hospital readmission. They are the only agents that can adequately control the fluid retention associated with HFrEF.

Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, does not decrease mortality risk in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), unlike other neurohormonal antagonists such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors.

Pearl PF0729: Cardioselective beta blockers: Mnemonic

Cardioselective Beta blockers Act At Nothing But Myocardium Exclusively.

* C: Celiprolol ( III )

* B: Bisoprolol

* A: Acebutolol

* A: Atenolol

* N: Nebivolol ( III )

* B: Betaxolol ( III )

* M: Metoprolol

* E: Esmolol

( III ) - Third generation beta blockers. All the others are second generation beta blockers

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked below is innervated by which of the following motor nerve fibres?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gamma

In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked shows intrafusal muscle fibres, which are innervated by gamma(γ) motor neurons.

Each muscle spindle is 3 to 10 mm long and consists of 3 to 12 tiny intrafusal muscle fibers that are pointed at their ends and attached to the glycocalyx of the surrounding large extrafusal muscle fibers. There are two kinds of sensory endings in each spindle, a single primary (group Ia) ending and up to eight secondary (group II) endings.

Intrafusal fibers are of 2 types: (1) nuclear bag fibers - subdivided as dynamic and static nuclear bag fibers and (2) nuclear chain fibers.

Each intrafusal muscle fiber is a tiny skeletal muscle fiber. Since there are either few or no actin and myosin filaments in the centre of each of these fibres, the centre does not contract when the ends do. It performs the role of a sensory receptor instead. The end portions that do contract are excited by small gamma(γ) motor nerve fibers which help control basic muscle tone.

There are two types of γ motor neurons- (a) dynamic that supplies dynamic nuclear bag fibers and (b) static that supply static nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain fibers.

Other options:

Option B: Alpha (α) motor fibers supply the extrafusal muscle fibers which are the regular contractile units of the muscle. They are on an average 14 micrometers in diameter and these fibers branch many times after they enter the muscle and innervate the large skeletal muscle fibers at the motor endplate. A single alpha nerve fibre can stimulate anywhere between three to several hundred skeletal muscle fibres, which are collectively called the motor unit.

Option C: Beta (β) motor fibers are for touch and pressure.

Option D: Delta (δ) motor fibers are for pain and temperature.
questions.learning: Gamma — In the given cross-section of a muscle spindle, the structure marked shows intrafusal muscle fibres, which are innervated by gamma(γ) motor neurons.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the most effective method for educating an urban slum community about the use of oral rehydration solution (ORS)?
questions.explanation: Health education in community settings, particularly in low-literacy areas like urban slums, requires methods that are practical and easy to follow. A Demonstration (Option D) is the most effective approach for teaching the preparation and use of ORS. This "learning by seeing" method allows community members to observe the exact measurements and mixing process, which ensures accuracy and builds confidence in their ability to perform the task at home. A Lecture (Option A) is often too passive and less effective for procedural skills. Roleplay (Option B) is good for teaching social behaviors but not technical prep. Flashcards (Option C) are useful visual aids but do not provide the step-by-step practical instruction of a live demonstration. Therefore, because ORS prep is a specific, life-saving skill that must be done correctly to be effective, demonstration is the definitive educational standard
questions.learning: Health education in community settings, particularly in low-literacy areas like urban slums, requires methods that are practical and easy to follow. A Demonstration (Option D) is the most effective approach for teaching the preparation and use of ORS.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is suspected to have MEN-1 syndrome. Which of the following is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor seen in this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma

MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets, and anterior pituitary. Gastrinoma is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor in MEN 1 syndrome.

Most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the first and second part of duodenum.

Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome.
questions.learning: Gastrinoma MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets, and anterior pituitary. Gastrinoma is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor in MEN 1 syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which tissue in the human body is most sensitive to the effects of radiation?
questions.explanation: The radiosensitivity of a tissue is generally proportional to its rate of cell division and inversely proportional to its degree of specialization (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau). The "bone marrow" (Option C) contains hematopoietic stem cells that are rapidly and continuously dividing, making it one of the "most radiation-sensitive" tissues in the body. Acute exposure to high doses of radiation can lead to bone marrow syndrome, characterized by severe pancytopenia and immune suppression. Skin (Option A) is also sensitive but less so than the bone marrow. Muscle tissue (Option B) and nervous tissue (Option D) are composed of highly specialized, non-dividing (permanent) cells, making them relatively "radioresistant". Understanding tissue sensitivity is crucial in clinical radiology and oncology for calculating safe diagnostic doses and for planning radiotherapy while minimizing collateral damage to vital organs. Protective measures, such as lead shielding, are specifically designed to protect the most sensitive areas from unnecessary exposure
questions.learning: The radiosensitivity of a tissue is generally proportional to its rate of cell division and inversely proportional to its degree of specialization (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female patient presents with dry mouth and a gritty sensation in the eyes. She has normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia. She also has enlarged salivary glands. What is the best investigation to arrive at a diagnosis?
options: Serum ACE levels and Chest X-ray
Schirmer test and auto antibodies measurement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Schirmer test and auto antibodies measurement

This question is packed with classic clues:

| Feature | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Dry mouth (xerostomia) | Salivary gland involvement

| Gritty eyes | Keratoconjunctivitis sicca

| Enlarged salivary glands | Lymphocytic infiltration

| Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia | Distal renal tubular acidosis (Type 1 RTA)

Put together → Primary Sjögren Syndrome with renal involvement

Sjögren is an autoimmune disease where:

• CD4+ T cells + B cells infiltrate exocrine glands
• Leads to:

• ↓ saliva → xerostomia
• ↓ tears → dry eyes

• Systemic involvement:

• Kidney → distal RTA → hypokalemia
• Lungs, nerves, joints

• Strong B-cell activation → ↑ risk of lymphoma

1. Schirmer Test

Measures tear production

• <5 mm wetting in 5 min → diagnostic

2. Autoantibodies

| Antibody | Significance

| -------- | ------------

| Anti-Ro (SSA) | Most sensitive

| Anti-La (SSB) | More specific

| ANA, RF | Often positive

A) Serum ACE levels and Chest X-ray

• Used for → Sarcoidosis
• Sarcoid can cause:

• Parotid enlargement
• Dryness (mimics Sjögren)

B) Improvement on trial with methylprednisolone

• Steroid response is NOT diagnostic
• Many autoimmune diseases respond to steroids

D) Salivary gland scintigraphy

• Assesses gland function
• Used as supportive evidence

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The following sign is seen in a patient presenting with rhinorrhea following a skull base fracture. Identify the sign.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Double Target Sign

The given image shows the Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign seen in CSF rhinorrhoea and suggests basal skull fracture due to trauma in this case.

Double target sign is seen patients with CSF rhinorrhea. The nasal discharge in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood. When this discharge is collected on a filter paper, it shows a double target sign with a central red spot and a peripheral lighter halo.

The following features help in differentiating CSF rhinorrhoea from nasal secretions:

Features
CSF Fluid
Nasal Secretions

Nasal or sinus surgery, head injury, or intracranial tumor

Flow of discharge

A few drops or a stream of fluid gushes down with bending forward or straining

cannot be sniffed back

Character of discharge

Thin, watery, and clear

Taste

Sweet

Note: Nasal discharge stiffens the handkerchief because of the presence of mucus.

A basilar skull fracture occurs due to direct impact behind the ear or crush injuries of the head and present with the following features:

* Hemotympanum

* Battle sign: bruising behind the ear

* Racoon eyes

* CSF rhinorrhoea

Pearl PF1086: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: Reservoir sign is also seen in acute mastoiditis/ coalescent mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Eonism
A. Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger

2. Exhibitionism
B. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies

3. Frotteurism
C. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

4. Necrophilia
D. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-C;2-A;3-D;4-B

The correct answer is option B: 1-C;2-A;3-D;4-B

1. Eonism
C. Sexual pleasure by wearing clothes of the opposite sex

2. Exhibitionism
A. Exposure of one’s genitals to an unsuspecting stranger

3. Frotteurism
D. Sexual gratification by rubbing private parts against another person

4. Necrophilia
B. Sexual gratification by intercourse with dead bodies

Paraphilias or perversions are sexual stimuli or acts that are deviations from normal sexual behaviors but are necessary for some people to experience arousal and orgasm.

Eonism (also known as transvestism) is a sexual perversion, where a person's whole personality is dominated by a desire to be identified as a member of the opposite sex. This is usually seen in males who obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female clothes. There is no hormonal/genital abnormality.

Exhibitionism is the urge to expose genitals to a stranger or unsuspecting person.

Frotteurism refers to the sexual gratification achieved by touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person. This behavior often occurs in busy and crowded places. It is predominantly described in men.

Necrophilia is an obsession with obtaining sexual gratification from dead bodies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 21 weeks of gestation is found to have a fetus diagnosed with meningomyelocele (a type of spina bifida) and is considering medical termination of pregnancy. In this situation, what legal and medical requirements must be fulfilled to proceed with MTP?
options: Consent of Husband with opinion of one doctor
Her consent with consent of 2 doctors
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, for an MTP performed between 20 and 24 weeks of gestation (such as in this 21-week case with a substantial fetal anomaly), the mandatory legal requirement is the opinion and consent of two registered medical practitioners. Most importantly, only the pregnant woman's own written consent is legally required; the consent of the husband or partner (Option A) is not a requirement under Indian law. Option C is incomplete as the patient's consent is the primary legal prerequisite. For terminations up to 20 weeks, only one doctor's opinion is required. Terminations beyond 24 weeks for fetal anomalies require the permission of a State-level Medical Board. Therefore, for this specific second-trimester scenario, the woman’s autonomous consent alongside the professional agreement of two doctors constitutes the full legal and medical requirement

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During first-trimester ultrasonography, which measurement is the most accurate parameter for determining gestational age?
questions.explanation: Accurate dating of pregnancy is fundamental to obstetric care. During the first trimester (specifically between 7 and 13 weeks), the Crown Rump Length (CRL) is universally recognized as the most reliable and accurate parameter for determining gestational age. The margin of error for CRL is remarkably low, typically within 3–5 days. Biparietal diameter (BPD, Option A) and head circumference (HC, Option B) become primary dating parameters during the second trimester (after 14 weeks), but they are less accurate than first-trimester CRL due to increased biological variability in fetal growth. Abdominal circumference (AC, Option D) is primarily used in the third trimester to estimate fetal weight and screen for growth restriction, rather than for initial dating. Once the CRL exceeds 84mm, dating is shifted to BPD. Therefore, CRL remains the gold standard for early pregnancy dating and establishing the "due date" for all subsequent monitoring
questions.learning: Accurate dating of pregnancy is fundamental to obstetric care. During the first trimester (specifically between 7 and 13 weeks), the Crown Rump Length (CRL) is universally recognized as the most reliable and accurate parameter for determining gestational age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the following instrument?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Unipolar cautery

The given instrument is a unipolar cautery/monopolar cautery.

Other options:

Option B: The bipolar cautery contains two tips, unlike unipolar cautery which has only one tip. The current flows between these two tips and hence it does not need a return electrode, unlike the unipolar cautery.

Option C: The harmonic scalpel (shown below) is a surgical instrument used to simultaneously cut and cauterize tissue. Ultrasonic energy is used in Harmonic scalpel where ultrasonic energy is converted to mechanical energy at the active blade.

Option D: LigaSure vessel sealing system (shown below) is a bipolar apparatus for sealing vascular tissue. It applies a high coaptive pressure during the generation of tissue temperature under 1000°C, hydrogen cross-links are first ruptured and then renatured, resulting in a vascular seal that has high tensile strength.
