questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid serves as the principal buffer in blood because of its ability to both accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine is the only amino acid that functions effectively as a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). This is because its imidazole side chain has a pKa of approximately 6.0, which is close enough to the blood's pH to allow it to both accept and donate protons. Arginine (Option B) has a pKa of 12.5, which is far too high to act as a buffer in the body. Tryptophan (Option C) and Tyrosine (Option D) have minimal buffering capacity because their side chains are either non-ionizable or have pKa values (10.1 for tyrosine) that are not relevant at physiological pH. Histidine residues are particularly abundant in hemoglobin, where they play a vital role in the Bohr effect, helping to maintain blood pH while regulating oxygen delivery to tissues
questions.learning: Histidine is the only amino acid that functions effectively as a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). This is because its imidazole side chain has a pKa of approximately 6.0, which is close enough to the blood's pH to allow it to both accept and donate protons.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following indications is not a standard therapeutic use of beta-blockers?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are not typically the preferred first-line choice for patients with Diabetes Mellitus and hypertension (Option B). This is because beta-blockers can mask the warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (like tachycardia and palpitations) and can impair glucose tolerance by inhibiting insulin release. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred in this demographic for their renoprotective effects. Essential tremors (Option A) are a classic indication for beta-blockers like Propranolol, as they reduce the amplitude of skeletal muscle tremors. Angina pectoris (Option C) is a major use, as they reduce myocardial oxygen demand by slowing the heart rate and contractility. Migraine prophylaxis (Option D) is another standard indication. While beta-blockers can be used in diabetics if necessary (especially cardioselective ones), they are not a "typical" or ideal first-line treatment compared to the other listed therapeutic uses. Therefore, Option B is the correct answer to this "not" question

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Water from a broken septic tank is collected in a container and breeding mosquitoes are seen. The image of the larva is given below. Identify the species of the mosquito.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Culex

The species of mosquito that breeds in dirty water is Culex.

Culex fatigans are found everywhere in India and they transmit Bancroftian filariasis. Culex mosquitoes are also vectors for Japanese encephalitis, West Nile fever, and viral arthritis.

It can be identified by the presence of unspotted wings and hunched back. The larva has a head that is suspended downwards at an angle to the water surface and a siphon tube is present.

It breeds in dirty water collections like stagnant drains, septic tanks, and burrow pits. The peak biting time is during midnight. The preferred biting site is the legs, mainly below the knee.
questions.learning: Culex — The species of mosquito that breeds in dirty water is Culex. Culex fatigans are found everywhere in India and they transmit Bancroftian filariasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with watery diarrhea and vomiting. The causative pathogen shows darting motility. What is the most appropriate selective culture media for isolating this pathogen?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, combined with the hallmark finding of "darting motility" under dark-field microscopy, is pathognomonic for Vibrio cholerae. Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) agar is the highly selective medium used for its primary isolation. The high alkalinity of TCBS (pH 8.6) inhibits the growth of most other intestinal commensals, while the sucrose allows for the differentiation of V. cholerae, which ferments it to produce distinct yellow colonies. Nutrient media (A) is a basal medium and lacks the selectivity required to isolate pathogens from fecal flora. Cetrimide agar (C) is selective for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and is irrelevant in this context. Potassium Tellurite Agar (D), specifically Monsur's medium, can be used for Vibrio isolation but TCBS is the most widely used and preferred selective medium globally. Consequently, given the specific motility and clinical signs, TCBS is the gold standard for laboratory confirmation of cholera
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, combined with the hallmark finding of "darting motility" under dark-field microscopy, is pathognomonic for Vibrio cholerae.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic valve replacement for mitral stenosis is on warfarin therapy 4mg/day. What is the appropriate next step in management? (NEET PG 2021)
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin and start LMWH.

Pregnant women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves require continuous anticoagulation because they are at high risk of valve thrombosis. Warfarin considerations in pregnancy:

• Warfarin crosses the placenta
• Near term, it increases the risk of:

• Fetal intracranial hemorrhage
• Maternal bleeding during labor

Therefore, at around 36 weeks gestation:

• Warfarin should be stopped
• Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) or unfractionated heparin should be started

Why LMWH is preferred:

• Does not cross the placenta
• Safer for the fetus
• Provides effective anticoagulation

Important point:

• Aspirin is not routinely added unless specifically indicated
• Continuing warfarin near delivery is unsafe
questions.learning: Pregnant women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves require continuous anticoagulation because they are at high risk of valve thrombosis. Warfarin considerations in pregnancy: • Warfarin crosses the placenta • Near term, it increases the risk of: •…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Thoracoscore?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Complication of surgery

The complication of surgery is not a component of thoracoscore.

Thoracoscore is used to assess the risk of operative mortality in a patient undergoing thoracic surgery. It includes 9 variables:

• Age
• Sex
• American Society of Anesthesiologists score (ASA)
• Performance status
• Dyspnoea score
• Priority of surgery
• Extent of surgery
• Malignant diagnosis
• Composite comorbidity score
questions.learning: Complication of surgery — The complication of surgery is not a component of thoracoscore. Thoracoscore is used to assess the risk of operative mortality in a patient undergoing thoracic surgery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A nursing assistant posted in the obstetric care unit was asked to monitor the progress of labour. After how much dilatation of the cervix, should she start the documentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5cm

The WHO Labour Care Guide begins the documentation of labour progression at 5 cm of cervical dilatation.

The WHO Labour Care Guide is a tool designed to help health personnel involved in labour care. It aims to

• Guide the monitoring and help in the documentation of the progress of labour.
• Guide the health professionals to offer supportive care throughout labour.
• Assist doctors in promptly identifying and addressing emerging labour complications.
• Prevent the use of unnecessary interventions in labour.
• Support audits and quality improvement.

The differences between the WHO-modified partograph and the latest WHO Labour Care Guide are tabulated below:

WHO modified partograph
WHO Labour Care Guide

Documentation of labour progression begins at 4 cm of cervical dilatation.
Documentation of labour progression begins at 5 cm of cervical dilatation.

Fixed 1 cm/hour ‘alert’ and ‘action’ lines
Time-based cut-offs for each centimetre of cervical dilatation to guide the obstetrician to take action. For example, at 5 cm of cervical dilatation, if there is no progress >6 hours, action needs to be taken.

Monitoring of labour is restricted to the first stage only.
Monitoring of the second stage of labour is included

No section on supportive care interventions
Addition of a section on supportive care of the mother- labour companionship, pain relief, oral fluid intake and posture

Documentation of strength, duration, and frequency of uterine contractions
Documentation of only the duration and frequency of uterine contractions

Note: Previously the answer to the question was 4 cm (according to the modified WHO patograph). However, this information is outdated, therefore the answer to this question has been revised per the latest WHO guidelines.
questions.learning: 5cm The WHO Labour Care Guide begins the documentation of labour progression at 5 cm of cervical dilatation. The WHO Labour Care Guide is a tool designed to help health personnel involved in labour care.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cholera causes diarrhea by binding to specific receptors on intestinal cells. Which factor facilitates the entry of cholera toxin through the intestinal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The cholera toxin, produced by Vibrio cholerae, consists of an A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits are responsible for binding to the host cell. The specific receptor on the intestinal epithelial cell surface that the cholera toxin binds to is the GM1 ganglioside. This binding facilitates the entry of the active A subunit into the cell. GLUT 1 (Option A) is a glucose transporter and is not involved in toxin binding. GM2 ganglioside (Option B) is a related molecule but is not the primary receptor for cholera toxin. Cephalin (Option C, phosphatidylethanolamine) is a common membrane phospholipid but lacks the specific carbohydrate structure required for toxin recognition. Once inside, the A subunit constitutively activates the Gs protein, leading to a massive increase in intracellular cAMP. This causes the hypersecretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen, resulting in the characteristic profuse "rice-water" diarrhea of cholera
questions.learning: The cholera toxin, produced by Vibrio cholerae, consists of an A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits are responsible for binding to the host cell.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In cases of paracetamol poisoning, N-acetylcysteine is used as an antidote. What is its mechanism of action in preventing toxicity?
questions.explanation: Paracetamol is metabolized into a toxic intermediate called NAPQI, which is normally detoxified by glutathione. In an overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, allowing NAPQI to accumulate and cause hepatic necrosis. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) prevents this by acting as a glutathione precursor, effectively replenishing glutathione levels to facilitate detoxification. NAC does not inhibit the formation of the toxin (Option A), nor does it directly remove paracetamol from the system (Option B). It also does not neutralize liver enzymes (Option D). NAC therapy is most effective when initiated within 8 hours of ingestion but may still provide benefit up to 36 hours post-overdose. Additionally, NAC directly binds to NAPQI and enhances the non-toxic sulfation metabolic pathway. This life-saving intervention is the cornerstone of managing paracetamol-induced acute liver failure
questions.learning: Paracetamol is metabolized into a toxic intermediate called NAPQI, which is normally detoxified by glutathione. In an overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, allowing NAPQI to accumulate and cause hepatic necrosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is Net Reproduction Rate?
options: The average number of children who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of surviving children who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
The average number of surviving daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The average number of surviving daughters who are going to be born to a newborn girl in her reproductive lifespan

The Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) is the average number of surviving daughters that a newborn girl is expected to bear during her reproductive years, taking into account both fertility and female mortality. An NRR of 1 indicates replacement-level fertility, where one generation of women exactly replaces itself.

Why not the other options?

• A. Average number of children: Describes Total Fertility Rate (TFR), not NRR.
• B. Average number of surviving children: Includes both sexes; NRR considers only surviving daughters.
• C. Average number of daughters: Equivalent to the Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR), which does not account for female mortality.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The HIV sentinel surveillance includes all of the following populations except ______________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. STD clinic attendees

Sentinel surveillance of HIV is usually not done for STD clinic attendees.

Sentinel surveillance is used to augment the notification systems used in the surveillance of diseases.

Till 2012-13, STD sites were also included in the HIV sentinel surveillance but from 2014-15, these sites were entirely discontinued, since the STD data had significant biases.

The study population for HIV sentinel surveillance includes:

• Female sex worker: Women who are engaged in consensual sex for money or payment in kind, as a means of livelihood in the last six months
• Men who had anal or oral sex with a male partner in the last month.
• Injection drug users: Men and women who use addictive substances or drugs for recreational or non-medical reasons, through injections, at least once in the last three months.
• Hijra/Transgender: Person whose identity does not conform unambiguously to conventional notions of male or female gender roles, but combines or moves between these.
• Single male migrants: Single male, living at a place other than the place of usual residence without his spouse or family, for the purposes of work and visiting his home town at least once a year.
• Long-distance truckers: Truckers who travel more than 800 km one way between source and destination.
• A pregnant woman of age 15-49 years and attending the antenatal clinic for the first time.
questions.learning: STD clinic attendees Sentinel surveillance of HIV is usually not done for STD clinic attendees. Sentinel surveillance is used to augment the notification systems used in the surveillance of diseases.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-day-old neonate brought to the outpatient department is found to have bilateral conjunctivitis. Chest X-ray done showed lung infiltrates. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for the infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia trachomatis

Chlamydia trachomatis is most likely responsible for the infection.

Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis usually manifests 1 week after birth. It is usually a venereal infection derived from the cervix or urethra of the mother during delivery.

On examination, the conjunctiva is swollen and edematous. The discharge is initially watery, later becomes purulent or bloody.

Newborns with suspected chlamydia infection should have samples drawn from both the conjunctivae and oropharynx. Since it is an obligate intracellular organism, swabs should also include conjunctival epithelial cells if possible. Subsequent Giemsa staining shows characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies formed by Chlamydia oculogenitalis.

Treatment involves administration of suspension of erythromycin ethylsuccinate 50 mg/kg daily in four divided doses before feeds for 2–3 weeks.

If left untreated, associated systemic diseases such as chlamydial otitis and pneumonia may develop later. In all cases, both parents must receive appropriate treatment for genital infection.

Neonatal conjunctivitis, also called ophthalmia neonatorum, typically presents during the first month of life. The age of the neonate is an important clue towards the etiology of the infection.

Age
Cause of conjunctivitis

First 24 hours
Chemical causes- erythromycin/gentamycin drops,

24 to 48 hours
Neisseria gonorrhea (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, coliforms

5 to 14 days
Chlamydia trachomatis, Herpes keratoconjunctivitis

5 to 18 days
Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Neonates are at higher risk of conjunctivitis due to predisposing factors such as:

• Decreased tear production
• Absence of IgA in tears
• Decreased immune function
• Absence of lymphoid tissue in the conjunctiva
• Decreased lysozyme activity.

Other risk factors for developing neonatal conjunctivitis are premature rupture of membranes, prolonged delivery, prematurity, poor prenatal care, mechanical ventilation, poor hygiene conditions, and history of midwife interference.

Other options :
Option B: Hemophilus influenza is one of the most common causes of acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children < 6 years of age and is responsible for causing conjunctivitis-otitis syndrome where conjunctivitis is followed by acute otitis media.

Option C: Streptococcus usually manifests 48-72 hours after birth. It is a common cause of acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children.

Option D: Mycoplasma, specifically M.genitalium can cause conjunctivitis due to contamination of the eye with genital infections in adults.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for pubertal development. On examination, she has early breast development with sparse, thin pubic hair. According to the Tanner staging, which stage does this correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage II

Tanner Stage II marks the onset of puberty. It is characterized by breast budding (thelarche) and the appearance of sparse, long, slightly pigmented pubic hair along the labia.

Key Tanner staging in girls:

• Stage I: Prepubertal; no breast tissue or pubic hair.
• Stage II: Breast bud (thelarche) with sparse, thin pubic hair. ✔️
• Stage III: Further breast enlargement; pubic hair becomes darker, coarser, and curlier.
• Stage IV: Secondary mound of areola and papilla; adult-type pubic hair but not yet on medial thighs.
• Stage V: Mature adult breast and pubic hair extending to the medial thighs.
questions.learning: Stage II Tanner Stage II marks the onset of puberty. It is characterized by breast budding (thelarche) and the appearance of sparse, long, slightly pigmented pubic hair along the labia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man is presbyopic. The power of his prescription glasses should be _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. +1.5D

The power of prescription glasses for a 50-year-old woman should be +1.5D.

Presbyopia is the condition of decreasing near vision due to an age-related decrease in the magnitude of accommodation.

Basic principles for correction in presbyopic patients are given below:

• Correct any refractive error for distance present in the patient first.
• Add the presbyopic correction(correction for near vision) of each eye to any distant correction that is present.
• For presbyopic correction, the weakest convex lens(plus lens) with which the patient can see clearly at the near point is prescribed, since over-correction will also result in eye fatigue symptoms.

Presbyopic spectacles may be unifocal, bifocal or Multifocal.

A rough prescription of presbyopic glasses can be made by the age of the patient in an emmetrope as follows:

Age
Power

45 years
+1 to +1.25D

50 years

+1.5 to 1.75D

55 years
+2 to +2.25D

60 years
+2.5 to +3D

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The next step to follow for a mother with Rh-negative pregnancy and antibody titre above critical level (husband Rh-positive) is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MCA PSV

In an Rh-negative pregnancy with a positive antibody screen and antibody titre above the critical level, the fetus is at risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).

The next step is to assess for fetal anemia non-invasively using the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) by Doppler.

• A. Umbilical artery Doppler: Mainly assesses placental resistance and fetal growth restriction, not fetal anemia.
• B. Cordocentesis: Invasive and used when fetal anemia is suspected/confirmed, particularly for diagnostic assessment and possible intrauterine transfusion.
• C. MCA PSV — Correct: MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM is suggestive of moderate-to-severe fetal anemia.
• D. Amniocentesis: Historically used for bilirubin assessment, but has largely been replaced by MCA Doppler for fetal anemia surveillance.
questions.learning: MCA PSV — In an Rh-negative pregnancy with a positive antibody screen and antibody titre above the critical level, the fetus is at risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The mascot depicts Sapna, a local school-going girl who will play a role in spreading awareness within the community. Which National Health Program is associated with this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. National leprosy eradication programme

The given image is of Sapna, a mascot for leprosy awareness, associated with the National Leprosy Eradication Program (NLEP).

Sapna refers to a local school-going girl who will help to spread awareness in the community.

National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) is a program of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the government of India. Characteristics of the NLEP emblem:

* The lotus in the NLEP emblem symbolizes beauty and purity.

* A partially affected thumb, a normal forefinger, and the shape of a house symbolize that leprosy can be cured and that a patient with leprosy can be a useful member of society.

* The rising sun symbolizes hope and optimism.

* The emblem captures the spirit of hope and positivity in the eradication of leprosy.

The vision of the NLEP is 'Leprosy-free India'. Disability prevention and medical rehabilitation (DPMR) is the priority of the programme. The mission of  NLEP is to provide quality services free of cost to all people through the integrated healthcare system.

The other developments under NLEP are:

* Mycobacterium Indicus Prani (MiP) vaccine for multibacillary leprosy patients and their contacts (it is in a project mode).

* Nikusth: is a real-time web-based system for data management for leprosy cases. It is a software for monitoring leprosy patients, with a patient tracking mechanism launched by the Health & Family Welfare Minister Government of India.

* Sparsh Leprosy Awareness Campaign (SLAC) was introduced in 2017 on the occasion of the anti-leprosy day (observed on the last Sunday of January) to promote awareness about various aspects of leprosy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a community, there are usually 40-50 reported cases of dengue every week. This week, there were 48 reported cases. This would classify as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endemic

The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease.

Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

Outbreak carries the same definition of an epidemic, but is often used for a more limited geographic area.

Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.
questions.learning: Endemic — The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease. Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: On finding a congenital heart block in a fetus, which of the following conditions would you evaluate for in the mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SLE

On finding a congenital heart block in the fetus, the mother should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Fetal and neonatal heart blocks occur due to myocarditis and fibrosis in the region between the AV node and the bundle of His. Congenital heart block primarily develops in fetuses of women with antibodies to the SS-A or SS-B antigens, and up to 50 percent of women with SLE test positive for these antibodies. So in pregnancies with either of these antibodies, fetal cardiac monitoring is performed between 18 and 26 weeks of gestation.

The cardiac lesion is permanent, and in most cases, a pacemaker is required. Maternal hydroxychloroquine therapy is associated with a reduced incidence of fetal heart block, particularly in women who have previously had an affected child.

Neonatal lupus erythematosus is thought to be caused by the transplacental passage of maternal antibodies. It is characterized by skin lesions known as lupus dermatitis in newborns, as well as various hematological and systemic abnormalities. In some cases, congenital heart block may also occur. Thrombocytopenia and hepatic involvement are also seen.

The most common cutaneous finding in neonatal lupus erythematosus is an erythematous, slightly scaly eruption on the face and periorbital skin (raccoon sign/owl eye/eye mask). The eruption can be exacerbated by UV exposure. The rash improves over the first few months of life and usually resolves without scarring by 12 months of age.

Avoidance of sunlight should be advised and low‐potency topical steroids may be of benefit.

The pregnancy outcomes are best in women with:

•  Dormant lupus activity for at least 6 months before conception
•  No lupus nephritis manifestation in the form of proteinuria or renal dysfunction
•  Absent anti-phospholipid syndrome or lupus anticoagulant
•  Superimposed preeclampsia does not develop
questions.learning: SLE On finding a congenital heart block in the fetus, the mother should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Fetal and neonatal heart blocks occur due to myocarditis and fibrosis in the region between the AV node and the bundle of His.

questions.text: After successful delivery of the baby, the obstetrician witnesses that the episiotomy performed has extended backwards beyond the perineal body. Which among the following structures is likely to be injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. External anal sphicter

External anal sphincter is the structure injured in an episiotomy extended posteriorly beyond the perineal body.

Perineal tear have been divided into four degrees:

• First degree- laceration is restricted to the skin of the fourchette
• Second degree- muscles of the perineal body are torn through
• Third degree- the tear extends partially backward through the external sphincter of the anus
• Fourth degree- the external anal sphincter is torn and anal mucosa is also involved

A central tear of the perineum is when the head penetrates first through the posterior vaginal wall, then through the perineal body and appears through the skin of the perineum. It usually occurs in patients with a contracted outlet.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ultrasound of a young woman with infertility is suggestive of a uterine anomaly. Which of the following is used to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hysteroscopy + laparoscopy

Among the given options, hysteroscopy with laparoscopy is used to confirm the diagnosis.

For infertility evaluation, hysteroscopy and laparoscopy can detect müllerian anomalies, screen for co-existent endometriosis, and exclude other tubal or uterine cavity pathology.

This approach can differentiate between a septate and a bicornuate uterus. On laparoscopy, the presence of a uterine fundus indicates that the uterus is septate, while its absence indicates it is bicornuate. The capacity of each horn in a bicornuate uterus and the depth and thickness of the uterine septum prior to surgical resection can also be assessed.

MRI is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of Mullerian anomalies. It clearly delineates both the internal and external uterine anatomy. Complex anomalies and common associations like renal or skeletal anomalies can also be evaluated. It is also less invasive than hysteroscopy and laparoscopy in diagnosing Mullerian anomalies.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) provides information about the interior contour of the uterine cavity but cannot accurately visualize the external contour of the uterus.

Option C: Laparoscopy alone as a diagnostic procedure cannot visualize the interior contour of a hollow viscus like the uterus. This can be done only with the help of hysteroscopy or imaging such as sonography, HSG, or MRI.

Option D: Transvaginal sonography is used for the initial detection of uterine anomalies causing infertility or spontaneous abortions. Complete evaluation of these anomalies is done by MRI.

Note:

• Hysteroscopy is the gold standard investigation to visualize the uterine cavity and tubal ostia. It also has therapeutic benefits in cases of endometrial polyps, submucous resection of myoma, hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, and resection of uterine septum.
• Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation to evaluate tubal factors of infertility.

Shirodkar 2. Purandare 3. Khanna A) Anterior superior iliac spine B) Rectus sheath C) Sacrum via lumbosacral fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-C, 2-B, 3-A

Fertility-preserving sling cervicopexy procedures are differentiated by the structure to which the sling is anchored.

•

Shirodkar sling is anchored posteriorly to the sacrum via the lumbo-sacral fascia.

•

Purandare sling is anchored to the rectus sheath.

•

Khanna sling is anchored laterally to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).

Therefore, the correct matching is 1-C, 2-B, 3-A.

•

Sling cervicopexy is a uterine-preserving procedure used in women desiring future fertility.

•

Posterior anchoring to sacrum provides strong apical support but needs careful dissection to avoid pre sacral bleeding.

•

Anterior anchoring to rectus sheath and lateral anchoring to ASIS are alternative designs with different vectors of support.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Sequentially arrange the steps involved in excitation-contraction coupling of smooth muscle cells. 1. Myosin phosphorylation 2. Increased influx of Ca2+ into the cell 3. Activation of calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase 4. Binding of myosin to actin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2-3-1-4

In smooth muscle excitation–contraction coupling, contraction is regulated by Ca²⁺-dependent phosphorylation of myosin rather than troponin (as in skeletal muscle).

Correct sequence:

1.      Increased influx of Ca²⁺ into the cell (via voltage-gated or receptor-operated channels).

2.      Ca²⁺ binds to calmodulin, activating calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase (MLCK).

3.      MLCK phosphorylates myosin light chains.

4.      Phosphorylated myosin binds to actin, initiating cross-bridge cycling and contraction.
questions.learning: 2-3-1-4 In smooth muscle excitation–contraction coupling, contraction is regulated by Ca²⁺-dependent phosphorylation of myosin rather than troponin (as in skeletal muscle).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with features of chronic pancreatitis with recurrent attacks and has a 10 mm dilatation of the pancreatic duct with intraductal calculi present. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy

In this case of chronic pancreatitis with recurrent attacks, 10 mm dilatation of the pancreatic duct, and intraductal calculi, longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (also known as Puestow procedure or lateral pancreaticojejunostomy) is the surgery of choice. This procedure involves opening the pancreatic duct along its length and connecting it to a loop of the jejunum, which helps to drain the obstructed pancreatic duct and alleviate pain.

Patients with chronic pancreatitis mainly experience pain due to ductal hypertension or parenchymal inflammation. Acute exacerbations in duct pressure lead to recurrent acute attacks. The pancreatic duct dilation observed on pancreatography for chronic pancreatitis is classically described as a chain of lakes, which reflects the presence of multiple dilations and stenoses. Response to treatment has been found to be dependent upon the degree of preoperative pancreatic fibrosis.

Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy, also known as the Puestow procedure or lateral pancreaticojejunostomy, is a surgical treatment primarily used for chronic pancreatitis with a dilated main pancreatic duct and intraductal calculi.

In longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy, a longitudinal incision is made along the length of the main pancreatic duct, typically from the tail to the head of the pancreas. The dilated pancreatic duct is then opened, and any intraductal calculi or obstructions are removed. The opened duct is then connected to a loop of the jejunum to create a side-to-side anastomosis. This allows for the drainage of pancreatic secretions directly into the jejunum, bypassing any narrowed or obstructed areas of the duct.

This procedure can effectively relieve pain and improve the quality of life for patients with chronic pancreatitis. However, it is important to note that it may not reverse the underlying pathology of chronic pancreatitis or prevent the progression of the disease. It is also not suitable for all patients with chronic pancreatitis, particularly those with a non-dilated pancreatic duct or isolated head involvement.

Other Options:

Pancreaticoduodenectomy: This procedure, also known as Whipple procedure, involves removing the head of the pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of the bile duct. It is typically performed for pancreatic cancer or tumors in the head of the pancreas, not for chronic pancreatitis with ductal obstruction and intraductal calculi.

ERCP and sphincterotomy: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy is a procedure that involves opening the sphincter of Oddi to facilitate the drainage of bile and pancreatic secretions. Although it may provide temporary relief, it is not a definitive treatment for chronic pancreatitis with large ductal dilatation and intraductal calculi. ERCP with sphincterotomy may be useful in some cases of chronic pancreatitis for the removal of small pancreatic duct stones, but for large ductal dilatation and intraductal calculi, longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy is more appropriate.

Coring of pancreas head: Coring of the pancreas head, also known as pancreatic head resection or Beger procedure, is a surgical technique used to treat chronic pancreatitis, particularly when the inflammation and fibrosis predominantly affect the head of the pancreas. The procedure involves removing the inflamed and fibrotic tissue from the head of the pancreas while preserving the duodenum, bile duct, and the main pancreatic duct. Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy is a more targeted and effective treatment for this patient's condition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Difference in trajectory between inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is due to:
options: Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration
Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration
Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration
Inspiration is active and expiration is passive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration

The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis.

It exists because a greater transpulmonary pressure is required to open a previously closed airway, due to a deficit of surfactant at the air-water interface, than to keep an open airway from closing, as then it has abundant surfactant.
questions.learning: Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During a planned dilatation and curettage (D&C) procedure, a Sims’ uterine sound is introduced, but no resistance is encountered. Based on this finding, what should be the next appropriate step in management from the given options?
questions.explanation: During a D&C, a sudden loss of resistance while using a uterine sound or curette is a classic sign of uterine perforation. This is a serious surgical complication. The immediate priority is to stop the procedure and assess for injury to internal organs, such as the bowel or bladder. Immediate laparoscopy (Option C) is the gold standard for visualizing the site of perforation and checking for secondary damage or internal bleeding. Continuing the procedure (Option A) or proceeding with the planned evacuation (Option B) is extremely dangerous, as it can worsen the injury or cause a bowel pull-through. Mifepristone and Misoprostol (Option D) are medical management options that have no role in the acute management of a surgical perforation. If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, an emergency laparotomy might be required, but in a controlled setting, laparoscopy is the preferred diagnostic and potentially therapeutic next step to ensure patient safety
questions.learning: During a D&C, a sudden loss of resistance while using a uterine sound or curette is a classic sign of uterine perforation. This is a serious surgical complication.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the clinic with a complaint of the feeling of insects crawling under the skin. Which of the following drug abuse can cause the symptoms of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cocaine

The feeling of insects crawling under the skin, also known as cocaine bugs or formication, is a feature of cocaine abuse.

Other features of acute cocaine intoxication are delusions of persecution, paranoia, and suspiciousness. It is essential to differentiate acute cocaine intoxication from acute schizophrenia which it closely resembles.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding a brain abscess? I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus. II. Presenting features include low grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits. III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice. IV. The aetiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

A brain abscess is a focal intracerebral infection consisting of a collection of pus surrounded by a vascularized capsule. It usually develops due to direct spread from adjacent infections, hematogenous dissemination, or penetrating cranial trauma/neurosurgery.

The following statements are true:

• I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus: Brain abscesses commonly result from:

• Direct extension from otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis
• Penetrating skull fractures or neurosurgery
• Hematogenous spread from distant infections

• II. Presenting features include low-grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits: Common clinical features include:

• Headache (most common symptom)
• Fever (may be absent)
• Altered mental status/confusion
• Focal neurological deficits
• Seizures
• Features of raised intracranial pressure

• IV. The etiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses: Although bacteria are the most common cause, brain abscess-like lesions can also occur due to:

• Fungi (Aspergillus, Candida)
• Protozoa (Toxoplasma gondii, especially in AIDS)
• Rarely viral infections can produce focal necrotizing lesions, though classic brain abscesses are predominantly bacterial.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice: Contrast-enhanced CT scan is usually the initial imaging investigation because it is rapid, widely available, and useful in emergency settings.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with subcutaneous emphysema, absent air entry on the right side, and unstable vital signs. What is the immediate management in this situation?
options: Insertion of wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space
Wide bore needle decompression and IV fluids
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—history of trauma, subcutaneous emphysema, absent air entry on one side, and hemodynamic instability—is highly suggestive of tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency. In this condition, air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space, leading to lung collapse, mediastinal shift, and reduced venous return, which can rapidly cause shock and death if not treated immediately. The first and most crucial step in management is emergency needle decompression using a wide bore needle. The currently preferred site is the 5th intercostal space in the anterior or mid-axillary line, as it is safer and more accessible in trauma patients. This procedure rapidly relieves intrathoracic pressure and stabilizes the patient. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Needle decompression with IV fluids: Fluids are supportive but do not address the primary problem immediately. (C) Intubation and PPV: May worsen tension pneumothorax if done before decompression. (D) e-FAST: Diagnostic tool; treatment should not be delayed in unstable patients

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: After undergoing a vasectomy, for how long is a patient advised to continue using alternative contraceptive methods??
questions.explanation: Sterility is not achieved immediately after a vasectomy because viable sperm remain in the distal portion of the vas deferens. Patients are advised to use alternative contraception for approximately 3 months or until they have had at least 20 ejaculations. Confirmation of sterility is mandatory through semen analysis, which must show azoospermia in two consecutive samples. Option A (1 month) and Option B (2 months) are insufficient timeframes, as studies show that while 80% of men are sterile by 6 weeks, nearly 10% still have sperm present at 10 weeks. Option D (6 months) is longer than the standard clinical recommendation for initial follow-up. Failure to adhere to this waiting period is a common cause of "failed" vasectomy and unintended pregnancy. Therefore, the 3-month guideline provides a safe buffer for the physiological clearance of stored sperm

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tooth is the first to erupt in the primary dentition?
questions.explanation: In the normal chronological sequence of dental development, the mandibular (lower) central incisors are the first teeth to erupt into the oral cavity. This typically occurs between the ages of 6 and 10 months. They are followed shortly by the maxillary (upper) central incisors (Option A) at approximately 8 to 12 months. The lateral incisors usually erupt next, followed by the first primary molars. The canines (Options C and D) erupt much later, generally between 16 and 22 months of age. The primary (deciduous) dentition consists of 20 teeth in total. Monitoring the eruption sequence is a key part of pediatric health surveillance, as significant delays or deviations from the normal pattern can indicate systemic conditions, nutritional deficiencies, or localized dental obstructions. Parents often seek guidance during this "teething" phase, which is marked by increased salivation and irritability. Therefore, the lower central incisor marks the functional beginning of the primary dentition

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a famous large prospective study that helped establish risk factors for coronary heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Framingham study

The Framingham Heart Study (FHS) is the landmark prospective cohort study that identified the major modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD) and laid the foundation for modern cardiovascular prevention.

• A. Adelaide study ✗

• Not a landmark study for CHD risk factors.

• B. Birmingham study ✗

• Not associated with establishing CHD risk factors.

• C. Framingham study ✓

• Began in 1948 in Framingham, Massachusetts, USA.
• Followed thousands of participants over decades to identify risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

• D. Pittsburg study ✗

• Not the classic prospective study for CHD risk factors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A diabetic patient came with the complaint of pedal edema due to congestive heart failure and was prescribed a medication that is preferred in the setting of cardiac and renal failure. What is the drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SGLT-2 inhibitor

In this case, a diabetic patient with cardiac and renal failure is started on a suitable medication. The drug is likely an sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor.

SGLT-2 inhibitors include canafliflozen, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. They act by inhibiting the SGLT-2 transporter which is present on the proximal segment of the renal tubule. It is responsible for the reabsorption of 80-90% of filtered glucose. It inhibits glucose reabsorption resulting in glycosuria and a change in the renal threshold.

SGLT2 inhibitors can lower blood pressure and cause a slight decrease in body weight. Drugs like empagliflozin and canagliflozin are found to reduce major cardiovascular events. SGLT2 inhibitors also exhibit a known nephro-protective effect.

The common side effects include urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections due to the high glucose content of the urine. There is a risk of the development of diabetic ketoacidosis. It increases the risk of fractures and lower limb amputations due to the creation of an imbalance with the minerals and circulating parathormone and vitamin D.

Other options :

Option A:  Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. It reduces the intestinal absorption of glucose by inhibiting the intestinal brush border enzyme, alpha-glucosidase. These drugs also increase GLP-1 levels in circulation. They reduce post-prandial glucose levels.

Option C: Linagliptin is a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor. It is used in type 2 diabetes as monotherapy or in combination therapy when metformin is not tolerated or contraindicated. It binds extensively to plasma proteins and is cleared primarily by the hepatobiliary system. Hence, no dosage adjustment is needed in renal failure. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors enhance the release of insulin postprandially, decrease glucagon, and thereby lower mealtime as well as fasting glucose. They are weight-neutral.

Option D: Liraglutide is also a GLP-1 receptor agonist and is given only in the subcutaneous injectable form. It was recently approved for the treatment of obesity.
